This paper describes an experimental analog VLSI chip for smooth surface interpolation from sparse depth data. An eight-node ID network was designed in 3J.lm CMOS and successfully tested. The network minimizes a second-order or "thin(cid:173) plate" energy of the surface. The circuit directly implements the cou(cid:173) pled depth/slope model of surface reconstruction (Harris, 1987). paragraphs: This paper addresses how to reconstruct a smooth surface when depth measurements are available only at scattered locations. The proposed solution is an experimental analog VLSI chip that performs interpolation. Its circuit represents a surface-reconstruction model in which depth and slope are coupled to determine the resulting shape.

The network minimizes a second-order energy, described as a thin-plate energy. This gives smoothness a specific role in filling the gaps between observations: the reconstructed surface is selected through the model’s energy objective. Implementing that objective in an analog circuit connects the mathematical formulation directly to a physical computing device.

The researchers designed and successfully tested an eight-node, one-dimensional network using 3-micrometer CMOS technology. That establishes a hardware demonstration at the stated scale. The chip can also produce Gaussian-like image smoothing, linking its interpolation behavior to another visual processing operation. The contribution is a tested circuit realization of the coupled depth-and-slope model, with both sparse-depth interpolation and smoothing as stated capabilities.
summary.tldr: A tested eight-node analog chip reconstructs smooth depth profiles by minimizing thin-plate energy and can also provide image smoothing.

title: An Analog VLSI Chip for Thin-Plate Surface Interpolation

paragraphs: This paper examines two commonly repeated claims about neural networks: that they remain effective after component damage, and that dense connectivity is necessary for efficient use of resources. The authors turn these broad intuitions into questions for formal analysis. Their organizing device is a hypothetical agent that removes connections, progressively making the network sparse.

Connection removal provides a way to investigate how computational ability depends on the network's wiring. The two claims concern different aspects of that dependence. Robustness asks whether computation survives damage, while resource efficiency asks whether extensive interconnection is necessary to make good use of the available neural elements.

The supplied text explicitly rejects an unrestricted robustness claim. A network that depends on a critical, highly specialized cell can lose its computational ability when that cell is damaged. This example shows why the arrangement of a computation matters alongside its overall connectivity. The paper's stated contribution is to formally examine these assumptions about sparsity, damage, and resource use, rather than treating robustness as an automatic property of neural computation.
summary.tldr: The paper formally examines whether neural networks tolerate connection loss and whether efficient computation requires dense connectivity.

title: The Devil and the Network: What Sparsity Implies to Robustness and Memory

abstract: Despite the fact that complex visual scenes contain multiple, overlapping objects, people perform object recognition with ease and accuracy. One operation that facilitates recognition is an early segmentation process in which features of objects are grouped and labeled according to which ob(cid:173) ject they belong. Current computational systems that perform this oper(cid:173) ation are based on predefined grouping heuristics. We describe a system called MAGIC that learn. how to group features based on a set of pre(cid:173) segmented examples. In many cases, MAGIC discovers grouping heuristics similar to those previously proposed, but it also has the capability of find(cid:173) ing nonintuitive structural regularities in images. Grouping is performed by a relaxation network that aUempts to dynamically bind related fea(cid:173) tures. Features transmit a complex-valued signal (amplitude and phase) to one another; binding can thus be represented by phase locking related features. MAGIC'S training procedure is a generalization of recurrent back propagation to complex-valued units. When a visual image contains multiple, overlapping objects, recognition is difficult because features in the image are not grouped according to which object they belong. Without the capability to form such groupings, it would be necessary to undergo a massive search through all subsets of image features. For this reason, most machine vision recognition systems include a component that performs feature grouping or image .egmentation (e.g., Guzman, 1968; Lowe, 1985; Marr, 1982).

paragraphs: MAGIC learns how to group image features according to the objects they belong to. This matters when several objects overlap, because recognition requires deciding which features go together. The system learns from examples whose segmentation is already provided, allowing the grouping rules themselves to be acquired through training.

Grouping takes place in a relaxation network whose features exchange complex-valued signals. Each signal has an amplitude and a phase, and related features become bound together by locking their phases. This supplies a changing representation of group membership within the network. Training extends recurrent backpropagation to units that operate with these complex-valued signals.

The paper reports that MAGIC often discovers grouping rules resembling previously proposed heuristics, while also being capable of finding less intuitive structural regularities. That result connects familiar image-grouping principles with a mechanism that can learn additional ones from examples. The approach makes segmentation a learned interaction among features, addressing the feature-assignment problem that otherwise complicates recognition in scenes with multiple objects.
summary.tldr: MAGIC learns image segmentation by synchronizing the phases of related features in a complex-valued recurrent network.

abstract: This paper presents a formulation for unsupervised learning of clus(cid:173) ters reflecting multiple causal structure in binary data. Unlike the standard mixture model, a multiple cause model accounts for ob(cid:173) served data by combining assertions from many hidden causes, each of which can pertain to varying degree to any subset of the observ(cid:173) able dimensions. A crucial issue is the mixing-function for combin(cid:173) ing beliefs from different cluster-centers in order to generate data reconstructions whose errors are minimized both during recognition and learning. We demonstrate a weakness inherent to the popular weighted sum followed by sigmoid squashing, and offer an alterna(cid:173) tive form of the nonlinearity. Results are presented demonstrating the algorithm's ability successfully to discover coherent multiple causal representat.ions of noisy test data and in images of printed characters.

paragraphs: A binary observation may reflect several hidden factors at once, whereas a standard mixture model assigns it to one component. This paper develops an unsupervised model in which multiple hidden causes jointly explain different subsets of observed dimensions. The key challenge is how their contributions should combine.

The authors examine the mixing function that turns beliefs about several cluster centers into a reconstruction. They identify a weakness in the common weighted-sum-plus-sigmoid construction and propose a different nonlinearity. Reconstruction errors guide both recognition of active causes and learning of the representations themselves.

Experiments recover coherent multiple-cause structure from noisy test data and printed-character images. The contribution is a representation that can compose latent explanations instead of forcing each example into a single exclusive cluster. Here hidden causes are components of a generative model; the empirical recovery does not automatically establish real-world causal identification from observational data.
summary.tldr: A revised nonlinear mixing rule lets an unsupervised binary-data model discover compositional hidden factors rather than exclusive clusters.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Mixtures of Multiple Causes in Binary Data

abstract: To compress text files, a neural predictor network P is used to ap(cid:173) proximate the conditional probability distribution of possible "next characters", given n previous characters. P's outputs are fed into standard coding algorithms that generate short codes for characters with high predicted probability and long codes for highly unpre(cid:173) dictable characters. Tested on short German newspaper articles, our method outperforms widely used Lempel-Ziv algorithms (used in UNIX functions such as "compress" and "gzip").

P's outputs are fed into standard coding algorithms that generate short codes for characters with high predicted probability and long codes for highly unpre(cid:173) dictable characters. Tested on short German newspaper articles, our method outperforms widely used Lempel-Ziv algorithms (used in UNIX functions such as "compress" and "gzip").

paragraphs: The paper uses neural prediction to compress text. A network observes a fixed number of preceding characters and estimates the probability of each possible next character. Its task is therefore to produce a distribution over what could follow, rather than simply choosing one character as the most likely continuation.

Those probabilities are passed to standard coding algorithms. Characters assigned high probability receive shorter codes, while surprising characters receive longer ones. This connects the quality of the learned language prediction to the amount of space needed for encoding: the predictor supplies expectations, and the coding procedure converts them into variable-length representations.

On short German newspaper articles, the method outperforms widely used Lempel-Ziv approaches associated with compress and gzip. That is the stated experimental setting for the comparison. The contribution shows that a neural estimate of character-level context can be useful as part of a practical compression pipeline, with the network handling probability estimation and an established coder handling the representation of those predictions.
summary.tldr: A neural next-character predictor drives text coding and outperforms common Lempel-Ziv methods on short German newspaper articles.

title: Predictive Coding with Neural Nets: Application to Text Compression

paragraphs: The paper describes implementing a neural network with the URAN custom chip, which combines analog and digital circuitry. The central practical issue is whether a trainable network can operate under the limited computational accuracy of the hardware. The authors report successful training of a multilayer perceptron despite that constraint.

The implementation is tested on recognition of spoken Korean words using a network with a large frame input layer. Recognition is carried out through forward retrieval, applying the network to the supplied input. This gives the hardware work a concrete application: the chip supports the computations of a network used to identify spoken words.

The paper also proposes a module containing eight or more chips to increase performance and capacity. That extension is presented as a suggested hardware arrangement, separate from the reported training and recognition work. Together, these elements connect device-level implementation to a usable neural system: learning remains possible with restricted arithmetic accuracy, and multiple chips offer a proposed route to accommodating a larger system.
summary.tldr: A mixed analog-digital URAN chip supports limited-accuracy neural learning and is tested on spoken Korean word recognition.

title: Implementation of Neural Hardware with the Neural VLSI of URAN in Applications with Reduced Representations

abstract: We present results on the use of neural network based autoassociators which act as novelty or anomaly detectors to detect imminent motor failures. The autoassociator is trained to reconstruct spectra obtained from the healthy motor. In laboratory tests, we have demonstrated that the trained autoassociator has a small reconstruction error on measurements recorded from healthy motors but a larger error on those recorded from a motor with a fault. We have designed and built a motor monitoring system using an autoassociator for anomaly detection and are in the process of testing the system at three industrial and commercial sites.

In laboratory tests, we have demonstrated that the trained autoassociator has a small reconstruction error on measurements recorded from healthy motors but a larger error on those recorded from a motor with a fault. paragraphs: This paper approaches motor-failure detection by teaching a neural network what healthy operation looks like. The network is an autoassociator: it learns to reproduce its input. Its training examples are spectra measured from a healthy motor, so successful reconstruction captures regularities in those measurements.

Once trained, the network compares a new spectrum with its reconstruction. The difference provides an anomaly signal. A spectrum resembling healthy examples should be reconstructed well, whereas an unfamiliar pattern associated with a fault can produce a larger error. This makes reconstruction error useful for identifying departures from normal operation.

Laboratory tests show the intended separation: healthy-motor measurements produce small errors, while measurements from a faulty motor produce larger ones. The authors also built a monitoring system around this approach and were testing it at three industrial and commercial sites. The laboratory findings support anomaly detection as a basis for failure monitoring; the deployment work described in the abstract was still undergoing testing.
summary.tldr: A network trained to reconstruct healthy motor spectra detects faults through increased reconstruction error.

title: A Neural Network Autoassociator for Induction Motor Failure Prediction

abstract: The hierarchical representation of data has various applications in do(cid:173) mains such as data mining, machine vision, or information retrieval. In this paper we introduce an extension of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm that learns mixture hierarchies in a computationally ef(cid:173) ficient manner. Efficiency is achieved by progressing in a bottom-up fashion, i.e. by clustering the mixture components of a given level in the hierarchy to obtain those of the level above. This cl ustering requires onl y knowledge of the mixture parameters, there being no need to resort to intermediate samples. In addition to practical applications, the algorithm allows a new interpretation of EM that makes clear the relationship with non-parametric kernel-based estimation methods, provides explicit con(cid:173) trol over the trade-off between the bias and variance of EM estimates, and offers new insights about the behavior of deterministic annealing methods commonly used with EM to escape local minima of the likelihood.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an extension of expectation-maximization for learning hierarchies of mixture models. Such hierarchies organize data at multiple levels, with applications including data mining, machine vision, and information retrieval. The method builds upward from an existing level by clustering its mixture components to produce the components at the level above.

The efficiency comes from operating directly on mixture parameters. Constructing the next level does not require intermediate samples, so the information already contained in the fitted components drives the clustering. This gives the bottom-up procedure a specific computational advantage and makes the hierarchy an organization of model components as well as a representation of data.

The authors also use the method to reinterpret EM. Their analysis clarifies its relationship to non-parametric kernel-based estimation and provides explicit control over the bias–variance trade-off in EM estimates. It further offers insight into deterministic annealing methods used with EM to escape local likelihood minima. These connections make the contribution both an efficient hierarchical learning procedure and a framework for understanding related estimation and optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: An EM extension efficiently builds mixture hierarchies by clustering component parameters and clarifies connections to kernel estimation and annealing.

title: Learning Mixture Hierarchies

abstract: Psychophysical and physiological evidence shows that sound local(cid:173) ization of acoustic signals is strongly influenced by their synchrony with visual signals. This effect, known as ventriloquism, is at work when sound coming from the side of a TV set feels as if it were coming from the mouth of the actors. The ventriloquism effect suggests that there is important information about sound location encoded in the synchrony between the audio and video signals. In spite of this evidence, audiovisual synchrony is rarely used as a source of information in computer vision tasks. In this paper we explore the use of audio visual synchrony to locate sound sources. We developed a system that searches for regions of the visual land(cid:173) scape that correlate highly with the acoustic signals and tags them as likely to contain an acoustic source. We discuss our experience implementing the system, present results on a speaker localization task and discuss potential applications of the approach.

paragraphs: The paper explores how matching timing across sound and vision can help a computer locate a sound source. Its motivation comes from the ventriloquism effect: synchronized visual events can influence where people perceive a sound to originate. An actor's visible mouth movements, for example, can make television audio seem to come from the actor.

The authors develop a system that searches a visual scene for regions whose activity correlates strongly with the acoustic signal. Those regions are marked as likely locations of a sound source. The underlying idea is that a visible event and a sound occurring together provide evidence of a shared source, making audiovisual timing useful for localization.

The paper discusses implementation experience and presents results on locating a speaker. It also considers possible applications of the approach. The contribution is a concrete way to use synchronization as a localization cue: the system produces candidate source regions from relationships between the two signals, preserving the distinction between a likely source and a conclusively identified one.
summary.tldr: A system locates likely sound sources by finding visual regions whose activity synchronizes with the audio.

title: Audio Vision: Using Audio-Visual Synchrony to Locate Sounds

abstract: We present techniques for rendering and animation of realistic scenes by analyzing and training on short video sequences. This work extends the new paradigm for computer animation, video tex(cid:173) tures, which uses recorded video to generate novel animations by replaying the video samples in a new order. Here we concentrate on video sprites, which are a special type of video texture. In video sprites, instead of storing whole images, the object of inter(cid:173) est is separated from the background and the video samples are stored as a sequence of alpha-matted sprites with associated veloc(cid:173) ity information. They can be rendered anywhere on the screen to create a novel animation of the object. We present methods to cre(cid:173) ate such animations by finding a sequence of sprite samples that is both visually smooth and follows a desired path. To estimate visual smoothness, we train a linear classifier to estimate visual similarity between video samples. If the motion path is known in advance, we use beam search to find a good sample sequence. We can specify the motion interactively by precomputing the sequence cost function using Q-Iearning.

paragraphs: This paper creates new animations from short recorded videos by selecting and rearranging samples. It focuses on video sprites: images of an object separated from its background, stored with transparency information and associated velocity. Because the object is isolated, these samples can be placed at different screen locations to generate new motion.

The central problem is choosing a sample sequence that follows a desired path while remaining visually smooth. The authors train a linear classifier to estimate visual similarity between samples. This learned comparison helps evaluate transitions, connecting the appearance of successive images to the choice of which recorded sample should come next.

The sequencing method depends on how motion is specified. When the path is available in advance, beam search finds a good sequence. For interactive motion control, Q-learning precomputes a sequence cost function. Together, these techniques connect recorded object appearance, desired movement, and transition quality, allowing the same source material to support animations whose sample order and screen path differ from the original video.
summary.tldr: Learned visual similarity, beam search, and Q-learning help rearrange video sprites into smooth animations that follow specified or interactive paths.

title: Machine Learning for Video-Based Rendering

abstract: We address the question of feature selection in the context of visual recognition. It is shown that, besides efﬁcient from a computational standpoint, the infomax principle is nearly optimal in the minimum Bayes error sense. The concept of marginal diversity is introduced, lead- ing to a generic principle for feature selection (the principle of maximum marginal diversity) of extreme computational simplicity. The relation- ships between infomax and the maximization of marginal diversity are identiﬁed, uncovering the existence of a family of classiﬁcation proce- dures for which near optimal (in the Bayes error sense) feature selection does not require combinatorial search. Examination of this family in light of recent studies on the statistics of natural images suggests that visual recognition problems are a subset of it.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to select useful features for visual recognition without an expensive search through combinations. Its starting point is the infomax principle, which favors retaining informative features. The authors show that this principle is computationally efficient and nearly optimal when judged by minimum Bayes error.

They introduce marginal diversity and use it to define a particularly simple feature-selection principle. By establishing relationships between marginal diversity and infomax, they identify a family of classification procedures for which nearly optimal feature selection does not require combinatorial search. The result ties a simple selection criterion to a decision-theoretic measure of quality.

The connection to visual recognition is qualified. Examining the identified family alongside studies of natural-image statistics suggests that visual recognition problems belong to it. Thus, the paper provides a theoretical route to inexpensive feature selection and an argument for its relevance to images. The near-optimality claim belongs to the identified framework, while the inclusion of visual recognition is presented as a suggestion supported by image statistics.
summary.tldr: Maximum marginal diversity connects simple feature selection to near-optimal Bayes error within an identified family of classification procedures.

title: Feature Selection by Maximum Marginal Diversity

abstract: In the multi-armed bandit problem, an online algorithm must choose from a set of strategies in a sequence of n trials so as to minimize the total cost of the chosen strategies. While nearly tight upper and lower bounds are known in the case when the strategy set is finite, much less is known when there is an infinite strategy set. Here we consider the case when the set of strategies is a subset of Rd , and the cost functions are continuous. In the d = 1 case, we improve on the best-known upper and lower bounds, closing the gap to a sublogarithmic factor. We also consider the case where d > 1 and the cost functions are convex, adapting a recent online convex optimization algorithm of Zinkevich to the sparser feedback model of the multi-armed bandit problem.

paragraphs: The paper investigates sequential decision-making when the available strategies form an infinite set. On each trial, an algorithm chooses a strategy and seeks to keep its accumulated cost low using bandit feedback. The strategies lie in a subset of a real coordinate space, and their cost functions are assumed to be continuous.

For a one-dimensional strategy space, the authors improve both upper and lower bounds. The remaining gap is reduced to a sublogarithmic factor, bringing the achievable guarantees and the established difficulty of the problem close together. This sharpens the theoretical picture for a setting where finite-strategy bandit results do not directly settle the problem.

The paper also considers higher-dimensional spaces under the additional assumption that the cost functions are convex. It adapts an online convex optimization algorithm to the more limited feedback available in a bandit problem. These contributions address both the precision of performance bounds in one dimension and the challenge of using convex optimization methods when feedback reveals less information.
summary.tldr: The paper nearly closes the bound gap for one-dimensional continuum bandits and adapts convex optimization to higher-dimensional bandit feedback.

title: Nearly Tight Bounds for the Continuum-Armed Bandit Problem

abstract: We present a probabilistic approach to language change in which word forms are represented by phoneme sequences that undergo stochastic edits along the branches of a phylogenetic tree. Our framework combines the advantages of the classical comparative method with the robustness of corpus-based probabilistic models. We use this framework to explore the consequences of two different schemes for defining probabilistic models of phonological change, evaluating these schemes using the reconstruction of ancient word forms in Romance languages. The result is an efficient inference procedure for automatically inferring ancient word forms from modern languages, which can be generalized to support inferences about linguistic phylogenies.

paragraphs: This paper treats the historical development of words as a probabilistic process. A word is represented as a sequence of phonemes, or speech sounds. Those sequences undergo random edits as they pass along the branches of a language family tree. Modern word forms can then provide evidence about the forms that preceded them.

The framework combines the comparative method's attention to relationships among languages with probabilistic modeling based on corpora. The authors investigate two ways of defining a probability model for sound change. They evaluate the consequences of those choices through the reconstruction of ancient word forms associated with Romance languages, connecting the modeling question to a concrete historical inference task.

The resulting procedure efficiently infers ancient forms from modern languages. Its contribution is a computational account that connects sound changes, language ancestry, and uncertainty within one framework. The authors also state that the procedure can be generalized to infer linguistic family trees, extending its possible role beyond reconstructing word forms along an existing tree.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model of sound changes along language family trees enables efficient reconstruction of ancient words from modern languages.

title: A Probabilistic Approach to Language Change

abstract: Sound localization by barn owls is commonly modeled as a matching procedure where localization cues derived from auditory inputs are compared to stored templates. While the matching models can explain properties of neural responses, no model explains how the owl resolves spatial ambiguity in the localization cues to produce accurate localization near the center of gaze. Here, we examine two models for the barn owl's sound localization behavior. First, we consider a maximum likelihood estimator in order to further evaluate the cue matching model. Second, we consider a maximum a posteriori estimator to test if a Bayesian model with a prior that emphasizes directions near the center of gaze can reproduce the owl's localization behavior. We show that the maximum likelihood estimator can not reproduce the owl's behavior, while the maximum a posteriori estimator is able to match the behavior. This result suggests that the standard cue matching model will not be sufficient to explain sound localization behavior in the barn owl. The Bayesian model provides a new framework for analyzing sound localization in the barn owl and leads to predictions about the owl's localization behavior.

These matching models can explain aspects of neural responses, but spatial ambiguity poses a behavioral problem: the same cues can leave uncertainty about direction. The paper asks how owls nevertheless localize accurately near the center of gaze.

The authors compare two estimators. Maximum likelihood provides a way to examine localization based on cue matching. Maximum a posteriori estimation adds a prior that favors directions near the center of gaze. This comparison tests whether including that directional preference helps account for behavior that the cue information alone does not explain.

title: Optimal models of sound localization by barn owls

abstract: This paper examines the generalization properties of online convex programming algorithms when the loss function is Lipschitz and strongly convex. Our main result is a sharp bound, that holds with high probability, on the excess risk of the output of an online algorithm in terms of the average regret. This allows one to use recent algorithms with logarithmic cumulative regret guarantees to achieve fast convergence rates for the excess risk with high probability. The bound also solves an open problem regarding the convergence rate of {\pegasos}, a recently proposed method for solving the SVM optimization problem.

paragraphs: Online optimization evaluates an algorithm through regret, which compares its accumulated losses with a reference choice. Statistical learning instead asks how well the resulting predictor generalizes. This paper connects these perspectives for online convex programming when the loss is both Lipschitz and strongly convex, making those properties explicit conditions of the analysis.

The main result is a sharp, high-probability upper bound on the output predictor's excess risk in terms of the algorithm's average regret. Excess risk measures how far predictive risk lies above the relevant optimum. The bound translates performance during online learning into a statement about the quality of the predictor it produces.

This connection allows algorithms with logarithmic cumulative regret guarantees to obtain fast excess-risk convergence rates with high probability. The same result resolves an open question about the convergence rate of Pegasos, an SVM optimization method. Its significance is a theoretical route from online regret guarantees to statistical learning guarantees under the stated loss assumptions.
summary.tldr: A high-probability bound converts online regret guarantees into fast excess-risk convergence for Lipschitz, strongly convex losses.

title: On the Generalization Ability of Online Strongly Convex Programming Algorithms

abstract: We propose Dirichlet-Bernoulli Alignment (DBA), a generative model for corpora in which each pattern (e.g., a document) contains a set of instances (e.g., paragraphs in the document) and belongs to multiple classes. By casting predefined classes as latent Dirichlet variables (i.e., instance level labels), and modeling the multi-label of each pattern as Bernoulli variables conditioned on the weighted empirical average of topic assignments, DBA automatically aligns the latent topics discovered from data to human-defined classes. DBA is useful for both pattern classification and instance disambiguation, which are tested on text classification and named entity disambiguation for web search queries respectively.

paragraphs: The paper addresses data with two linked levels of structure: each example contains multiple instances, and the example can belong to several classes. A document containing paragraphs illustrates the first relationship. The modeling challenge is to connect assignments inside the example with the multiple labels attached to the example as a whole.

Dirichlet-Bernoulli Alignment is a generative model that makes this connection explicit. It represents predefined classes through latent Dirichlet variables at the instance level. It then models the example's labels with Bernoulli variables conditioned on a weighted empirical average of topic assignments. This links the topics inferred from data to the human-defined class system.

That alignment allows the model to support both classification of complete examples and disambiguation of their constituent instances. The authors test these uses through text classification and named-entity disambiguation in web search queries, respectively. The contribution is a shared probabilistic account of the two levels, so information about whole-example labels and instance-level assignments participates in one model rather than being treated as unrelated outputs.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet-Bernoulli Alignment connects instance-level latent topics with multiple human-defined labels for each complete example.

title: Dirichlet-Bernoulli Alignment: A Generative Model for Multi-Class Multi-Label Multi-Instance Corpora

abstract: We tackle the fundamental problem of Bayesian active learning with noise, where we need to adaptively select from a number of expensive tests in order to identify an unknown hypothesis sampled from a known prior distribution. In the case of noise-free observations, a greedy algorithm called generalized binary search (GBS) is known to perform near-optimally. We show that if the observations are noisy, perhaps surprisingly, GBS can perform very poorly. We develop EC2, a novel, greedy active learning algorithm and prove that it is competitive with the optimal policy, thus obtaining the first competitiveness guarantees for Bayesian active learning with noisy observations. Our bounds rely on a recently discovered diminishing returns property called adaptive submodularity, generalizing the classical notion of submodular set functions to adaptive policies. Our results hold even if the tests have non–uniform cost and their noise is correlated. We also propose EffECXtive, a particularly fast approximation of EC2, and evaluate it on a Bayesian experimental design problem involving human subjects, intended to tease apart competing economic theories of how people make decisions under uncertainty.

paragraphs: The paper considers how to choose costly tests sequentially to identify an unknown hypothesis drawn from a known prior distribution. Each test can influence which test should come next, but observations may be noisy. The authors show that generalized binary search, a greedy method with near-optimal behavior without noise, can perform very poorly when noise is introduced.

They develop EC2, a new greedy active-learning algorithm, and prove bounds comparing its performance with that of the optimal policy. The analysis uses adaptive submodularity, a diminishing-returns property for decisions made as observations arrive. The guarantees accommodate tests with unequal costs and correlated noise, so they do not require every test to have the same price or independent errors.

The paper also proposes EffECXtive, a particularly fast approximation of EC2. It evaluates this approximation in experimental design with human subjects, selecting information intended to distinguish economic theories of decision-making under uncertainty. The theoretical contribution concerns EC2's competitiveness, while the experimental component explores a faster approximation in a concrete test-selection problem.
summary.tldr: EC2 provides competitiveness guarantees for Bayesian test selection with noisy observations, unequal test costs, and correlated noise.

title: Near-Optimal Bayesian Active Learning with Noisy Observations

abstract: Recent work in reinforcement learning has emphasized the power of L1 regularization to perform feature selection and prevent overfitting. We propose formulating the L1 regularized linear fixed point problem as a linear complementarity problem (LCP). This formulation offers several advantages over the LARS-inspired formulation, LARS-TD. The LCP formulation allows the use of efficient off-the-shelf solvers, leads to a new uniqueness result, and can be initialized with starting points from similar problems (warm starts). We demonstrate that warm starts, as well as the efficiency of LCP solvers, can speed up policy iteration. Moreover, warm starts permit a form of modified policy iteration that can be used to approximate a greedy" homotopy path, a generalization of the LARS-TD homotopy path that combines policy evaluation and optimization."

paragraphs: The paper addresses reinforcement learning methods that use L1 regularization to select features and reduce overfitting. Its main contribution is to express the regularized linear fixed-point problem as a linear complementarity problem. This reformulation changes how the problem can be solved and analyzed.

Compared with the LARS-TD formulation, the new approach permits efficient existing solvers, supports a new uniqueness result, and allows warm starts. That capability matters for policy iteration because successive evaluation and improvement steps create related problems whose solutions can inform later computation.

They also use warm starts to enable a form of modified policy iteration that approximates a greedy homotopy path. This generalizes the path considered by LARS-TD by bringing policy evaluation and policy optimization into the same construction, extending the role of the regularized solution path.
summary.tldr: A linear complementarity formulation enables efficient solvers and warm starts for L1-regularized policy evaluation and improvement.

title: Linear Complementarity for Regularized Policy Evaluation and Improvement

abstract: In order to study the properties of total visual input in humans, a single subject wore a camera for two weeks capturing, on average, an image every 20 seconds (www.research.microsoft.com/~jojic/aihs). The resulting new dataset contains a mix of indoor and outdoor scenes as well as numerous foreground objects. Our first analysis goal is to create a visual summary of the subject’s two weeks of life using unsupervised algorithms that would automatically discover recurrent scenes, familiar faces or common actions. Direct application of existing algorithms, such as panoramic stitching (e.g. Photosynth) or appearance-based clustering models (e.g. the epitome), is impractical due to either the large dataset size or the dramatic variation in the lighting conditions. As a remedy to these problems, we introduce a novel image representation, the “stel epitome,” and an associated efficient learning algorithm. In our model, each image or image patch is characterized by a hidden mapping T, which, as in previous epitome models, defines a mapping between the image-coordinates and the coordinates in the large all-I-have-seen" epitome matrix. The limited epitome real-estate forces the mappings of different images to overlap, with this overlap indicating image similarity. However, in our model the image similarity does not depend on direct pixel-to-pixel intensity/color/feature comparisons as in previous epitome models, but on spatial configuration of scene or object parts, as the model is based on the palette-invariant stel models. As a result, stel epitomes capture structure that is invariant to non-structural changes, such as illumination, that tend to uniformly affect pixels belonging to a single scene or object part."

paragraphs: A subject wore a camera for two weeks, producing an image roughly every twenty seconds. The paper seeks an unsupervised summary of this visual record, with the goal of discovering recurring scenes, familiar faces, or common actions. Dataset size and substantial lighting variation make direct use of existing stitching and appearance-clustering approaches impractical.

The proposed representation, called a stel epitome, maps images or patches into a shared epitome matrix. Its limited space forces mappings from different images to overlap, with overlap expressing similarity. The crucial change is how similarity is represented: it depends on the spatial arrangement of scene or object parts rather than direct comparisons of pixel intensities, colors, or features.

The model is based on palette-invariant representations and comes with an efficient learning algorithm. It captures structure despite non-structural changes, such as illumination changes that tend to affect pixels within a part uniformly. This makes structural recurrence the basis of the visual summary, addressing a major difficulty in recognizing related content across a long and visually variable record.
summary.tldr: A structural epitome summarizes recurring visual structure while accommodating appearance changes such as illumination.

title: Structural epitome: a way to summarize one’s visual experience

abstract: Bayesian filtering of stochastic stimuli has received a great deal of attention re- cently. It has been applied to describe the way in which biological systems dy- namically represent and make decisions about the environment. There have been no exact results for the error in the biologically plausible setting of inference on point process, however. We present an exact analysis of the evolution of the mean- squared error in a state estimation task using Gaussian-tuned point processes as sensors. This allows us to study the dynamics of the error of an optimal Bayesian decoder, providing insights into the limits obtainable in this task. This is done for Markovian and a class of non-Markovian Gaussian processes. We find that there is an optimal tuning width for which the error is minimized. This leads to a char- acterization of the optimal encoding for the setting as a function of the statistics of the stimulus, providing a mathematically sound primer for an ecological theory of sensory processing.

paragraphs: Estimating a changing stimulus from a sequence of discrete events is relevant to understanding how biological systems represent their surroundings. This paper examines that problem using point-process sensors with Gaussian tuning. Its focus is the estimation error of an optimal Bayesian decoder and how that error develops over time.

The authors derive an exact analysis of mean-squared error for this setting. Their treatment includes Markovian Gaussian processes and a class of non-Markovian Gaussian processes. The latter extends the analysis beyond the Markovian case without claiming coverage of every possible process. Tracking error analytically provides a way to examine the achievable limits of the specified state-estimation task.

A central finding is that some tuning width minimizes the error. Thus, the width of the sensors' response functions is a meaningful design variable, with the optimal encoding depending on the stimulus statistics. The result gives a mathematical basis for relating sensory encoding to properties of the environment being sensed.
summary.tldr: An exact filtering-error analysis identifies stimulus-dependent optimal sensor tuning for specified classes of Gaussian processes.

title: Analytical Results for the Error in Filtering of Gaussian Processes

abstract: The L_1 regularized Gaussian maximum likelihood estimator has been shown to have strong statistical guarantees in recovering a sparse inverse covariance matrix, or alternatively the underlying graph structure of a Gaussian Markov Random Field, from very limited samples. We propose a novel algorithm for solving the resulting optimization problem which is a regularized log-determinant program. In contrast to other state-of-the-art methods that largely use first order gradient information, our algorithm is based on Newton's method and employs a quadratic approximation, but with some modifications that leverage the structure of the sparse Gaussian MLE problem. We show that our method is superlinearly convergent, and also present experimental results using synthetic and real application data that demonstrate the considerable improvements in performance of our method when compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: A sparse inverse covariance matrix represents a pattern of relationships in a Gaussian model and can describe the graph of a Gaussian Markov random field. L1-regularized maximum likelihood already has strong statistical guarantees for recovering this structure from limited samples. This paper focuses on making the associated optimization problem easier to solve computationally.

The optimization is a regularized log-determinant program. The authors introduce a Newton-based algorithm that uses a quadratic approximation, incorporating more local information about the objective than a first-order gradient method. They modify the procedure to exploit the particular structure of sparse Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation.

The method is shown to converge superlinearly, and experiments on synthetic and real application data demonstrate considerable performance improvements over other state-of-the-art methods. The statistical estimator supplies the existing motivation for the problem; the paper's contribution is an improved solver for it. Its findings show how adapting second-order optimization to the structure of this estimator can translate into substantial computational benefits.
summary.tldr: A structure-aware Newton algorithm solves sparse inverse-covariance estimation with superlinear convergence and strong experimental performance.

title: Sparse Inverse Covariance Matrix Estimation Using Quadratic Approximation

abstract: Neurons in the neocortex code and compute as part of a locally interconnected population. Large-scale multi-electrode recording makes it possible to access these population processes empirically by fitting statistical models to unaveraged data. What statistical structure best describes the concurrent spiking of cells within a local network? We argue that in the cortex, where firing exhibits extensive correlations in both time and space and where a typical sample of neurons still reflects only a very small fraction of the local population, the most appropriate model captures shared variability by a low-dimensional latent process evolving with smooth dynamics, rather than by putative direct coupling. We test this claim by comparing a latent dynamical model with realistic spiking observations to coupled generalised linear spike-response models (GLMs) using cortical recordings. We find that the latent dynamical approach outperforms the GLM in terms of goodness-of-fit, and reproduces the temporal correlations in the data more accurately. We also compare models whose observations models are either derived from a Gaussian or point-process models, finding that the non-Gaussian model provides slightly better goodness-of-fit and more realistic population spike counts.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to describe neurons firing together in a local cortical population. Recordings capture correlations across neurons and across time, but the observed neurons still represent only a small fraction of the surrounding network. The authors argue that this sampling situation favors a model of shared hidden activity over interpreting observed relationships as direct coupling.

Their proposed explanation uses a low-dimensional latent process with smooth dynamics to capture shared variability. A spiking observation model links that hidden process to the recorded events. The authors compare this latent dynamical approach with coupled generalized linear spike-response models using cortical recordings, testing which description better captures the observed population activity.

The latent dynamical model achieves better goodness-of-fit and reproduces temporal correlations more accurately in these comparisons. The paper also examines Gaussian and point-process observation models. The non-Gaussian version gives a slightly better fit and more realistic population spike counts. These findings support the shared-process approach in the recordings studied and show that the observation model also affects how faithfully population activity is represented.
summary.tldr: A shared latent dynamical process models recorded cortical population spiking better than coupled GLMs in the reported comparisons.

title: Empirical models of spiking in neural populations

abstract: A hallmark of modern machine learning is its ability to deal with high dimensional problems by exploiting structural assumptions that limit the degrees of freedom in the underlying model. A deep understanding of the capabilities and limits of high dimensional learning methods under specific assumptions such as sparsity, group sparsity, and low rank has been attained. Efforts (Negahban et al., 2010, Chandrasekaran et al., 2010} are now underway to distill this valuable experience by proposing general unified frameworks that can achieve the twin goals of summarizing previous analyses and enabling their application to notions of structure hitherto unexplored. Inspired by these developments, we propose and analyze a general computational scheme based on a greedy strategy to solve convex optimization problems that arise when dealing with structurally constrained high-dimensional problems. Our framework not only unifies existing greedy algorithms by recovering them as special cases but also yields novel ones. Finally, we extend our results to infinite dimensional problems by using interesting connections between smoothness of norms and behavior of martingales in Banach spaces.

paragraphs: High-dimensional learning becomes more manageable when a model has fewer effective degrees of freedom than its number of variables suggests. Sparsity, group sparsity, and low rank are examples of such structure. The paper seeks a common computational framework that can capture established approaches and support forms of structure beyond those already studied.

The authors propose and analyze a general greedy scheme for convex optimization problems arising from structural constraints. A greedy strategy builds a solution through successive choices. Here, the framework is broad enough to recover existing greedy algorithms as special cases and also produce new algorithms, linking methods that might otherwise require separate treatments.

The analysis also extends to infinite-dimensional problems. This extension uses connections between the smoothness of norms and the behavior of martingales in Banach spaces. The contribution is therefore both computational and theoretical: it supplies a shared algorithmic approach and develops mathematical tools for understanding its behavior across a wider range of structured problems.
summary.tldr: A general greedy optimization framework unifies existing algorithms for structured high-dimensional problems, yields new ones, and extends to infinite dimensions.

title: Greedy Algorithms for Structurally Constrained High Dimensional Problems

abstract: We present a new graph-based approach for incorporating domain knowledge in reinforcement learning applications. The domain knowledge is given as a weighted graph, or a kernel matrix, that loosely indicates which states should have similar optimal actions. We first introduce a bias into the policy search process by deriving a distribution on policies such that policies that disagree with the provided graph have low probabilities. This distribution corresponds to a Markov Random Field. We then present a reinforcement and an apprenticeship learning algorithms for finding such policy distributions. We also illustrate the advantage of the proposed approach on three problems: swing-up cart-balancing with nonuniform and smooth frictions, gridworlds, and teaching a robot to grasp new objects.

paragraphs: The paper studies how reinforcement learning can use domain knowledge about which states should receive similar actions. That knowledge is supplied as a weighted graph or kernel matrix. It need only loosely indicate similarities in optimal behavior, making it a guide for policy learning rather than a complete specification of what to do.

The authors translate this information into a probability distribution over policies. Policies that disagree with the graph receive lower probability, introducing a bias toward the supplied relationships. The resulting distribution is a Markov random field. They then develop both reinforcement learning and apprenticeship learning algorithms for finding policy distributions of this kind.

The approach is illustrated through cart balancing with varying friction, gridworlds, and teaching a robot to grasp new objects. These examples demonstrate advantages of incorporating the supplied relationships into learning. The central contribution is a common probabilistic mechanism for turning state-similarity knowledge into preferences over policies, together with algorithms that use those preferences in two learning settings.
summary.tldr: A Markov random field biases policy learning toward similar actions in states linked by supplied domain knowledge.

title: Algorithms for Learning Markov Field Policies

abstract: Discovering hierarchical regularities in data is a key problem in interacting with large datasets, modeling cognition, and encoding knowledge. A previous Bayesian solution---Kingman's coalescent---provides a convenient probabilistic model for data represented as a binary tree. Unfortunately, this is inappropriate for data better described by bushier trees. We generalize an existing belief propagation framework of Kingman's coalescent to the beta coalescent, which models a wider range of tree structures. Because of the complex combinatorial search over possible structures, we develop new sampling schemes using sequential Monte Carlo and Dirichlet process mixture models, which render inference efficient and tractable. We present results on both synthetic and real data that show the beta coalescent outperforms Kingman's coalescent on real datasets and is qualitatively better at capturing data in bushy hierarchies.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering represents relationships through a tree of groups within groups. A binary tree requires every branching point to split into two, which can be an awkward description of data with broader groupings. This paper replaces a Bayesian model restricted to binary trees, Kingman’s coalescent, with the more flexible beta coalescent.

The authors extend an existing belief propagation framework to this broader family of tree structures. Greater flexibility also creates a difficult search problem because there are many possible hierarchies to consider. To make inference manageable, they develop sampling schemes using sequential Monte Carlo and Dirichlet process mixture models. These methods address the computational challenge created by the richer structural model.

Results on synthetic and real data assess the approach. The authors report that the beta coalescent outperforms Kingman’s coalescent on the real datasets and gives qualitatively better representations of bushy hierarchies. The findings support allowing broader branches when those better match the data, while the sampling contribution makes that modeling choice computationally tractable.
summary.tldr: Beta-coalescent clustering supports broader hierarchical branches and outperforms a binary-tree model on the reported real datasets.

title: Binary to Bushy: Bayesian Hierarchical Clustering with the Beta Coalescent

abstract: Adaptive stochastic optimization optimizes an objective function adaptively under uncertainty. Adaptive stochastic optimization plays a crucial role in planning and learning under uncertainty, but is, unfortunately, computationally intractable in general. This paper introduces two conditions on the objective function, the marginal likelihood rate bound and the marginal likelihood bound, which enable efficient approximate solution of adaptive stochastic optimization. Several interesting classes of functions satisfy these conditions naturally, e.g., the version space reduction function for hypothesis learning. We describe Recursive Adaptive Coverage (RAC), a new adaptive stochastic optimization algorithm that exploits these conditions, and apply it to two planning tasks under uncertainty. In constrast to the earlier submodular optimization approach, our algorithm applies to adaptive stochastic optimization algorithm over both sets and paths.

This makes it relevant to planning and learning, but the general problem is computationally intractable. The paper asks which properties of an objective allow useful approximate solutions to be found efficiently.

It introduces two conditions, called the marginal likelihood rate bound and the marginal likelihood bound. These provide the structure exploited by a new algorithm, Recursive Adaptive Coverage. The abstract identifies several classes of functions that naturally satisfy the conditions, including version space reduction for hypothesis learning, where the objective concerns narrowing the set of candidate explanations.

summary.tldr: Recursive Adaptive Coverage uses two objective conditions to enable efficient approximate adaptive optimization over both sets and paths.

title: Adaptive Stochastic Optimization: From Sets to Paths

abstract: Many real world graphs, such as the graphs of molecules, exhibit structure at multiple different scales, but most existing kernels between graphs are either purely local or purely global in character. In contrast, by building a hierarchy of nested subgraphs, the Multiscale Laplacian Graph kernels (MLG kernels) that we define in this paper can account for structure at a range of different scales. At the heart of the MLG construction is another new graph kernel, called the Feature Space Laplacian Graph kernel (FLG kernel), which has the property that it can lift a base kernel defined on the vertices of two graphs to a kernel between the graphs. The MLG kernel applies such FLG kernels to subgraphs recursively. To make the MLG kernel computationally feasible, we also introduce a randomized projection procedure, similar to the Nystro ̈m method, but for RKHS operators.

paragraphs: Graphs can contain meaningful patterns at several scales, as illustrated by molecular graphs. A similarity measure focused only on local neighborhoods or only on the whole graph can miss this layered organization. The Multiscale Laplacian Graph kernel addresses the problem by constructing a hierarchy of nested subgraphs and accounting for structure across that hierarchy.

Its main building block is the Feature Space Laplacian Graph kernel. This kernel converts a base similarity measure between vertices into a similarity measure between graphs. The multiscale construction applies that operation recursively to subgraphs, allowing comparisons at different levels to contribute to the overall representation of graph similarity.

The paper also introduces a randomized projection procedure to make the construction computationally feasible. It resembles the Nyström method but operates on reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space operators. The contribution combines a way to represent graph structure at multiple scales with a computational mechanism for using it, addressing both the scope of the comparison and the cost of carrying it out.
summary.tldr: The Multiscale Laplacian Graph kernel recursively compares nested subgraphs to capture structure across scales, using randomized projection for computational feasibility.

title: The Multiscale Laplacian Graph Kernel

abstract: This study introduces a novel feature selection approach CMICOT, which is a further evolution of filter methods with sequential forward selection (SFS) whose scoring functions are based on conditional mutual information (MI). We state and study a novel saddle point (max-min) optimization problem to build a scoring function that is able to identify joint interactions between several features. This method fills the gap of MI-based SFS techniques with high-order dependencies. In this high-dimensional case, the estimation of MI has prohibitively high sample complexity. We mitigate this cost using a greedy approximation and binary representatives what makes our technique able to be effectively used. The superiority of our approach is demonstrated by comparison with recently proposed interaction-aware filters and several interaction-agnostic state-of-the-art ones on ten publicly available benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Feature selection needs to recognize when several features provide useful information jointly. Methods that score features without adequately representing these interactions can overlook high-order dependencies. This paper introduces CMICOT, a filter method that extends sequential forward selection using scores based on conditional mutual information.

The authors formulate a new max-min, or saddle-point, optimization problem to construct the scoring function. Its purpose is to identify interactions among several features as the selected set grows. Directly estimating mutual information in this high-dimensional setting requires prohibitively many samples. CMICOT reduces that burden through a greedy approximation and binary representatives, making the proposed interaction-sensitive score usable in practice.

Experiments compare the method with recently proposed interaction-aware filters and several leading filters that do not account for interactions, using ten public benchmark datasets. The authors report superior performance in these comparisons. The contribution combines a scoring formulation for high-order dependence with an approximation strategy that addresses the statistical cost of estimating it.
summary.tldr: CMICOT selects features using an interaction-sensitive information score made practical through greedy approximation and binary representatives.

title: Efficient High-Order Interaction-Aware Feature Selection Based on Conditional Mutual Information

abstract: We address the problem of multi-class classification in the case where the number of classes is very large. We propose a double sampling strategy on top of a multi-class to binary reduction strategy, which transforms the original multi-class problem into a binary classification problem over pairs of examples. The aim of the sampling strategy is to overcome the curse of long-tailed class distributions exhibited in majority of large-scale multi-class classification problems and to reduce the number of pairs of examples in the expanded data. We show that this strategy does not alter the consistency of the empirical risk minimization principle defined over the double sample reduction. Experiments are carried out on DMOZ and Wikipedia collections with 10,000 to 100,000 classes where we show the efficiency of the proposed approach in terms of training and prediction time, memory consumption, and predictive performance with respect to state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Classification becomes difficult to manage when the possible labels number in the tens of thousands. One approach converts the original task into binary classification over pairs of examples. This changes the form of the learning problem, but can create a very large expanded dataset. Uneven class frequencies add another challenge because many classes have relatively little data.

The paper introduces a double sampling strategy on top of this pair-based reduction. Its goals are to reduce the number of training pairs and address the long-tailed class distributions common in large classification problems. The theoretical result shows that this sampling does not change the consistency of empirical risk minimization for the double sample reduction.

Experiments use the DMOZ and Wikipedia collections with between 10,000 and 100,000 classes. The evaluation considers training time, prediction time, memory use, and predictive performance against state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution connects computational savings with a statistical justification: aggressive pair selection can make the reduction more manageable while preserving the stated consistency property.
summary.tldr: A double sampling strategy makes pair-based classification with many classes more manageable while preserving the reduction’s stated statistical consistency.

title: Aggressive Sampling for Multi-class to Binary Reduction with Applications to Text Classification

abstract: Dealing with sparse rewards is one of the biggest challenges in Reinforcement Learning (RL). We present a novel technique called Hindsight Experience Replay which allows sample-efficient learning from rewards which are sparse and binary and therefore avoid the need for complicated reward engineering. It can be combined with an arbitrary off-policy RL algorithm and may be seen as a form of implicit curriculum. We demonstrate our approach on the task of manipulating objects with a robotic arm. In particular, we run experiments on three different tasks: pushing, sliding, and pick-and-place, in each case using only binary rewards indicating whether or not the task is completed. Our ablation studies show that Hindsight Experience Replay is a crucial ingredient which makes training possible in these challenging environments. We show that our policies trained on a physics simulation can be deployed on a physical robot and successfully complete the task. The video presenting our experiments is available at https://goo.gl/SMrQnI.

Hindsight Experience Replay is proposed as a way to learn efficiently when rewards simply indicate success or failure. Its practical aim is to make these simple reward definitions usable without designing a more complicated reward signal.

The technique can be combined with any off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm and can be interpreted as an implicit curriculum. The authors evaluate it using a robotic arm on pushing, sliding, and pick-and-place tasks. In all three cases, the reward is binary and reports only whether the requested task has been completed.

Ablation studies identify Hindsight Experience Replay as a crucial component that makes training possible in these challenging environments. The authors also deploy policies learned in physics simulation on a physical robot and report successful task completion. These results connect learning from minimal feedback to physical execution, showing that the approach's benefits in the reported tasks extend beyond simulated training.
summary.tldr: Hindsight Experience Replay enables efficient learning from sparse binary rewards and supports successful transfer from simulated manipulation to a physical robot.

title: Hindsight Experience Replay

abstract: Computing partition function is the most important statistical inference task arising in applications of Graphical Models (GM). Since it is computationally intractable, approximate methods have been used in practice, where mean-field (MF) and belief propagation (BP) are arguably the most popular and successful approaches of a variational type. In this paper, we propose two new variational schemes, coined Gauged-MF (G-MF) and Gauged-BP (G-BP), improving MF and BP, respectively. Both provide lower bounds for the partition function by utilizing the so-called gauge transformation which modifies factors of GM while keeping the partition function invariant. Moreover, we prove that both G-MF and G-BP are exact for GMs with a single loop of a special structure, even though the bare MF and BP perform badly in this case. Our extensive experiments indeed confirm that the proposed algorithms outperform and generalize MF and BP.

paragraphs: The partition function is a central quantity for inference in graphical models, but computing it exactly is generally intractable. Mean-field methods and belief propagation provide widely used variational approximations. This paper introduces modified versions of both methods, called Gauged-MF and Gauged-BP, to improve their treatment of this quantity.

The key operation is a gauge transformation: it changes the model’s factors while leaving the partition function unchanged. This creates flexibility in how the model is represented without changing the target quantity. Both proposed schemes use that flexibility to provide lower bounds on the partition function.

The authors prove that the methods are exact for graphical models containing a single loop with a particular structure, a case where the unmodified methods perform poorly. That guarantee is specific to the stated class of models. Extensive experiments also support the broader usefulness of the approach, showing improvements over mean-field and belief propagation. The work demonstrates how a target-preserving transformation can improve the approximation used to compute it.
summary.tldr: Gauge transformations improve mean-field and belief-propagation partition-function bounds, with exactness proved for a special single-loop structure.

title: Gauging Variational Inference

abstract: This paper introduces Wasserstein variational inference, a new form of approximate Bayesian inference based on optimal transport theory. Wasserstein variational inference uses a new family of divergences that includes both f-divergences and the Wasserstein distance as special cases. The gradients of the Wasserstein variational loss are obtained by backpropagating through the Sinkhorn iterations. This technique results in a very stable likelihood-free training method that can be used with implicit distributions and probabilistic programs. Using the Wasserstein variational inference framework, we introduce several new forms of autoencoders and test their robustness and performance against existing variational autoencoding techniques.

paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian inference seeks a manageable representation of a probability distribution that is difficult to work with directly. This paper introduces Wasserstein variational inference, an approach grounded in optimal transport. It uses a new family of divergences that contains both f-divergences and Wasserstein distance as special cases.

The method obtains gradients of its variational objective by backpropagating through Sinkhorn iterations. This connects the transport-based comparison of distributions to a trainable optimization procedure. The authors report a very stable likelihood-free training method that can work with implicit distributions and probabilistic programs, making the framework relevant when training does not rely on evaluating a likelihood.

The authors also use the framework to introduce several new autoencoder forms and evaluate their robustness and performance against existing variational autoencoding techniques. These applications show how the inference construction can lead to concrete representation-learning models. The abstract reports the stability of the training method and the comparative evaluation, without claiming that every proposed autoencoder outperforms the existing alternatives.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein variational inference uses optimal-transport divergences and differentiable Sinkhorn iterations for stable likelihood-free Bayesian approximation.

title: Wasserstein Variational Inference

abstract: In this paper, we consider the $k$-center/median/means clustering with outliers problems (or the $(k, z)$-center/median/means problems) in the distributed setting. Most previous distributed algorithms have their communication costs linearly depending on $z$, the number of outliers. Recently Guha et al.[10] overcame this dependence issue by considering bi-criteria approximation algorithms that output solutions with $2z$ outliers. For the case where $z$ is large, the extra $z$ outliers discarded by the algorithms might be too large, considering that the data gathering process might be costly. In this paper, we improve the number of outliers to the best possible $(1+\epsilon)z$, while maintaining the $O(1)$-approximation ratio and independence of communication cost on $z$. The problems we consider include the $(k, z)$-center problem, and $(k, z)$-median/means problems in Euclidean metrics. Implementation of the our algorithm for $(k, z)$-center shows that it outperforms many previous algorithms, both in terms of the communication cost and quality of the output solution.

In this paper, we improve the number of outliers to the best possible $(1+\epsilon)z$, while maintaining the $O(1)$-approximation ratio and independence of communication cost on $z$. paragraphs: Clustering distributed data becomes harder when many observations may be outliers. Algorithms must coordinate across machines while deciding which points to exclude. Earlier approaches often communicated an amount of data proportional to the outlier budget, z. Another approach removed that dependence but could discard twice as many points as the budget allowed.

This paper reduces the permitted number of discarded points to (1 + epsilon) times z while retaining a constant-factor approximation and communication cost independent of z. That brings the exclusion allowance closer to the intended budget, which matters when gathering data is costly and discarding many extra observations is undesirable.

The theoretical results cover k-center with outliers and Euclidean k-median and k-means with outliers. An implementation for k-center outperforms many previous algorithms in both communication cost and solution quality. The contribution therefore improves the tradeoff between distributed coordination and data retention, while still allowing a small multiplicative increase in the outlier budget rather than requiring exactly z exclusions.
summary.tldr: Distributed clustering algorithms retain constant-factor guarantees and communication independent of the outlier budget while discarding at most (1 + epsilon) times that budget.

title: Distributed $k$-Clustering for Data with Heavy Noise

abstract: Shift-and-invert preconditioning, as a classic acceleration technique for the leading eigenvector computation, has received much attention again recently, owing to fast least-squares solvers for efficiently approximating matrix inversions in power iterations. In this work, we adopt an inexact Riemannian gradient descent perspective to investigate this technique on the effect of the step-size scheme. The shift-and-inverted power method is included as a special case with adaptive step-sizes. Particularly, two other step-size settings, i.e., constant step-sizes and Barzilai-Borwein (BB) step-sizes, are examined theoretically and/or empirically. We present a novel convergence analysis for the constant step-size setting that achieves a rate at $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{p+1}}})$, where $\lambda_{i}$ represents the $i$-th largest eigenvalue of the given real symmetric matrix and $p$ is the multiplicity of $\lambda_{1}$. Our experimental studies show that the proposed algorithm can be significantly faster than the shift-and-inverted power method in practice.

paragraphs: The paper studies faster computation of a real symmetric matrix’s leading eigenvector. It focuses on shift-and-invert preconditioning, an acceleration technique whose practical appeal has grown with fast least-squares solvers that approximate the matrix inversions used in power iterations. The authors examine this technique through the perspective of inexact Riemannian gradient descent.

That perspective makes the choice of step size central. The shifted-and-inverted power method appears as a special case with adaptive step sizes. The paper then studies constant step sizes and Barzilai-Borwein step sizes, using theoretical analysis, experiments, or both. This connects a familiar eigenvector procedure to a broader set of optimization choices.

For constant step sizes, the authors prove a convergence rate of approximately the square root of λ₁ divided by λ₁ − λₚ₊₁, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here p is the multiplicity of the largest eigenvalue, so the expression accounts for repeated leading eigenvalues. Experiments show that the proposed algorithm can be significantly faster than the shifted-and-inverted power method in practice.
summary.tldr: Viewing shift-and-invert eigenvector computation as gradient descent reveals useful step-size choices, with convergence analysis and empirical speed gains.

title: Gradient Descent Meets Shift-and-Invert Preconditioning for Eigenvector Computation

abstract: Asynchronous Gibbs sampling has been recently shown to be fast-mixing and an accurate method for estimating probabilities of events on a small number of variables of a graphical model satisfying Dobrushin's condition~\cite{DeSaOR16}. We investigate whether it can be used to accurately estimate expectations of functions of {\em all the variables} of the model. Under the same condition, we show that the synchronous (sequential) and asynchronous Gibbs samplers can be coupled so that the expected Hamming distance between their (multivariate) samples remains bounded by $O(\tau \log n),$ where $n$ is the number of variables in the graphical model, and $\tau$ is a measure of the asynchronicity. A similar bound holds for any constant power of the Hamming distance. Hence, the expectation of any function that is Lipschitz with respect to a power of the Hamming distance, can be estimated with a bias that grows logarithmically in $n$. Going beyond Lipschitz functions, we consider the bias arising from asynchronicity in estimating the expectation of polynomial functions of all variables in the model. Using recent concentration of measure results~\cite{DaskalakisDK17,GheissariLP17,GotzeSS18}, we show that the bias introduced by the asynchronicity is of smaller order than the standard deviation of the function value already present in the true model. We perform experiments on a multi-processor machine to empirically illustrate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Asynchronous Gibbs sampling had already been shown to estimate probabilities involving small groups of variables accurately under Dobrushin's condition. This paper asks whether it can also estimate expectations of functions involving every variable in a graphical model. The distinction matters because accuracy for local events does not itself settle accuracy for global quantities.

Under the same condition, the authors couple sequential and asynchronous samplers so that their samples differ in an expected O(τ log n) coordinates, where n counts variables and τ measures asynchronicity.
