Using concentration results, the authors show that the bias caused by asynchronicity is smaller in order than the standard deviation already present under the true model. Multiprocessor experiments illustrate the theory. The results establish conditional accuracy guarantees for broader, global quantities while explicitly relating asynchronous error to ordinary statistical variation.
summary.tldr: Under Dobrushin's condition, asynchronous Gibbs sampling has controlled bias for broad classes of functions involving all model variables.

title: HOGWILD!-Gibbs can be PanAccurate

abstract: Embedding complex objects as vectors in low dimensional spaces is a longstanding problem in machine learning. We propose in this work an extension of that approach, which consists in embedding objects as elliptical probability distributions, namely distributions whose densities have elliptical level sets. We endow these measures with the 2-Wasserstein metric, with two important benefits: (i) For such measures, the squared 2-Wasserstein metric has a closed form, equal to a weighted sum of the squared Euclidean distance between means and the squared Bures metric between covariance matrices. The latter is a Riemannian metric between positive semi-definite matrices, which turns out to be Euclidean on a suitable factor representation of such matrices, which is valid on the entire geodesic between these matrices. (ii) The 2-Wasserstein distance boils down to the usual Euclidean metric when comparing Diracs, and therefore provides a natural framework to extend point embeddings. We show that for these reasons Wasserstein elliptical embeddings are more intuitive and yield tools that are better behaved numerically than the alternative choice of Gaussian embeddings with the Kullback-Leibler divergence. In particular, and unlike previous work based on the KL geometry, we learn elliptical distributions that are not necessarily diagonal. We demonstrate the advantages of elliptical embeddings by using them for visualization, to compute embeddings of words, and to reflect entailment or hypernymy.

paragraphs: Conventional embeddings represent each object as a point in a low-dimensional space. This paper extends that representation to elliptical probability distributions, whose equal-density contours have elliptical shapes. An object can therefore have both a location and a covariance structure, and the authors compare these representations using the 2-Wasserstein distance.

Their method also learns distributions with covariance matrices that need not be diagonal. Applications to visualization, word embeddings, and entailment or hypernymy illustrate how the richer representation can express relationships beyond the locations of isolated points.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein distances extend point embeddings to elliptical distributions with tractable geometry and support for non-diagonal covariance.

title: Generalizing Point Embeddings using the Wasserstein Space of Elliptical Distributions

abstract: Neural networks have been used prominently in several machine learning and statistics applications. In general, the underlying optimization of neural networks is non-convex which makes analyzing their performance challenging. In this paper, we take another approach to this problem by constraining the network such that the corresponding optimization landscape has good theoretical properties without significantly compromising performance. In particular, for two-layer neural networks we introduce Porcupine Neural Networks (PNNs) whose weight vectors are constrained to lie over a finite set of lines. We show that most local optima of PNN optimizations are global while we have a characterization of regions where bad local optimizers may exist. Moreover, our theoretical and empirical results suggest that an unconstrained neural network can be approximated using a polynomially-large PNN.
originalAbstract: Neural networks have been used prominently in several machine learning and statistics applications. In general, the underlying optimization of neural networks is non-convex which makes analyzing their performance challenging. In this paper, we take another approach to this problem by constraining the network such that the corresponding optimization landscape has good theoretical properties without significantly compromising performance. In particular, for two-layer neural networks we introduce Porcupine Neural Networks (PNNs) whose weight vectors are constrained to lie over a finite set of lines. We show that most local optima of PNN optimizations are global while we have a characterization of regions where bad local optimizers may exist. Moreover, our theoretical and empirical results suggest that an unconstrained neural network can be approximated using a polynomially-large PNN.

paragraphs: Neural network optimization is difficult to analyze because its objective is generally nonconvex. This paper approaches the problem by restricting the network so that the optimization landscape has more tractable theoretical properties. For two-layer networks, it introduces Porcupine Neural Networks, whose weight vectors must lie along a finite collection of lines.

The restriction provides structure for studying local optima. The authors show that most local optima of the resulting optimization problems are global, and they characterize regions where inferior local optima may occur. This is a qualified landscape result: it identifies broad favorable behavior while retaining an explicit place for bad local solutions.

The paper also examines whether this constrained family can represent the behavior of unconstrained networks without excessive growth. Its theoretical and empirical results suggest that a polynomially large Porcupine Neural Network can approximate an unconstrained network. Together, the findings support structured network restrictions as a way to study optimization while retaining useful expressive capacity, rather than assuming that favorable landscape properties require abandoning approximation quality.
summary.tldr: Constraining two-layer network weights to finitely many lines yields analyzable landscapes where most local optima are global.

title: Porcupine Neural Networks: Approximating Neural Network Landscapes

abstract: This paper studies first order methods for solving smooth minimax optimization problems $\min_x \max_y g(x,y)$ where $g(\cdot,\cdot)$ is smooth and $g(x,\cdot)$ is concave for each $x$. In terms of $g(\cdot,y)$, we consider two settings -- strongly convex and nonconvex -- and improve upon the best known rates in both. For strongly-convex $g(\cdot, y),\ \forall y$, we propose a new direct optimal algorithm combining Mirror-Prox and Nesterov's AGD, and show that it can find global optimum in $\widetilde{O}\left(1/k^2 \right)$ iterations, improving over current state-of-the-art rate of $O(1/k)$. We use this result along with an inexact proximal point method to provide $\widetilde{O}\left(1/k^{1/3} \right)$ rate for finding stationary points in the nonconvex setting where $g(\cdot, y)$ can be nonconvex. This improves over current best-known rate of $O(1/k^{1/5})$. Finally, we instantiate our result for finite nonconvex minimax problems, i.e., $\min_x \max_{1\leq i\leq m} f_i(x)$, with nonconvex $f_i(\cdot)$, to obtain convergence rate of $O(m^{1/3}\sqrt{\log m}/k^{1/3})$.

For the strongly convex case, they combine Mirror-Prox with Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent. Their method improves the reported convergence rate from order 1/k to approximately 1/k squared, with logarithmic factors suppressed, toward a global optimum. Here k tracks the number of iterations, so the faster decay means stronger accuracy guarantees as computation increases.

They improve the rate for finding stationary points from order 1/k to the one-fifth power to approximately 1/k to the one-third power. They also specialize the analysis to minimizing the maximum of finitely many nonconvex functions, explicitly accounting for the number of functions.
summary.tldr: New first-order minimax methods improve convergence guarantees in both strongly convex–concave and nonconvex–concave settings.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Smooth Minimax Optimization

abstract: Retrosynthesis is one of the fundamental problems in organic chemistry. The task is to identify reactants that can be used to synthesize a specified product molecule. Recently, computer-aided retrosynthesis is finding renewed interest from both chemistry and computer science communities. Most existing approaches rely on template-based models that define subgraph matching rules, but whether or not a chemical reaction can proceed is not defined by hard decision rules. In this work, we propose a new approach to this task using the Conditional Graph Logic Network, a conditional graphical model built upon graph neural networks that learns when rules from reaction templates should be applied, implicitly considering whether the resulting reaction would be both chemically feasible and strategic. We also propose an efficient hierarchical sampling to alleviate the computation cost. While achieving a significant improvement of 8.2% over current state-of-the-art methods on the benchmark dataset, our model also offers interpretations for the prediction.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis works backward from a desired product molecule to reactants that could produce it. Many computational approaches use reaction templates expressed as graph-matching rules. The paper argues that matching such a rule is insufficient to determine whether a reaction should proceed, because chemical feasibility and strategic usefulness cannot be captured solely by hard decisions.

The proposed Conditional Graph Logic Network learns when reaction-template rules should apply. It is a conditional graphical model built on graph neural networks, combining molecular graph representations with rule-based reaction structure. In learning which rules to apply, the model implicitly considers whether the proposed reaction is chemically feasible and useful for the synthesis objective.

The authors also introduce hierarchical sampling to reduce computational cost. On the benchmark dataset, the model reports an 8.2% improvement over the compared state-of-the-art methods and provides interpretations of its predictions. The contribution is a learned approach to template application: reaction rules still structure the prediction, while a conditional model learns how to choose among their possible uses.
summary.tldr: A Conditional Graph Logic Network learns when reaction templates should apply, improving benchmark retrosynthesis predictions while providing interpretations.

title: Retrosynthesis Prediction with Conditional Graph Logic Network

abstract: “Thinking in pictures,” [1] i.e., spatial-temporal reasoning, effortless and instantaneous for humans, is believed to be a significant ability to perform logical induction and a crucial factor in the intellectual history of technology development. Modern Artificial Intelligence (AI), fueled by massive datasets, deeper models, and mighty computation, has come to a stage where (super-)human-level performances are observed in certain specific tasks. However, current AI's ability in “thinking in pictures” is still far lacking behind. In this work, we study how to improve machines' reasoning ability on one challenging task of this kind: Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM). Specifically, we borrow the very idea of “contrast effects” from the field of psychology, cognition, and education to design and train a permutation-invariant model. Inspired by cognitive studies, we equip our model with a simple inference module that is jointly trained with the perception backbone. Combining all the elements, we propose the Contrastive Perceptual Inference network (CoPINet) and empirically demonstrate that CoPINet sets the new state-of-the-art for permutation-invariant models on two major datasets. We conclude that spatial-temporal reasoning depends on envisaging the possibilities consistent with the relations between objects and can be solved from pixel-level inputs.

paragraphs: The paper studies visual reasoning through Raven's Progressive Matrices, a task used here to investigate reasoning about relationships in visual inputs. Its motivation is that strong performance on specialized AI tasks does not automatically establish the ability to reason spatially and temporally. The authors focus on improving this particular form of perceptual inference.

Their Contrastive Perceptual Inference network, CoPINet, draws on contrast effects discussed in psychology, cognition, and education. They use this idea to design and train a permutation-invariant model, so the modeled collection is not treated differently merely because its elements are reordered. The authors interpret their results as supporting reasoning from pixels by considering possibilities consistent with relationships among objects. The empirical achievement is specifically within the evaluated visual-reasoning tasks and model category; its significance is the demonstrated combination of perception, contrast, and jointly learned inference.
summary.tldr: CoPINet combines contrast-inspired learning with joint perception and inference, achieving leading results among permutation-invariant models on two visual-reasoning datasets.

title: Learning Perceptual Inference by Contrasting

abstract: Given a set of a reference RGBD views of an indoor environment, and a new viewpoint, our goal is to predict the view from that location. Prior work on new-view generation has predominantly focused on significantly constrained scenarios, typically involving artificially rendered views of isolated CAD models. Here we tackle a much more challenging version of the problem. We devise an approach that exploits known geometric properties of the scene (per-frame camera extrinsics and depth) in order to warp reference views into the new ones. The defects in the generated views are handled by a novel RGBD inpainting network, PerspectiveNet, that is fine-tuned for a given scene in order to obtain images that are geometrically consistent with all the views in the scene camera system. Experiments conducted on the ScanNet and SceneNet datasets reveal performance superior to strong baselines.

Here we tackle a much more challenging version of the problem. The defects in the generated views are handled by a novel RGBD inpainting network, PerspectiveNet, that is fine-tuned for a given scene in order to obtain images that are geometrically consistent with all the views in the scene camera system. Experiments conducted on the ScanNet and SceneNet datasets reveal performance superior to strong baselines.

paragraphs: PerspectiveNet tackles the problem of predicting what an indoor environment would look like from a new viewpoint. Its inputs are reference images with color and depth, together with the desired viewpoint. The work addresses real indoor scenes, extending beyond the constrained settings of isolated computer-rendered objects that dominated much earlier work.

The approach uses known camera extrinsics and depth to geometrically warp the reference views toward the requested view. These warped images contain defects that a dedicated RGBD inpainting network handles. This separates the use of available scene geometry from the learned task of repairing the incomplete or imperfect views produced by warping.

The inpainting network is fine-tuned for each scene to obtain images consistent with the geometry across that scene’s camera system. This scene-specific adaptation is part of the proposed method, alongside its reliance on known depth and camera geometry. Experiments on ScanNet and SceneNet report performance above strong baselines, supporting the combination of geometric warping and learned completion for indoor view synthesis.
summary.tldr: PerspectiveNet combines geometric warping with scene-specific RGBD inpainting to synthesize consistent indoor views from reference images and known geometry.

title: PerspectiveNet: A Scene-consistent Image Generator for New View Synthesis in Real Indoor Environments

abstract: Statistical tests are at the heart of many scientific tasks. To validate their hypothesis, researchers in medical and social sciences use individuals' data. The sensitivity of participants' data requires the design of statistical tests that ensure the privacy of the individuals in the most efficient way. In this paper, we use the framework of property testing to design algorithms to test the properties of the distribution that the data is drawn from with respect to differential privacy. In particular, we investigate testing two fundamental properties of distributions: (1) testing the equivalence of two distributions when we have unequal numbers of samples from the two distributions. (2) Testing independence of two random variables. In both cases, we show that our testers achieve near optimal sample complexity (up to logarithmic factors). Moreover, our dependence on the privacy parameter is an additive term, which indicates that differential privacy can be obtained in most regimes of parameters for free.

paragraphs: Statistical testing often uses sensitive information about individuals, making privacy part of the algorithm-design problem. This paper studies distribution property testing under differential privacy. The goal is to decide whether a distribution has a specified property while using samples efficiently and providing the required protection for individual data.

The authors address two tasks. One tests whether two distributions are equivalent when the available sample counts differ between them. The other tests whether two random variables are independent. For both problems, they construct private testers with sample complexity that is near optimal up to logarithmic factors.

A central result is that dependence on the privacy parameter appears as an additive term in the sample requirement. The authors interpret this as allowing privacy essentially for free in most parameter regimes: the privacy-related term need not dominate the overall sample cost. This is a statement about the sample-complexity tradeoff, with the benefit depending on the regime in which the test operates.
summary.tldr: Private equivalence and independence testers achieve near-optimal sample complexity with an additive privacy-related cost.

title: Private Testing of Distributions via Sample Permutations

abstract: Many reinforcement learning (RL) tasks have specific properties that can be leveraged to modify existing RL algorithms to adapt to those tasks and further improve performance, and a general class of such properties is the multiple reward channel. In those environments the full reward can be decomposed into sub-rewards obtained from different channels. Existing work on reward decomposition either requires prior knowledge of the environment to decompose the full reward, or decomposes reward without prior knowledge but with degraded performance. In this paper, we propose Distributional Reward Decomposition for Reinforcement Learning (DRDRL), a novel reward decomposition algorithm which captures the multiple reward channel structure under distributional setting. Empirically, our method captures the multi-channel structure and discovers meaningful reward decomposition, without any requirements on prior knowledge. Consequently, our agent achieves better performance than existing methods on environments with multiple reward channels.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning environments provide a total reward that combines several underlying reward channels. Treating that total as a single signal can leave useful structure unexploited. The paper studies how to discover a decomposition into meaningful sub-rewards so an agent can make use of the environment's multiple-channel organization during learning.

Existing approaches described in the abstract face a tradeoff: they either need prior knowledge to specify the decomposition or discover one without that knowledge at the cost of weaker performance. Distributional Reward Decomposition for Reinforcement Learning, or DRDRL, seeks to capture the channel structure within a distributional reinforcement learning setting.

The experiments show that DRDRL discovers meaningful reward decompositions without requiring prior knowledge of the environment's channels. The resulting agent performs better than existing methods in environments with multiple reward channels. The evidence supports using learned reward structure in that class of tasks; it is an empirical result tied to environments where such a decomposition is relevant.
summary.tldr: DRDRL discovers meaningful reward channels without prior knowledge and improves empirical performance in environments with multiple reward channels.

title: Distributional Reward Decomposition for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new framework for designing fast parallel algorithms for fundamental statistical subset selection tasks that include feature selection and experimental design. Such tasks are known to be weakly submodular and are amenable to optimization via the standard greedy algorithm. Despite its desirable approximation guarantees, however, the greedy algorithm is inherently sequential and in the worst case, its parallel runtime is linear in the size of the data. Recently, there has been a surge of interest in a parallel optimization technique called adaptive sampling which produces solutions with desirable approximation guarantees for submodular maximization in exponentially faster parallel runtime. Unfortunately, we show that for general weakly submodular functions such accelerations are impossible. The major contribution in this paper is a novel relaxation of submodularity which we call differential submodularity. We first prove that differential submodularity characterizes objectives like feature selection and experimental design. We then design an adaptive sampling algorithm for differentially submodular functions whose parallel runtime is logarithmic in the size of the data and achieves strong approximation guarantees. Through experiments, we show the algorithm's performance is competitive with state-of-the-art methods and obtains dramatic speedups for feature selection and experimental design problems.

paragraphs: Feature selection and experimental design involve choosing a useful subset from many candidates. Greedy algorithms offer approximation guarantees for these tasks, but their choices depend sequentially on earlier choices. Consequently, even with parallel hardware, their worst-case parallel runtime can grow linearly with the size of the data.

Adaptive sampling can greatly reduce parallel runtime for submodular objectives. The paper first shows that the same acceleration is impossible for general weakly submodular functions, the broader class associated with these statistical tasks. It then introduces differential submodularity and proves that objectives such as feature selection and experimental design possess this more useful structure.

Using that structure, the authors develop an adaptive sampling algorithm with logarithmic parallel runtime in the data size and strong approximation guarantees. The contribution is both a boundary on what weak submodularity alone permits and a route around that boundary for relevant objectives. Experiments report competitive solution performance and substantial speedups for feature selection and experimental design.
summary.tldr: Differential submodularity enables fast parallel subset selection with approximation guarantees for feature selection and experimental design.

title: Fast Parallel Algorithms for Statistical Subset Selection Problems

abstract: We present a novel intrinsically motivated agent that learns how to control the environment in a sample efficient manner, that is with as few environment interactions as possible, by optimizing learning progress. It learns what can be controlled, how to allocate time and attention as well as the relations between objects using surprise-based motivation. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated in a synthetic and robotic manipulation environment yielding considerably improved performance and smaller sample complexity compared to an intrinsically motivated, non-hierarchical and state-of-the-art hierarchical baseline. In a nutshell, our work combines several task-level planning agent structures (backtracking search on task-graph, probabilistic road-maps, allocation of search efforts) with intrinsic motivation to achieve learning from scratch.

paragraphs: This paper presents an agent that learns from scratch how to control its environment while trying to use as few interactions as possible. Its learning objective emphasizes progress: the agent directs its activity toward improving what it can do. Surprise provides an internal source of motivation for discovering controllable aspects of the environment and relationships between objects.

The approach combines that motivation with planning at the level of tasks. Its components include backtracking search over a task graph, probabilistic roadmaps, and mechanisms for allocating search effort. Together, these structures address both what the agent should attempt and how much time and attention to devote to different possibilities. Planning and exploration are therefore linked through the agent's own learning progress.

Experiments in synthetic and robotic manipulation environments show considerably better performance and lower sample complexity than the stated non-hierarchical and hierarchical baselines. Here, lower sample complexity means learning with fewer environment interactions. The findings support combining structured task planning with intrinsic motivation as a practical route to more efficient learning in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: An intrinsically motivated agent combines task planning with surprise-driven learning to improve control using fewer environment interactions.

title: Control What You Can: Intrinsically Motivated Task-Planning Agent

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) have attracted substantial attention as an elegant probabilistic model that captures the balance between quality and diversity within sets. DPPs are conventionally parameterized by a positive semi-definite kernel matrix, and this symmetric kernel encodes only repulsive interactions between items. These so-called symmetric DPPs have significant expressive power, and have been successfully applied to a variety of machine learning tasks, including recommendation systems, information retrieval, and automatic summarization, among many others. Efficient algorithms for learning symmetric DPPs and sampling from these models have been reasonably well studied. However, relatively little attention has been given to nonsymmetric DPPs, which relax the symmetric constraint on the kernel. Nonsymmetric DPPs allow for both repulsive and attractive item interactions, which can significantly improve modeling power, resulting in a model that may better fit for some applications. We present a method that enables a tractable algorithm, based on maximum likelihood estimation, for learning nonsymmetric DPPs from data composed of observed subsets. Our method imposes a particular decomposition of the nonsymmetric kernel that enables such tractable learning algorithms, which we analyze both theoretically and experimentally. We evaluate our model on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating improved predictive performance compared to symmetric DPPs, which have previously shown strong performance on modeling tasks associated with these datasets.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model sets while balancing item quality and diversity. Their conventional symmetric, positive semidefinite kernels encode repulsive interactions, helping represent items that tend not to appear together. Some applications also involve attraction between items, motivating a model that can express both kinds of relationships.

This paper develops a tractable way to learn nonsymmetric determinantal point processes from observed subsets. Relaxing symmetry permits attractive as well as repulsive interactions. The authors impose a particular decomposition of the kernel that makes maximum likelihood learning tractable, then investigate the resulting method theoretically and experimentally. The decomposition is the mechanism that makes the richer model practical to fit.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show improved predictive performance relative to symmetric models that already perform strongly on those tasks. These results indicate that allowing attraction can improve modeling for some applications. The contribution combines additional expressive capacity with a learning procedure, so the benefit goes beyond merely defining a broader family of set distributions.
summary.tldr: A structured nonsymmetric kernel enables tractable learning of set models with both attractive and repulsive item interactions.

title: Learning Nonsymmetric Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Attention modules have been demonstrated effective in strengthening the representation ability of a neural network via reweighting spatial or channel features or stacking both operations sequentially. However, designing the structures of different attention operations requires a bulk of computation and extensive expertise. In this paper, we devise an Auto Learning Attention (AutoLA) method, which is the first attempt on automatic attention design. Specifically, we define a novel attention module named high order group attention (HOGA) as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where each group represents a node, and each edge represents an operation of heterogeneous attentions. A typical HOGA architecture can be searched automatically via the differential AutoLA method within 1 GPU day using the ResNet-20 backbone on CIFAR10. Further, the searched attention module can generalize to various backbones as a plug-and-play component and outperforms popular manually designed channel and spatial attentions for many vision tasks, including image classification on CIFAR100 and ImageNet, object detection and human keypoint detection on COCO dataset. The code will be released.

paragraphs: Attention modules strengthen visual networks by changing the emphasis placed on spatial locations or feature channels. Designing how these operations interact can demand substantial computation and expertise. Auto Learning Attention, or AutoLA, addresses that design problem by automatically searching for an attention module’s structure.

The authors introduce high order group attention, called HOGA, and represent it as a directed acyclic graph. Groups form the graph’s nodes, while connections represent different attention operations. A differentiable search method chooses an architecture within this representation. Using a ResNet-20 backbone on CIFAR10, the reported search for a typical HOGA module takes no more than one GPU day.

The resulting module can be inserted into different network backbones as a reusable component. Evaluations cover image classification on CIFAR100 and ImageNet, plus object detection and human keypoint detection on COCO. The searched module outperforms popular manually designed spatial and channel attention modules across the reported tasks. These findings support automatic attention design as a way to discover structures that remain useful beyond the original search setting.
summary.tldr: AutoLA automatically searches attention structures that transfer across network backbones and outperform popular handcrafted attention modules on several vision tasks.

title: Auto Learning Attention

abstract: Sample-based planning is a powerful family of algorithms for generating intelligent behavior from a model of the environment. Generating good candidate actions is critical to the success of sample-based planners, particularly in continuous or large action spaces. Typically, candidate action generation exhausts the action space, uses domain knowledge, or more recently, involves learning a stochastic policy to provide such search guidance. In this paper we explore explicitly learning a candidate action generator by optimizing a novel objective, marginal utility. The marginal utility of an action generator measures the increase in value of an action over previously generated actions. We validate our approach in both curling, a challenging stochastic domain with continuous state and action spaces, and a location game with a discrete but large action space. We show that a generator trained with the marginal utility objective outperforms hand-coded schemes built on substantial domain knowledge, trained stochastic policies, and other natural objectives for generating actions for sampled-based planners.

paragraphs: A sample-based planner evaluates candidate actions using a model of its environment. When actions are continuous or extremely numerous, deciding which candidates to consider becomes crucial. Exhaustive generation is difficult, while hand-designed rules and learned stochastic policies offer different ways to focus the planner’s search.

This paper trains the candidate generator using marginal utility: the improvement in action value relative to actions already generated. The objective makes a candidate’s usefulness depend on the alternatives already available to the planner. It therefore targets the value of adding an option to a planning process, giving the generator an objective directly connected to the quality of the candidate collection.

The authors evaluate the approach in curling, which has continuous states and actions and stochastic outcomes, and in a location game with a large discrete action space. In these evaluations, marginal-utility training outperforms domain-informed hand-coded generators, trained stochastic policies, and other natural generation objectives. These findings support explicitly learning how to contribute useful additional choices to a planner’s search.
summary.tldr: Training action generators for marginal improvement over existing candidates improves sample-based planning in two challenging action-space settings.

title: Marginal Utility for Planning in Continuous or Large Discrete Action Spaces

abstract: Many recent reinforcement learning (RL) methods learn stochastic policies with entropy regularization for exploration and robustness. However, in continuous action spaces, integrating entropy regularization with expressive policies is challenging and usually requires complex inference procedures. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel regularization method that is compatible with a broad range of expressive policy architectures. An appealing feature is that, the estimation of our regularization terms is simple and efficient even when the policy distributions are unknown. We show that our approach can effectively promote the exploration in continuous action spaces. Based on our regularization, we propose an off-policy actor-critic algorithm. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art regularized RL methods in continuous control tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning policies often use randomness to support exploration, with entropy regularization encouraging stochastic behavior. In continuous action spaces, however, computing or incorporating entropy can become difficult for expressive policy architectures. The paper targets this obstacle: how to encourage useful randomness without requiring complex inference procedures tied to the policy's distribution.

The authors propose a regularizer compatible with a broad range of expressive policies. Its terms can be estimated simply and efficiently even when the policy distributions are unknown. This property matters because it lets the learning procedure encourage stochasticity without needing the same distributional access that makes conventional entropy regularization challenging in these settings.

Using the regularizer, the paper constructs an off-policy actor–critic algorithm and shows that the approach can promote exploration in continuous action spaces. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art regularized reinforcement-learning methods on continuous-control tasks. These findings support the regularizer as a practical component for expressive policies, with the reported gains applying to the tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: An efficiently estimated regularizer promotes exploration with expressive continuous-action policies, including policies with unknown distributions.

title: Promoting Stochasticity for Expressive Policies via a Simple and Efficient Regularization Method

abstract: Visual processing in the retina has been studied in great detail at all levels such that a comprehensive picture of the retina's cell types and the many neural circuits they form is emerging. However, the currently best performing models of retinal function are black-box CNN models which are agnostic to such biological knowledge. In particular, these models typically neglect the role of the many inhibitory circuits involving amacrine cells and the biophysical mechanisms underlying synaptic release. Here, we present a computational model of temporal processing in the inner retina, including inhibitory feedback circuits and realistic synaptic release mechanisms. Fit to the responses of bipolar cells, the model generalized well to new stimuli including natural movie sequences, performing on par with or better than a benchmark black-box model. In pharmacology experiments, the model replicated in silico the effect of blocking specific amacrine cell populations with high fidelity, indicating that it had learned key circuit functions. Also, more in depth comparisons showed that connectivity patterns learned by the model were well matched to connectivity patterns extracted from connectomics data. Thus, our model provides a biologically interpretable data-driven account of temporal processing in the inner retina, filling the gap between purely black-box and detailed biophysical modeling.

It incorporates inhibitory feedback involving amacrine cells and realistic mechanisms for synaptic release. These biological structures are often absent from strong black-box CNN models, despite detailed knowledge of retinal cell types and circuits.

The researchers fit the model to bipolar-cell responses and test it on new stimuli, including natural movies. It generalizes well, matching or exceeding a benchmark black-box model. This shows that the incorporated biological structure can coexist with strong predictive performance in the evaluated temporal-processing tasks.

summary.tldr: A biologically constrained retinal model predicts new responses and reproduces intervention effects while learning connectivity consistent with anatomical data.

title: System Identification with Biophysical Constraints: A Circuit Model of the Inner Retina

abstract: We introduce a new theoretical framework to analyze deep learning optimization with connection to its generalization error. Existing frameworks such as mean field theory and neural tangent kernel theory for neural network optimization analysis typically require taking limit of infinite width of the network to show its global convergence. This potentially makes it difficult to directly deal with finite width network; especially in the neural tangent kernel regime, we cannot reveal favorable properties of neural networks {\it beyond kernel methods}. To realize more natural analysis, we consider a completely different approach in which we formulate the parameter training as a transportation map estimation and show its global convergence via the theory of the {\it infinite dimensional Langevin dynamics}. This enables us to analyze narrow and wide networks in a unifying manner. Moreover, we give generalization gap and excess risk bounds for the solution obtained by the dynamics. The excess risk bound achieves the so-called fast learning rate. In particular, we show an exponential convergence for a classification problem and a minimax optimal rate for a regression problem.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework linking neural-network optimization to generalization. The motivation is that common optimization analyses use infinite-width limits to establish global convergence, making finite-width networks harder to address directly. The authors seek a framework that can analyze both narrow and wide networks within the same mathematical treatment.

They formulate parameter training as estimation of a transportation map and analyze it through infinite-dimensional Langevin dynamics. Within this formulation, they establish global convergence. The infinite-dimensional dynamics provide the analytical machinery while the framework accommodates networks of different widths, avoiding a dependence on treating network width itself as infinite.

The analysis also bounds the generalization gap and excess risk of the solution produced by the dynamics. The excess-risk bound attains a fast learning rate. More specifically, the authors show exponential convergence for a classification problem and a minimax-optimal rate for a regression problem. These results connect successful optimization with statistical performance in the problems analyzed, extending the framework beyond convergence alone.
summary.tldr: A transportation-map formulation analyzes global convergence and generalization for narrow and wide networks through infinite-dimensional Langevin dynamics.

title: Generalization bound of globally optimal non-convex neural network training: Transportation map estimation by infinite dimensional Langevin dynamics

abstract: Unsupervised learning from continuous visual streams is a challenging problem that cannot be naturally and efficiently managed in the classic batch-mode setting of computation. The information stream must be carefully processed accordingly to an appropriate spatio-temporal distribution of the visual data, while most approaches of learning commonly assume uniform probability density. In this paper we focus on unsupervised learning for transferring visual information in a truly online setting by using a computational model that is inspired to the principle of least action in physics. The maximization of the mutual information is carried out by a temporal process which yields online estimation of the entropy terms. The model, which is based on second-order differential equations, maximizes the information transfer from the input to a discrete space of symbols related to the visual features of the input, whose computation is supported by hidden neurons. In order to better structure the input probability distribution, we use a human-like focus of attention model that, coherently with the information maximization model, is also based on second-order differential equations. We provide experimental results to support the theory by showing that the spatio-temporal filtering induced by the focus of attention allows the system to globally transfer more information from the input stream over the focused areas and, in some contexts, over the whole frames with respect to the unfiltered case that yields uniform probability distributions.

paragraphs: Learning from a continuous visual stream requires deciding how to process information across both space and time. The paper argues that treating visual input as uniformly distributed can overlook this structure. It develops an unsupervised online learning model that transfers information from incoming images into discrete symbols associated with visual features.

The learning process is inspired by the principle of least action and uses second-order differential equations. It maximizes mutual information through entropy estimates updated over time, with hidden neurons supporting feature computation. A human-like focus-of-attention model, also expressed through second-order differential equations, shapes the spatial and temporal distribution of the input.

Experiments support the claim that this attention-based filtering improves information transfer over the areas receiving attention compared with unfiltered, uniformly distributed input. In some tested contexts, the improvement extends to entire frames. The distinction matters: the reported benefit across whole images is conditional, while the broader approach connects where the model attends with how it learns from a continuing stream.
summary.tldr: An online visual-learning model uses attention to improve information transfer over focused regions and, in some contexts, whole frames.

title: Focus of Attention Improves Information Transfer in Visual Features

abstract: Deep learning has exhibited superior performance for various tasks, especially for high-dimensional datasets, such as images. To understand this property, we investigate the approximation and estimation ability of deep learning on {\it anisotropic Besov spaces}.The anisotropic Besov space is characterized by direction-dependent smoothness and includes several function classes that have been investigated thus far.We demonstrate that the approximation error and estimation error of deep learning only depend on the average value of the smoothness parameters in all directions. Consequently, the curse of dimensionality can be avoided if the smoothness of the target function is highly anisotropic.Unlike existing studies, our analysis does not require a low-dimensional structure of the input data.We also investigate the minimax optimality of deep learning and compare its performance with that of the kernel method (more generally, linear estimators).The results show that deep learning has better dependence on the input dimensionality if the target function possesses anisotropic smoothness, and it achieves an adaptive rate for functions with spatially inhomogeneous smoothness.

Consequently, the curse of dimensionality can be avoided if the smoothness of the target function is highly anisotropic.Unlike existing studies, our analysis does not require a low-dimensional structure of the input data.We also investigate the minimax optimality of deep learning and compare its performance with that of the kernel method (more generally, linear estimators).The results show that deep learning has better dependence on the input dimensionality if the target function possesses anisotropic smoothness, and it achieves an adaptive rate for functions with spatially inhomogeneous smoothness.

paragraphs: High-dimensional learning can be difficult because the amount of information needed often grows sharply with the number of inputs. This paper investigates a different source of effective simplicity: the target function may vary unevenly across directions. Some inputs can require detailed modelling while others have much smoother effects, even without low-dimensional structure in the data.

The analysis uses anisotropic Besov spaces, function classes that describe direction-dependent smoothness. The authors show that deep learning’s approximation and estimation errors depend on an average of the smoothness parameters across directions. Consequently, sufficiently strong anisotropy can allow the method to avoid the curse of dimensionality under the conditions studied.

The paper also examines minimax optimality and compares deep learning with kernel methods and, more broadly, linear estimators. Its results show better dependence on input dimensionality when the target has anisotropic smoothness, together with adaptive rates when smoothness varies across locations. The explanation for favourable learning behaviour therefore comes from the structure of the target function itself.
summary.tldr: Deep learning can adapt to uneven target-function smoothness, reducing dimensionality costs without assuming low-dimensional input data.

title: Deep learning is adaptive to intrinsic dimensionality of model smoothness in anisotropic Besov space

abstract: One of the main challenges in model-based reinforcement learning (RL) is to decide which aspects of the environment should be modeled. The value-equivalence (VE) principle proposes a simple answer to this question: a model should capture the aspects of the environment that are relevant for value-based planning. Technically, VE distinguishes models based on a set of policies and a set of functions: a model is said to be VE to the environment if the Bellman operators it induces for the policies yield the correct result when applied to the functions. As the number of policies and functions increase, the set of VE models shrinks, eventually collapsing to a single point corresponding to a perfect model. A fundamental question underlying the VE principle is thus how to select the smallest sets of policies and functions that are sufficient for planning. In this paper we take an important step towards answering this question. We start by generalizing the concept of VE to order-$k$ counterparts defined with respect to $k$ applications of the Bellman operator. This leads to a family of VE classes that increase in size as $k \rightarrow \infty$. In the limit, all functions become value functions, and we have a special instantiation of VE which we call proper VE or simply PVE. Unlike VE, the PVE class may contain multiple models even in the limit when all value functions are used. Crucially, all these models are sufficient for planning, meaning that they will yield an optimal policy despite the fact that they may ignore many aspects of the environment. We construct a loss function for learning PVE models and argue that popular algorithms such as MuZero can be understood as minimizing an upper bound for this loss. We leverage this connection to propose a modification to MuZero and show that it can lead to improved performance in practice.

However, adding more such requirements eventually forces an ordinary value-equivalent model to match the environment perfectly.

Those models can omit environmental details while remaining sufficient to produce an optimal policy.

They use this connection to propose a modification to MuZero that can improve practical performance. The theoretical contribution identifies a broader class of planning-sufficient models, while the algorithmic connection shows how that distinction can inform model learning.
summary.tldr: Proper value equivalence characterizes models that can ignore environmental details yet remain sufficient for optimal planning.

title: Proper Value Equivalence

abstract: Tractably modelling distributions over manifolds has long been an important goal in the natural sciences. Recent work has focused on developing general machine learning models to learn such distributions. However, for many applications these distributions must respect manifold symmetries—a trait which most previous models disregard. In this paper, we lay the theoretical foundations for learning symmetry-invariant distributions on arbitrary manifolds via equivariant manifold flows. We demonstrate the utility of our approach by learning quantum field theory-motivated invariant SU(n) densities and by correcting meteor impact dataset bias.

paragraphs: Many scientific distributions live on manifolds, spaces whose geometry differs from an ordinary unconstrained coordinate system. Learning a probability distribution on such a space requires accounting for that geometry. In some applications, the distribution must also respect symmetries: transformations of the space should leave the probability description unchanged.

This paper establishes theoretical foundations for learning symmetry-invariant distributions on arbitrary manifolds through equivariant manifold flows. Equivariance means the flow's transformations behave consistently with the relevant symmetries. The approach connects this behavior of the model to invariance of the distribution being learned, addressing a requirement that many earlier general models disregard.

The authors demonstrate the approach on invariant SU(n) densities motivated by quantum field theory and on correcting bias in a meteor impact dataset. These applications illustrate why symmetry is a modeling constraint with practical consequences, rather than merely a geometric detail. The contribution provides a foundation for incorporating such constraints into distribution learning, with demonstrations spanning a physics-motivated setting and observational data.
summary.tldr: Equivariant manifold flows provide a theoretical framework for learning distributions that respect both manifold geometry and required symmetries.

title: Equivariant Manifold Flows

abstract: Given a matrix $D$ describing the pairwise dissimilarities of a data set, a common task is to embed the data points into Euclidean space. The classical multidimensional scaling (cMDS) algorithm is a widespread method to do this. However, theoretical analysis of the robustness of the algorithm and an in-depth analysis of its performance on non-Euclidean metrics is lacking. In this paper, we derive a formula, based on the eigenvalues of a matrix obtained from $D$, for the Frobenius norm of the difference between $D$ and the metric $D_{\text{cmds}}$ returned by cMDS. This error analysis leads us to the conclusion that when the derived matrix has a significant number of negative eigenvalues, then $\|D-D_{\text{cmds}}\|_F$, after initially decreasing, willeventually increase as we increase the dimension. Hence, counterintuitively, the quality of the embedding degrades as we increase the dimension. We empirically verify that the Frobenius norm increases as we increase the dimension for a variety of non-Euclidean metrics. We also show on several benchmark datasets that this degradation in the embedding results in the classification accuracy of both simple (e.g., 1-nearest neighbor) and complex (e.g., multi-layer neural nets) classifiers decreasing as we increase the embedding dimension.Finally, our analysis leads us to a new efficiently computable algorithm that returns a matrix $D_l$ that is at least as close to the original distances as $D_t$ (the Euclidean metric closest in $\ell_2$ distance). While $D_l$ is not metric, when given as input to cMDS instead of $D$, it empirically results in solutions whose distance to $D$ does not increase when we increase the dimension and the classification accuracy degrades less than the cMDS solution.

paragraphs: Classical multidimensional scaling embeds data into Euclidean space from pairwise dissimilarities. This paper shows why adding embedding dimensions can sometimes make that representation worse. The authors derive a formula for the Frobenius error between the original dissimilarities and the distances produced by classical multidimensional scaling.

The formula depends on eigenvalues of a matrix derived from the input. When that matrix has a significant number of negative eigenvalues, error can initially decrease and then increase as dimensions are added. Experiments verify this behavior for several non-Euclidean metrics. On benchmark datasets, the resulting degradation also reduces classification accuracy for both nearest-neighbor and multilayer neural-network classifiers.

The analysis motivates an efficiently computed replacement matrix that is at least as close to the original distances as the closest Euclidean metric in the stated comparison. The replacement is itself not a metric. When used as input to classical multidimensional scaling, it empirically prevents distance error from increasing with dimension and reduces the degradation in classification accuracy.
summary.tldr: Classical multidimensional scaling can worsen as dimensions increase, and a derived preprocessing method empirically reduces this degradation.

title: How can classical multidimensional scaling go wrong?

abstract: Medical report generation, which aims to automatically generate a long and coherent report of a given medical image, has been receiving growing research interests. Existing approaches mainly adopt a supervised manner and heavily rely on coupled image-report pairs. However, in the medical domain, building a large-scale image-report paired dataset is both time-consuming and expensive. To relax the dependency on paired data, we propose an unsupervised model Knowledge Graph Auto-Encoder (KGAE) which accepts independent sets of images and reports in training. KGAE consists of a pre-constructed knowledge graph, a knowledge-driven encoder and a knowledge-driven decoder. The knowledge graph works as the shared latent space to bridge the visual and textual domains; The knowledge-driven encoder projects medical images and reports to the corresponding coordinates in this latent space and the knowledge-driven decoder generates a medical report given a coordinate in this space. Since the knowledge-driven encoder and decoder can be trained with independent sets of images and reports, KGAE is unsupervised. The experiments show that the unsupervised KGAE generates desirable medical reports without using any image-report training pairs. Moreover, KGAE can also work in both semi-supervised and supervised settings, and accept paired images and reports in training. By further fine-tuning with image-report pairs, KGAE consistently outperforms the current state-of-the-art models on two datasets.

paragraphs: Generating a medical report from an image usually requires training examples that pair each image with its corresponding report. Collecting those matched examples is expensive and time-consuming. This paper proposes Knowledge Graph Auto-Encoder, or KGAE, which can instead train on separate collections of medical images and reports.

The central device is a preconstructed knowledge graph that supplies a shared representation for visual and textual information. A knowledge-driven encoder maps an image or report to coordinates in that shared space. A knowledge-driven decoder then turns a coordinate into report text. This common space provides the bridge that paired examples would otherwise help establish.

The experiments report desirable generated reports without any image-report training pairs. KGAE also accepts paired data, allowing the same framework to operate in semi-supervised and supervised settings. After additional fine-tuning on matched images and reports, it consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art models on two datasets. The findings therefore support both learning without pairs and using pairs to improve an already trained system.
summary.tldr: KGAE uses a shared knowledge-graph representation to learn medical report generation from separate image and report collections.

title: Auto-Encoding Knowledge Graph for Unsupervised Medical Report Generation

abstract: Riemannian space forms, such as the Euclidean space, sphere and hyperbolic space, are popular and powerful representation spaces in machine learning. For instance, hyperbolic geometry is appropriate to represent graphs without cycles and has been used to extend Graph Neural Networks. Recently, some pseudo-Riemannian space forms that generalize both hyperbolic and spherical geometries have been exploited to learn a specific type of nonparametric embedding called ultrahyperbolic. The lack of geodesic between every pair of ultrahyperbolic points makes the task of learning parametric models (e.g., neural networks) difficult. This paper introduces a method to learn parametric models in ultrahyperbolic space. We experimentally show the relevance of our approach in the tasks of graph and node classification.

For instance, hyperbolic geometry is appropriate to represent graphs without cycles and has been used to extend Graph Neural Networks. Recently, some pseudo-Riemannian space forms that generalize both hyperbolic and spherical geometries have been exploited to learn a specific type of nonparametric embedding called ultrahyperbolic. The lack of geodesic between every pair of ultrahyperbolic points makes the task of learning parametric models (e.g., neural networks) difficult. This paper introduces a method to learn parametric models in ultrahyperbolic space. We experimentally show the relevance of our approach in the tasks of graph and node classification.

paragraphs: The geometry of a representation space affects which structures it can naturally describe. This paper considers ultrahyperbolic spaces, drawn from pseudo-Riemannian geometry and generalizing both hyperbolic and spherical geometries. Earlier work had used these spaces for a particular type of nonparametric embedding, motivating the question of how to learn parametric models there.

A central difficulty is that not every pair of ultrahyperbolic points is connected by a geodesic. This creates an obstacle for constructing neural networks in the space. The paper introduces a method for learning parametric ultrahyperbolic models, addressing the transition from learning individual embeddings to learning a model that operates within this geometry.

The authors evaluate their approach on graph classification and node classification, with experiments demonstrating its relevance to both tasks. The contribution expands the geometric settings available for neural representation learning. Its stated empirical result is that the method is useful in those classification settings; the abstract does not claim that ultrahyperbolic geometry is uniformly preferable to other representation spaces.
summary.tldr: The paper enables parametric neural models in ultrahyperbolic space and demonstrates their relevance to graph and node classification.

title: Ultrahyperbolic Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a method for object-aware 3D egocentric pose estimation that tightly integrates kinematics modeling, dynamics modeling, and scene object information. Unlike prior kinematics or dynamics-based approaches where the two components are used disjointly, we synergize the two approaches via dynamics-regulated training. At each timestep, a kinematic model is used to provide a target pose using video evidence and simulation state. Then, a prelearned dynamics model attempts to mimic the kinematic pose in a physics simulator. By comparing the pose instructed by the kinematic model against the pose generated by the dynamics model, we can use their misalignment to further improve the kinematic model. By factoring in the 6DoF pose of objects (e.g., chairs, boxes) in the scene, we demonstrate for the first time, the ability to estimate physically-plausible 3D human-object interactions using a single wearable camera. We evaluate our egocentric pose estimation method in both controlled laboratory settings and real-world scenarios.

At each timestep, a kinematic model is used to provide a target pose using video evidence and simulation state. Then, a prelearned dynamics model attempts to mimic the kinematic pose in a physics simulator. By comparing the pose instructed by the kinematic model against the pose generated by the dynamics model, we can use their misalignment to further improve the kinematic model. By factoring in the 6DoF pose of objects (e.g., chairs, boxes) in the scene, we demonstrate for the first time, the ability to estimate physically-plausible 3D human-object interactions using a single wearable camera. We evaluate our egocentric pose estimation method in both controlled laboratory settings and real-world scenarios.

paragraphs: Estimating a person's 3D pose from a wearable camera requires connecting visual evidence to plausible body motion. This paper combines kinematic pose prediction, dynamics modeling, and information about nearby objects. Its central idea is to let a physics-based model help train the model that proposes poses, linking the two components through direct feedback.

The authors demonstrate physically plausible human-object interaction estimates using a single wearable camera and evaluate the approach in both laboratory and real-world settings. The contribution is the tightly integrated training process that connects appearance, motion, and object context.
summary.tldr: Physics-simulation feedback trains a video-based pose predictor to estimate plausible human-object interactions from a wearable camera.

title: Dynamics-regulated kinematic policy for egocentric pose estimation

abstract: We study a constructive procedure that approximates Gateaux derivatives for statistical functionals by finite-differencing, with attention to causal inference functionals. We focus on the case where probability distributions are not known a priori but need also to be estimated from data, leading to empirical Gateaux derivatives, and study relationships between empirical, numerical, and analytical Gateaux derivatives. Starting with a case study of counterfactual mean estimation, we verify the exact relationship between finite-differences and the analytical Gateaux derivative. We then derive requirements on the rates of numerical approximation in perturbation and smoothing that preserve statistical benefits. We study more complicated functionals such as dynamic treatment regimes and the linear-programming formulation for policy optimization infinite-horizon Markov decision processes. In the case of the latter, this approach can be used to approximate bias adjustments in the presence of arbitrary constraints, illustrating the usefulness of constructive approaches for Gateaux derivatives. We find that, omitting unfavorable dimension dependence of smoothing, although rate-double robustness permits for coarser rates of perturbation size than implied by generic approximation analysis of finite-differences for the case of the counterfactual mean, this is not the case for the infinite-horizon MDP policy value.

paragraphs: A Gateaux derivative describes how a statistical quantity changes when its underlying probability distribution is perturbed. This paper studies a constructive way to approximate such derivatives using finite differences, with particular attention to causal inference. The complication is that the distribution itself must be estimated from data, so statistical estimation and numerical approximation interact.

Starting with counterfactual mean estimation, the authors establish the exact relationship between finite differences and the analytical derivative. They then derive requirements on perturbation and smoothing rates that preserve statistical benefits. The analysis extends to dynamic treatment regimes and policy optimization in infinite-horizon Markov decision processes. For the latter, the method can approximate bias adjustments even with arbitrary constraints.

The conclusions depend on the functional being estimated. Setting aside unfavorable dimension dependence from smoothing, rate-double robustness allows coarser perturbation rates for the counterfactual mean than generic finite-difference analysis suggests. The same benefit does not hold for infinite-horizon policy value. This distinction explains why a numerical derivative procedure needs statistical analysis tailored to its target rather than a single approximation rule applied everywhere.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes when finite-difference approximations to distributional derivatives preserve statistical benefits in causal inference.

title: Empirical Gateaux Derivatives for Causal Inference

abstract: This work offers a novel theoretical perspective on why, despite numerous attempts, adversarial approaches to generative modeling (e.g., GANs) have not been as successful for certain generation tasks, particularly sequential tasks such as Natural Language Generation, as they have in others, such as Computer Vision. In particular, on sequential data such as text, maximum-likelihood approaches are significantly more utilized than GANs. We show that, while it may seem that maximizing likelihood is inherently different than minimizing distinguishability, this distinction is largely an artifact of the limited representational capacity of the model family, for a wide class of adversarial objectives. We give a theoretical model in which minimizing KL-divergence (i.e., maximizing likelihood) is a more efficient approach to effectively minimizing the same distinguishability criteria that adversarial models seek to optimize. Reductions show that minimizing distinguishability can be seen as simply boosting likelihood for certain families of models including n-gram models and neural networks with a softmax output layer. To achieve a full polynomial-time reduction, a novel next-token distinguishability model is considered. Some preliminary empirical evidence is also provided to substantiate our theoretical analyses.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial models try to make generated data difficult to distinguish from real data, whereas likelihood-based models learn to assign high probability to observed examples. This paper investigates why likelihood methods have been more widely successful for sequential generation, especially text. It asks how different these two objectives really are when model capacity is taken into account.

For a broad class of adversarial objectives, the authors argue that much of the apparent distinction comes from the limited expressiveness of the model family. They develop a theoretical setting in which minimizing KL divergence, corresponding to maximizing likelihood, more efficiently reduces the distinguishability criteria targeted by adversarial training.

The analysis gives reductions relating distinguishability minimization to improving likelihood for model families including n-grams and neural networks with softmax outputs. A next-token distinguishability formulation enables a full polynomial-time reduction. Preliminary empirical evidence supports the theoretical account. These results offer a qualified explanation for likelihood training's effectiveness on sequential data, rather than establishing that adversarial modeling is unnecessary for every generation problem.
summary.tldr: The paper gives theoretical settings where likelihood training efficiently achieves distinguishability objectives associated with adversarial text generation.

title: Are GANs overkill for NLP?

abstract: Many data have an underlying dependence on spatial location; it may be weather on the Earth, a simulation on a mesh, or a registered image. Yet this feature is rarely taken advantage of, and violates common assumptions made by many neural network layers, such as translation equivariance. Further, many works that do incorporate locality fail to capture fine-grained structure. To address this, we introduce the Spatial Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) layer, a sparsely-gated layer that learns spatial structure in the input domain and routes experts at a fine-grained level to utilize it. We also develop new techniques to train SMoEs, including a self-supervised routing loss and damping expert errors. Finally, we show strong results for SMoEs on numerous tasks, and set new state-of-the-art results for medium-range weather prediction and post-processing ensemble weather forecasts.

paragraphs: For some data, location is part of the phenomenon being modeled. Weather, mesh-based simulations, and registered images can contain patterns whose significance depends on where they occur. The paper argues that common neural-network assumptions, including translation equivariance, can fail to reflect this dependence, while existing locality-aware approaches may miss fine detail.

Spatial Mixture-of-Experts introduces a sparsely gated layer that learns spatial structure and routes computation to experts at a fine-grained level. The routing mechanism lets the model use location-dependent structure in deciding which experts should handle the input. The authors also develop training techniques, including a self-supervised routing loss and damping of expert errors.

The method produces strong results across numerous tasks and achieves reported state-of-the-art performance for medium-range weather prediction and post-processing ensemble weather forecasts. These findings support making spatial specialization an explicit part of the network. The contribution includes both the layer that assigns experts according to learned spatial structure and techniques for training that layer effectively.
summary.tldr: Spatial Mixture-of-Experts learns fine-grained location-dependent routing and achieves strong results, including in weather forecasting.

title: Spatial Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Self-supervised learning of graph neural networks (GNNs) aims to learn an accurate representation of the graphs in an unsupervised manner, to obtain transferable representations of them for diverse downstream tasks. Predictive learning and contrastive learning are the two most prevalent approaches for graph self-supervised learning. However, they have their own drawbacks. While the predictive learning methods can learn the contextual relationships between neighboring nodes and edges, they cannot learn global graph-level similarities. Contrastive learning, while it can learn global graph-level similarities, its objective to maximize the similarity between two differently perturbed graphs may result in representations that cannot discriminate two similar graphs with different properties. To tackle such limitations, we propose a framework that aims to learn the exact discrepancy between the original and the perturbed graphs, coined as Discrepancy-based Self-supervised LeArning (D-SLA). Specifically, we create multiple perturbations of the given graph with varying degrees of similarity, and train the model to predict whether each graph is the original graph or the perturbed one. Moreover, we further aim to accurately capture the amount of discrepancy for each perturbed graph using the graph edit distance. We validate our D-SLA on various graph-related downstream tasks, including molecular property prediction, protein function prediction, and link prediction tasks, on which ours largely outperforms relevant baselines.

paragraphs: Graph self-supervised learning seeks useful representations without supervised labels. The paper identifies a tension between two common approaches: predictive learning captures local relationships but misses global similarities, while contrastive learning can push perturbed graphs too close together. That pressure may obscure differences between structurally similar graphs that have different properties.

D-SLA trains a model to recognize and measure changes to a graph. It creates several perturbations with different degrees of similarity and asks the model to distinguish original graphs from modified ones. It also uses graph edit distance to target the amount of discrepancy. The objective therefore emphasizes how much a graph has changed, alongside whether a change occurred.

The authors evaluate the learned representations on molecular property prediction, protein function prediction, and link prediction. They report that D-SLA largely outperforms relevant baselines across these tasks. The findings support learning discrepancies as a useful self-supervised signal: representations can capture graph-level relationships while retaining distinctions that may matter for subsequent predictions.
summary.tldr: D-SLA learns graph representations by distinguishing original graphs from perturbations and estimating how much each perturbation changes them.

title: Graph Self-supervised Learning with Accurate Discrepancy Learning

abstract: Modern neural networks often have great expressive power and can be trained to overfit the training data, while still achieving a good test performance. This phenomenon is referred to as “benign overfitting”. Recently, there emerges a line of works studying “benign overfitting” from the theoretical perspective. However, they are limited to linear models or kernel/random feature models, and there is still a lack of theoretical understanding about when and how benign overfitting occurs in neural networks. In this paper, we study the benign overfitting phenomenon in training a two-layer convolutional neural network (CNN). We show that when the signal-to-noise ratio satisfies a certain condition, a two-layer CNN trained by gradient descent can achieve arbitrarily small training and test loss. On the other hand, when this condition does not hold, overfitting becomes harmful and the obtained CNN can only achieve a constant level test loss. These together demonstrate a sharp phase transition between benign overfitting and harmful overfitting, driven by the signal-to-noise ratio. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that precisely characterizes the conditions under which benign overfitting can occur in training convolutional neural networks.
