paragraphs: Explaining a Vision Transformer often means identifying important input tokens, influential modules, or the features it represents. Transformer Doctor instead investigates how internal information integration can produce errors. Its starting point is a hypothesis inspired by information integration and conjunctive errors in biological vision.

The hypothesis distinguishes dynamic integration between tokens from static integration within a token. The authors present experimental evidence for both forms of integration and for associated conjunctive errors. This provides a framework for diagnosing mistakes in terms of how information is combined, extending analysis beyond identifying which components contribute to a prediction.

The treatment follows the same distinction. Heuristic constraints address dynamic integration, while rule-based constraints address static integration. Quantitative and qualitative experiments show that these interventions can correct internal errors and improve model performance. The paper's contribution is the full connection from a proposed account of error formation to interventions aimed at those errors, with experimental support for the hypothesis rather than a claim that it exhaustively explains Transformer behavior.
summary.tldr: Transformer Doctor diagnoses information-integration errors in Vision Transformers and applies targeted constraints that improve performance.

title: Transformer Doctor: Diagnosing and Treating Vision Transformers

abstract: This paper is motivated by an interesting phenomenon: the performance of object detection lags behind that of instance segmentation (i.e., performance imbalance) when investigating the intermediate results from the beginning transformer decoder layer of MaskDINO (i.e., the SOTA model for joint detection and segmentation). This phenomenon inspires us to think about a question: will the performance imbalance at the beginning layer of transformer decoder constrain the upper bound of the final performance? With this question in mind, we further conduct qualitative and quantitative pre-experiments, which validate the negative impact of detection-segmentation imbalance issue on the model performance. To address this issue, this paper proposes DI-MaskDINO model, the core idea of which is to improve the final performance by alleviating the detection-segmentation imbalance. DI-MaskDINO is implemented by configuring our proposed De-Imbalance (DI) module and Balance-Aware Tokens Optimization (BATO) module to MaskDINO. DI is responsible for generating balance-aware query, and BATO uses the balance-aware query to guide the optimization of the initial feature tokens. The balance-aware query and optimized feature tokens are respectively taken as the Query and Key&Value of transformer decoder to perform joint object detection and instance segmentation. DI-MaskDINO outperforms existing joint object detection and instance segmentation models on COCO and BDD100K benchmarks, achieving +1.2 $AP^{box}$ and +0.9 $AP^{mask}$ improvements compared to SOTA joint detection and segmentation model MaskDINO. In addition, DI-MaskDINO also obtains +1.0 $AP^{box}$ improvement compared to SOTA object detection model DINO and +3.0 $AP^{mask}$ improvement compared to SOTA segmentation model Mask2Former.

Their preliminary qualitative and quantitative experiments indicate that this imbalance negatively affects the model's eventual results, motivating an intervention at the beginning of decoding.

Balance-Aware Tokens Optimization then uses this query to improve the initial feature tokens. Comparisons with specialist models also show gains of 1.0 box AP over DINO and 3.0 mask AP over Mask2Former. The findings support improving early task balance as a route to better final predictions.
summary.tldr: DI-MaskDINO improves joint detection and segmentation by correcting an early imbalance between the two tasks in MaskDINO's decoder.

title: DI-MaskDINO: A Joint Object Detection and Instance Segmentation Model

abstract: 3D generation guided by text-to-image diffusion models enables the creation of visually compelling assets. However previous methods explore generation based on image or text. The boundaries of creativity are limited by what can be expressed through words or the images that can be sourced. We present YouDream, a method to generate high-quality anatomically controllable animals. YouDream is guided using a text-to-image diffusion model controlled by 2D views of a 3D pose prior. Our method is capable of generating novel imaginary animals that previous text-to-3D generative methods are unable to create. Additionally, our method can preserve anatomic consistency in the generated animals, an area where prior approaches often struggle. Moreover, we design a fully automated pipeline for generating commonly observed animals. To circumvent the need for human intervention to create a 3D pose, we propose a multi-agent LLM that adapts poses from a limited library of animal 3D poses to represent the desired animal. A user study conducted on the outcomes of YouDream demonstrates the preference of the animal models generated by our method over others. Visualizations and code are available at https://youdream3d.github.io/.

YouDream adds explicit anatomical control for animal generation through a 3D pose prior. The authors report that this approach can create novel imaginary animals beyond the capabilities of previous text-to-3D methods. It can also preserve anatomical consistency, a difficulty for earlier approaches. The pose prior supplies a structural basis for the desired animal while diffusion guidance contributes to the generated asset's visual appearance.

A multi-agent language-model system adapts poses from a limited library of animal poses, avoiding the need for a person to construct the 3D pose. A user study finds a preference for YouDream's generated animals over the compared alternatives. The work combines controllable generation with automation for more familiar animal forms.
summary.tldr: YouDream uses 3D pose guidance to generate anatomically controllable animals and automates pose adaptation for common animals.

title: YouDream: Generating Anatomically Controllable Consistent Text-to-3D Animals

abstract: The increasing size of language models necessitates a thorough analysis across multiple dimensions to assess trade-offs among crucial hardware metrics such as latency, energy consumption, GPU memory usage, and performance. Identifying optimal model configurations under specific hardware constraints is becoming essential but remains challenging due to the computational load of exhaustive training and evaluation on multiple devices. To address this, we introduce HW-GPT-Bench, a hardware-aware benchmark that utilizes surrogate predictions to approximate various hardware metrics across 13 devices of architectures in the GPT-2 family, with architectures containing up to 1.55B parameters. Our surrogates, via calibrated predictions and reliable uncertainty estimates, faithfully model the heteroscedastic noise inherent in the energy and latency measurements. To estimate perplexity, we employ weight-sharing techniques from Neural Architecture Search (NAS), inheriting pretrained weights from the largest GPT-2 model. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of HW-GPT-Bench by simulating optimization trajectories of various multi-objective optimization algorithms in just a few seconds.

paragraphs: Choosing a language-model architecture involves trade-offs among predictive performance, latency, energy consumption, and GPU memory. Measuring every candidate on multiple devices would require substantial training and evaluation work. HW-GPT-Bench provides a way to explore these choices through predictions of hardware behavior for GPT-2-family architectures containing up to 1.55 billion parameters.

The benchmark uses surrogate models to approximate hardware metrics across 13 devices. Their calibrated predictions include uncertainty estimates and account for measurement noise whose magnitude varies, particularly in latency and energy measurements. To estimate perplexity, the benchmark uses weight sharing from neural architecture search, drawing pretrained weights from the largest GPT-2 model.

The authors demonstrate that the benchmark can simulate the progress of several multi-objective optimization algorithms within seconds. This makes it useful for studying how architecture search balances competing requirements under hardware constraints. Its contribution is a fast evaluation framework grounded in predicted hardware behavior and shared model weights, enabling broader exploration without exhaustively training and measuring every candidate.
summary.tldr: HW-GPT-Bench combines hardware surrogates and shared weights to rapidly study language-model architecture trade-offs across 13 devices.

title: HW-GPT-Bench: Hardware-Aware Architecture Benchmark for Language Models

abstract: Recently, a wide range of memory-efficient LLM training algorithms have gained substantial popularity. These methods leverage the low-rank structure of gradients to project optimizer states into a subspace using projection matrix found by singular value decomposition (SVD). However, convergence of these algorithms is highly dependent on the update rules of their projection matrix. In this work, we provide the \emph{first} convergence guarantee for arbitrary update rules of projection matrix. This guarantee is generally applicable to optimizers that can be analyzed with Hamiltonian Descent, including most common ones, such as LION, Adam. Inspired by our theoretical understanding, we propose Online Subspace Descent, a new family of subspace descent optimizer without SVD. Instead of updating projection matrix with eigenvectors, Online Subspace Descent updates projection matrix wtih online PCA. Online Subspace Descent is flexible and introduces only minimum overhead to training. We demonstrate that, for the task of pretraining LLaMA models ranging from 60M to 1B parameters on the C4 dataset, Online Subspace Descent achieves lower perplexity than state-of-the-art low-rank training methods across different settings and narrows the gap with full-rank baselines.

paragraphs: Memory-efficient language-model training can reduce optimizer storage by projecting it into a lower-dimensional subspace. Existing approaches often obtain the projection through singular value decomposition, but their convergence depends strongly on how that projection changes. This paper studies the theoretical consequences of updating the subspace during training.

The authors provide a convergence guarantee that accommodates arbitrary projection-matrix update rules within their analysis. It applies to optimizers that can be studied through Hamiltonian Descent, including common methods such as Adam and LION. Motivated by this result, they introduce Online Subspace Descent, which updates the projection using online principal component analysis instead of singular value decomposition and adds minimal training overhead.

The experiments pretrain LLaMA models ranging from 60 million to one billion parameters on C4. Across different tested settings, Online Subspace Descent achieves lower perplexity than leading low-rank training methods and moves closer to full-rank baselines. The findings connect a more flexible theoretical treatment of changing subspaces with a practical method for improving the quality of memory-efficient training.
summary.tldr: Online Subspace Descent updates training subspaces with online PCA, backed by convergence analysis and improved low-rank language-model training results.

title: Memory-Efficient LLM Training with Online Subspace Descent

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating a structured multivariate density, subject to Markov conditions implied by an undirected graph. In the worst case, without Markovian assumptions, this problem suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Our main result shows how the curse of dimensionality can be avoided or greatly alleviated under the Markov property, and applies to arbitrary graphs. While existing results along these lines focus on sparsity or manifold assumptions, we introduce a new graphical quantity called ``graph resilience'' and show that it dictates the optimal sample complexity. Surprisingly, although one might expect the sample complexity of this problem to scale with local graph parameters such as the degree, this turns out not to be the case. Through explicit examples, we compute uniform deviation bounds and illustrate how the curse of dimensionality in density estimation can thus be circumvented. Notable examples where the rate improves substantially include sequential, hierarchical, and spatial data.

paragraphs: Estimating a joint probability density becomes difficult as the number of variables grows. Without structural assumptions, the required data can suffer from the curse of dimensionality. This paper studies densities whose conditional independence relationships obey the Markov conditions of an undirected graph, using that structure to characterize the difficulty of estimation.

The central contribution is a graph quantity called graph resilience. The authors show that it determines the optimal sample complexity of the structured estimation problem, with results applying to arbitrary graphs. This differs from an explanation based only on sparsity, manifold structure, or local graph properties. In particular, quantities such as node degree do not by themselves describe the relevant sample-complexity behavior.

The paper derives uniform deviation bounds for explicit examples and shows how graph structure can avoid or substantially lessen dimensionality-related difficulty. Sequential, hierarchical, and spatial data provide notable cases with improved rates. The result ties the possible statistical benefit to the assumed Markov structure rather than promising the same improvement for every high-dimensional distribution.
summary.tldr: Graph resilience characterizes optimal sample complexity for graph-structured density estimation and explains when dimensionality-related difficulty can be reduced.

title: Breaking the curse of dimensionality in structured density estimation

abstract: One of the central goals of neuroscience is to gain a mechanistic understanding of how the dynamics of neural circuits give rise to their observed function. A popular approach towards this end is to train recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to reproduce experimental recordings of neural activity. These trained RNNs are then treated as surrogate models of biological neural circuits, whose properties can be dissected via dynamical systems analysis. How reliable are the mechanistic insights derived from this procedure? While recent advances in population-level recording technologies have allowed simultaneous recording of up to tens of thousands of neurons, this represents only a tiny fraction of most cortical circuits. Here we show that observing only a subset of neurons in a circuit can create mechanistic mismatches between a simulated teacher network and a data-constrained student, even when the two networks have matching single-unit dynamics. In particular, we show that partial observation of models of low-dimensional cortical dynamics based on functionally feedforward or low-rank connectivity can lead to surrogate models with spurious attractor structure. In total, our results illustrate the challenges inherent in accurately uncovering neural mechanisms from single-trial data, and suggest the need for new methods of validating data-constrained models for neural dynamics.
originalAbstract: One of the central goals of neuroscience is to gain a mechanistic understanding of how the dynamics of neural circuits give rise to their observed function. A popular approach towards this end is to train recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to reproduce experimental recordings of neural activity. These trained RNNs are then treated as surrogate models of biological neural circuits, whose properties can be dissected via dynamical systems analysis. How reliable are the mechanistic insights derived from this procedure? While recent advances in population-level recording technologies have allowed simultaneous recording of up to tens of thousands of neurons, this represents only a tiny fraction of most cortical circuits. Here we show that observing only a subset of neurons in a circuit can create mechanistic mismatches between a simulated teacher network and a data-constrained student, even when the two networks have matching single-unit dynamics. In particular, we show that partial observation of models of low-dimensional cortical dynamics based on functionally feedforward or low-rank connectivity can lead to surrogate models with spurious attractor structure. In total, our results illustrate the challenges inherent in accurately uncovering neural mechanisms from single-trial data, and suggest the need for new methods of validating data-constrained models for neural dynamics.

paragraphs: Neuroscientists sometimes train recurrent neural networks to reproduce recorded neural activity and then analyze those networks to infer how a biological circuit works. This paper examines the reliability of that procedure when recordings cover only part of a circuit. Even large recordings can represent a small fraction of the neurons in the system of interest.

The authors study simulated teacher networks and student networks fitted to their observed activity. They show that partial observation can produce a student with different underlying mechanisms even when individual-unit dynamics match. In particular, partially observed systems with functionally feedforward or low-rank connectivity can yield fitted models containing spurious attractor structure.

An attractor inferred from the student can therefore suggest a dynamical explanation that does not faithfully describe the teacher. The result establishes that agreement with observed activity can coexist with mechanistic mismatch in these settings. It highlights the challenge of recovering neural mechanisms from single-trial data and motivates additional ways of validating data-constrained dynamical models before using their internal structure to explain neural computation.
summary.tldr: Fitting partially observed neural activity can produce recurrent models with spurious attractors despite matching individual-unit dynamics.

title: Partial observation can induce mechanistic mismatches in data-constrained models of neural dynamics

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is essential for model trustworthiness which aims to sensitively identity semantic OOD samples and robustly generalize for covariate-shifted OOD samples. However, we discover that the superior OOD detection performance of state-of-the-art methods is achieved by secretly sacrificing the OOD generalization ability. The classification accuracy frequently collapses catastrophically when even slight noise is encountered. Such a phenomenon violates the motivation of trustworthiness and significantly limits the model's deployment in the real world. What is the hidden reason behind such a limitation? In this work, we theoretically demystify the "\textit{sensitive-robust}" dilemma that lies in previous OOD detection methods. Consequently, a theory-inspired algorithm is induced to overcome such a dilemma. By decoupling the uncertainty learning objective from a Bayesian perspective, the conflict between OOD detection and OOD generalization is naturally harmonized and a dual-optimized performance could be expected. Empirical studies show that our method achieves superior performance on commonly used benchmarks. To our best knowledge, this work is the first principled OOD detection method that achieves state-of-the-art OOD detection performance without sacrificing OOD generalization ability. Our code is available at https://github.com/QingyangZhang/DUL.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection must distinguish two different kinds of change. A model should recognize inputs with unfamiliar semantic content, while still classifying familiar content when its appearance is altered by changes such as noise. The paper finds that strong detection results in existing methods can come at the expense of this second ability.

The authors report that classification accuracy can collapse even under slight noise and develop a theoretical account of the resulting sensitivity-versus-robustness dilemma. Their proposed algorithm follows from this analysis. It separates the uncertainty-learning objective from a Bayesian perspective, aiming to resolve the conflict between detecting semantic novelty and generalizing under changes in input conditions.

Experiments on commonly used benchmarks show superior performance, with state-of-the-art detection achieved without sacrificing generalization in the reported evaluations. The contribution is therefore a joint treatment of two requirements that should both support trustworthiness. Its findings argue for evaluating whether a detector preserves useful classification under shifts, alongside how well it identifies unfamiliar semantic inputs. The empirical success supports the proposed decoupling as a way to improve both.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian decoupling of uncertainty learning improves detection of unfamiliar inputs while preserving generalization under input shifts in benchmark evaluations.

title: The Best of Both Worlds: On the Dilemma of Out-of-distribution Detection

abstract: We study convex resource allocation problems with $m$ hard constraints under $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-joint differential privacy (Joint-DP or JDP) in an offline setting. To approximately solve the problem, we propose a generic algorithm called Noisy Dual Mirror Descent. The algorithm applies noisy Mirror Descent to a dual problem from relaxing the hard constraints for private shadow prices, and then uses the shadow prices to coordinate allocations in the primal problem. Leveraging weak duality theory, we show that the optimality gap is upper bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sqrt{m\ln(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon})$, and constraint violation is no more than $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sqrt{m\ln(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon})$ per constraint. When strong duality holds, both preceding results can be improved to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon})$ by better utilizing the geometric structure of the dual space, which is neglected by existing works. To complement our results under strong duality, we derive a minimax lower bound $\Omega(\frac{m}{\varepsilon})$ for any JDP algorithm outputting feasible allocations. The lower bound matches our upper bounds up to some logarithmic factors for $\varepsilon\geq \max(1, 1/(n\gamma))$, where $n\gamma$ is the available resource level. Numerical studies further confirm the effectiveness of our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies offline convex resource allocation under joint differential privacy with m hard constraints. The task is to produce useful allocations while satisfying a privacy requirement and controlling departures from the resource constraints. Its proposed algorithm, Noisy Dual Mirror Descent, coordinates allocations through privately computed shadow prices.

The algorithm relaxes the constraints to form a dual problem, applies noisy mirror descent to obtain prices, and uses those prices in the original allocation problem. Under weak duality, both the optimality gap and the violation per constraint are bounded at order √(m ln(1/δ))/ε. Under strong duality, exploiting the dual space’s geometry improves both bounds to order √ln(1/δ)/ε, up to logarithmic factors.

They report matching upper and lower bounds up to logarithmic factors when ε ≥ max(1, 1/(nγ)), where nγ is the available resource level. Numerical studies support the algorithm’s effectiveness. The stronger guarantees therefore depend on explicit duality and parameter conditions.
summary.tldr: Noisy Dual Mirror Descent uses private shadow prices for resource allocation, with stronger near-optimal guarantees under stated conditions.

title: Noisy Dual Mirror Descent: A Near Optimal Algorithm for Jointly-DP Convex Resource Allocation

abstract: Mobile devices such as smartphones, laptops, and tablets can often connect to multiple access networks (e.g., Wi-Fi, LTE, and 5G) simultaneously.Recent advancements facilitate seamless integration of these connections below the transport layer, enhancing the experience for apps that lack inherent multi-path support.This optimization hinges on dynamically determining the traffic distribution across networks for each device, a process referred to as multi-access traffic splitting.This paper introduces NetworkGym, a high-fidelity network environment simulator that facilitates generating multiple network traffic flows and multi-access traffic splitting.This simulator facilitates training and evaluating different RL-based solutions for the multi-access traffic splitting problem.Our initial explorations demonstrate that the majority of existing state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms (e.g. CQL) fail to outperform certain hand-crafted heuristic policies on average.This illustrates the urgent need to evaluate offline RL algorithms against a broader range of benchmarks, rather than relying solely on popular ones such as D4RL.We also propose an extension to the TD3+BC algorithm, named Pessimistic TD3 (PTD3), and demonstrate that it outperforms many state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms.PTD3's behavioral constraint mechanism, which relies on value-function pessimism, is theoretically motivated and relatively simple to implement.We open source our code and offline datasets at github.com/hmomin/networkgym.

paragraphs: Devices can maintain connections to multiple networks, such as Wi-Fi and cellular services, at the same time. Making useful joint use of those connections requires deciding how to distribute each device's traffic as conditions change. NetworkGym provides a high-fidelity simulation environment for training and evaluating reinforcement-learning solutions to this traffic-splitting problem.

The simulator supports multiple traffic flows and splitting across access networks. Initial evaluations find that most tested state-of-the-art offline reinforcement-learning algorithms, including CQL, do not outperform certain handcrafted heuristics on average. This result motivates broader evaluation beyond familiar benchmarks: success elsewhere does not establish that an algorithm will handle this networking task well.

The paper also introduces Pessimistic TD3, an extension of TD3+BC that uses value-function pessimism as a behavioral constraint. The mechanism has theoretical motivation and is described as relatively simple to implement. It outperforms many evaluated offline reinforcement-learning methods. Together, the simulator, offline datasets, and algorithm provide a concrete setting for studying where offline learning succeeds or struggles in network traffic management.
summary.tldr: NetworkGym benchmarks multi-network traffic splitting and introduces a pessimistic offline learning method that outperforms many tested alternatives.

title: NetworkGym: Reinforcement Learning Environments for Multi-Access Traffic Management in Network Simulation

abstract: Multi-object 3D Grounding involves locating 3D boxes based on a given query phrase from a point cloud. It is a challenging and significant task that has numerous applications in visual understanding, human-computer interaction, and robotics. To tackle this challenge, we introduce D-LISA, a two-stage approach that incorporates three innovations. First, a dynamic vision module that enables a variable and learnable number of box proposals. Second, a dynamic camera positioning that extracts features for each proposal. Third, a language-informed spatial attention module that better reasons over the proposals to output the final prediction. Empirically, experiments show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on multi-object 3D grounding by 12.8% (absolute) and is competitive in single-object 3D grounding.

paragraphs: Multi-object 3D grounding means finding the objects described by a phrase within a point cloud and returning their three-dimensional boxes. The task connects language to spatial scene understanding and is relevant to interaction and robotics. D-LISA addresses it with a two-stage approach that makes both candidate construction and reasoning more adaptable.

Three components define the method. A dynamic vision module learns a variable number of proposed boxes. Dynamic camera positioning extracts features for each proposal. A language-informed spatial attention module then reasons over the proposals to produce the final prediction. Together, these components connect candidate locations, their extracted visual features, and the wording used to identify the desired objects.

Experiments report a 12.8% absolute improvement over state-of-the-art methods on multi-object grounding, while remaining competitive on single-object grounding. The result supports the combined approach for locating multiple language-specified objects. It also indicates that the method's emphasis on multiple candidates can coexist with useful performance when a query concerns only one object.
summary.tldr: D-LISA improves multi-object 3D grounding through adaptive box proposals, dynamic feature extraction, and language-guided spatial reasoning.

title: Multi-Object 3D Grounding with Dynamic Modules and Language-Informed Spatial Attention

abstract: Though vision transformers (ViTs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of settings, they exhibit surprising failures when performing tasks involving visual relations. This begs the question: how do ViTs attempt to perform tasks that require computing visual relations between objects? Prior efforts to interpret ViTs tend to focus on characterizing relevant low-level visual features. In contrast, we adopt methods from mechanistic interpretability to study the higher-level visual algorithms that ViTs use to perform abstract visual reasoning. We present a case study of a fundamental, yet surprisingly difficult, relational reasoning task: judging whether two visual entities are the same or different. We find that pretrained ViTs fine-tuned on this task often exhibit two qualitatively different stages of processing despite having no obvious inductive biases to do so: 1) a perceptual stage wherein local object features are extracted and stored in a disentangled representation, and 2) a relational stage wherein object representations are compared. In the second stage, we find evidence that ViTs can learn to represent somewhat abstract visual relations, a capability that has long been considered out of reach for artificial neural networks. Finally, we demonstrate that failures at either stage can prevent a model from learning a generalizable solution to our fairly simple tasks. By understanding ViTs in terms of discrete processing stages, one can more precisely diagnose and rectify shortcomings of existing and future models.

paragraphs: This paper studies how vision transformers decide whether two visual entities are the same or different. The result provides a more precise diagnostic picture: a failed relational judgment can reflect problems forming object representations, problems comparing them, or both.
summary.tldr: Vision transformers fine-tuned on same-or-different tasks often separate object perception from relational comparison, revealing distinct sources of generalization failure.

title: Beyond the Doors of Perception: Vision Transformers Represent Relations Between Objects

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable generalization and instruction-following capabilities with instruction tuning. The advancements in LLMs and instruction tuning have led to the development of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). However, the competency of the LLMs and instruction tuning have been less explored in the molecular domain. Thus, we propose LLaMo: Large Language Model-based Molecular graph assistant, which is an end-to- end trained large molecular graph-language model. To bridge the discrepancy between the language and graph modalities, we present the multi-level graph projector that transforms graph representations into graph tokens by abstracting the output representations of each GNN layer and motif representations with the cross-attention mechanism. We also introduce machine-generated molecular graph instruction data to instruction-tune the large molecular graph-language model for general-purpose molecule and language understanding. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that LLaMo shows the best performance on diverse tasks, such as molecular description generation, property prediction, and IUPAC name prediction. The code of LLaMo is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/LLaMo.

paragraphs: Instruction-tuned language models have broad text capabilities, but molecular graphs require representations that do not naturally match ordinary language tokens. LLaMo is an end-to-end molecular graph-language assistant designed to connect those modalities.

A multilevel graph projector gathers representations from different graph-neural-network layers and molecular motifs, using cross-attention to form graph tokens. Machine-generated molecular instructions then support tuning for molecule-related language and prediction tasks.

Experiments report the best performance among the evaluated methods on molecular description generation, property prediction, and IUPAC-name prediction. The abstract does not provide scores or assess laboratory validation of generated claims. The contribution is a graph-to-language architecture plus instruction data and task evaluations, rather than evidence that the assistant can reliably determine every chemical property or replace experimental characterization.
summary.tldr: LLaMo connects molecular graphs to language-model instruction following through multilevel graph tokens.

title: LLaMo: Large Language Model-based Molecular Graph Assistant

abstract: Outputs from large language models (LLMs) are often rated as highly original yet show low variability (or greater homogeneity) compared to human responses, a pattern we refer to as the *LLM creativity paradox*. Yet, prior work suggests that assessments of originality and variability may reflect stylistic features of LLM outputs rather than underlying conceptual novelty. The goal of the present study was to investigate this issue using outputs from seven distinct LLMs on a modified Alternative Uses Task. We scored verbatim and "humanized" LLM responses—reworded to reduce verbosity but maintain core ideas—using four automated metrics (supervised OCSAI and CLAUS models, and two unsupervised semantic-distance tools) and compared them with responses from 30 human participants. As expected, verbatim LLM responses were rated as substantially more original than human responses (median $d = 1.46$) but showed markedly lower variability (median $d = 0.85$). Humanizing the responses strongly decreased originality and weakly increased variability, indicating that part of the LLM creativity paradox is driven by stylistic cues. Nevertheless, even after humanization, originality scores of LLM responses remained higher (median $d = 0.80$) and their variability lower ($d = 0.57$) than those of human responses. These findings suggest that automated assessment tools can be partially misled by the style of LLM outputs, highlighting the need for caution when using automated methods to evaluate machine-generated ideas, particularly in real-world applications such as providing feedback or guiding creative workflows.

paragraphs: This study asks whether automated creativity assessments respond to ideas themselves or to the way language models express them. It investigates a recurring pattern: model responses receive high originality scores while varying less than human responses. The authors call this combination the LLM creativity paradox.

The researchers collected responses from seven language models on a modified Alternative Uses Task and compared them with responses from thirty people. Four automated tools scored both the original model outputs and versions rewritten to reduce verbosity while preserving their central ideas. This comparison tests how changing presentation affects assessments without intentionally changing the proposed concepts.

Rewording substantially reduced originality scores and slightly increased variability. However, the rewritten model responses still scored as more original and less variable than human responses. Style therefore explains part of the measured paradox, rather than eliminating it. The findings support caution when automated scores inform creative feedback: a change in wording can alter the assessment even when the underlying idea remains.
summary.tldr: Automated creativity scores partly reward language-model writing style, although differences from human responses persist after rewording.

title: AI is Misled by GenAI: Stylistic Bias in Automated Assessment of Creativity in Large Language Models

abstract: The lack of fine-grained, large-scale datasets on water availability presents a critical barrier to applying machine learning (ML) for agricultural water management. Since there are multiple natural and anthropogenic factors that influence water availability, incorporating diverse multimodal features can significantly improve modeling performance. However, integrating such heterogeneous data is challenging due to spatial misalignments, inconsistent formats, semantic label ambiguities, and class imbalances. To address these challenges, we introduce IRRISIGHT, a large-scale, multimodal dataset spanning 20 U.S. states. It consists of 1.4 million pixel-aligned 224×224 patches that fuse satellite imagery with rich environmental attributes. We develop a robust geospatial fusion pipeline that aligns raster, vector, and point-based data on a unified 10m grid, and employ domain-informed structured prompts to convert tabular attributes into natural language. With irrigation type classification as a representative problem, the dataset is AI-ready, offering a spatially disjoint train/test split and extensive benchmarking with both vision and vision–language models. Our results demonstrate that multimodal representations substantially improve model performance, establishing a foundation for future research on water availability.https://github.com/Nibir088/IRRISIGHThttps://huggingface.co/datasets/OBH30/IRRISIGHT

paragraphs: IRRISIGHT addresses the shortage of detailed, large-scale data for studying agricultural water availability. Water conditions depend on natural factors and human activity, so satellite images alone need not capture all relevant information. Combining sources is difficult because geographic alignment, data formats, labels, and class frequencies can differ.

The dataset contains 1.4 million aligned image patches, each 224 by 224 pixels, spanning 20 U.S. states. Its processing pipeline brings raster, vector, and point data onto a shared 10-meter grid and combines satellite imagery with environmental attributes. Structured prompts informed by domain knowledge also turn tabular attributes into natural-language descriptions, supporting models that process both images and text.

The authors use irrigation-type classification as a representative task and benchmark vision and vision–language models. Training and test regions are spatially separate, making geographic separation part of the evaluation design. The results show substantial performance improvements from multimodal representations. The contribution combines a reusable data resource with a scalable alignment pipeline, creating a foundation for further machine-learning research on water availability.
summary.tldr: IRRISIGHT combines satellite imagery and environmental data at scale, with irrigation benchmarks showing benefits from multimodal inputs.

title: IRRISIGHT: A Large-Scale Multimodal Dataset and Scalable Pipeline to Address Irrigation and Water Management in Agriculture

abstract: Discrete diffusion models enable parallel token sampling for faster inference than autoregressive approaches. However, prior diffusion models use a decoder-only architecture, which requires sampling algorithms that invoke the full network at every denoising step and incur high computational cost. Our key insight is that discrete diffusion models perform two types of computation: 1) representing clean tokens and 2) denoising corrupted tokens, which enables us to use separate modules for each task. We propose an encoder-decoder architecture to accelerate discrete diffusion inference, which relies on an encoder to represent clean tokens and a lightweight decoder to iteratively refine a noised sequence. We also show that this architecture enables faster training of block diffusion models, which partition sequences into blocks for better quality and are commonly used in diffusion language model inference. We introduce a framework for **E**fficient **E**ncoder-**D**ecoder **D**iffusion (E2D2), consisting of an architecture with specialized training and sampling algorithms, and we show that E2D2 achieves superior trade-offs between generation quality and inference throughput on summarization, translation, and mathematical reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but repeated denoising can still be computationally expensive. Earlier decoder-only designs invoke the entire network at each denoising step. This paper identifies two distinct jobs inside that computation: representing clean tokens and refining tokens that remain corrupted.

E2D2 separates those jobs into an encoder and a lightweight decoder. The encoder represents clean tokens, while the smaller decoder repeatedly improves the noisy sequence. The framework includes training and sampling algorithms specialized for this architecture. Its central efficiency idea is to assign iterative refinement to a lighter component instead of repeatedly using the full network.

The authors also show that the architecture accelerates training for block diffusion models, which divide sequences into blocks to improve quality. Evaluations cover summarization, translation, and mathematical reasoning, where E2D2 achieves better trade-offs between generation quality and inference throughput. The contribution is therefore both architectural and procedural: separating computation enables more efficient generation and training while maintaining a competitive relationship between speed and output quality.
summary.tldr: E2D2 separates clean-token encoding from lightweight iterative denoising to improve diffusion language models' training efficiency and quality–throughput trade-offs.

title: Encoder-Decoder Diffusion Language Models for Efficient Training and Inference

abstract: Recent work on large language models has demonstrated the use of model-free reinforcement learning (RL) to train reasoning-like capabilities. The emergence of "thinking" through model-free RL is interesting as thinking actions neither produce reward nor change the external world state to one where the agent is more likely to get reward. This paper seeks to build a domain-independent understanding of when model-free RL will lead to such "thinking" as a strategy for reward maximization. To build this understanding, we first introduce a theoretical model which we call a thought Markov decision process (MDP). Thought MDPs minimally extend the classical MDP model to include an abstract notion of thought state and thought action. Using the thought MDP model, we prove the importance of policy initialization in determining whether or not thinking emerges and show formally that thought actions are equivalent to the agent choosing to perform a step of policy improvement before continuing to act. We then show that open-source LLMs satisfy the conditions that our theory predicts are necessary for model-free RL to produce thinking-like behavior. Finally, we hypothesize sufficient conditions that would enable thinking to be learned outside of language generation and introduce a toy domain where a combination of multi-task pre-training and designated thought actions enable more data-efficient RL compared to non-thinking agents.

paragraphs: This paper asks when model-free reinforcement learning can produce useful thinking behavior. The puzzle is that thought actions do not directly earn rewards or change the external world into a more rewarding state. To study this, the authors introduce thought Markov decision processes, which extend ordinary MDPs with internal thought states and actions.

Within that framework, they prove that policy initialization matters for whether thinking emerges. They also show that taking a thought action is equivalent to choosing a policy-improvement step before continuing to act. This gives internal computation a formal role in reward maximization, even though it has no direct external effect.

The authors find that open-source language models satisfy conditions their theory identifies as necessary for model-free learning to produce thinking-like behavior. They separately hypothesize sufficient conditions for learning thinking outside language generation. In a toy domain, multi-task pretraining combined with designated thought actions improves reinforcement-learning data efficiency over non-thinking agents. These results distinguish theoretical necessities, proposed sufficient conditions, and empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: Thought MDPs explain how initialization can enable model-free reinforcement learning to learn internal actions that improve subsequent decisions.

title: When Can Model-Free Reinforcement Learning be Enough for Thinking?

abstract: Recent interest in building foundation models for knowledge graphs has highlighted a fundamental challenge: knowledge graph data is scarce. The best-known knowl- edge graphs are primarily human-labeled, created by pattern-matching, or extracted using early NLP techniques. While human-generated knowledge graphs are in short supply, automatically extracted ones are of questionable quality. We present KGGen, a novel text-to-knowledge-graph generator that uses language models to extract high-quality graphs from plain text with a novel entity resolution approach that clusters related entities, significantly reducing the sparsity problem that plagues existing extractors. Unlike other KG generators, KGGen clusters and de-duplicates related entities to reduce sparsity in extracted KGs. Along with KGGen, we release Measure of Information in Nodes and Edges (MINE), the first benchmark to test an extractor’s ability to produce a useful KG from plain text. We benchmark our new tool against leading existing generators such as Microsoft’s GraphRAG; we achieve comparable retrieval accuracy on the generated graphs and better information re- tention. Moreover, our graphs exhibit more concise and generalizable entities and relations. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/stair-lab/kg-gen/.

paragraphs: Knowledge-graph modeling faces a data problem: manually produced graphs are scarce, while automatically extracted graphs can have questionable quality. KGGen uses language models to convert plain text into knowledge graphs. Its main focus is making the extracted entities and relationships useful together, rather than leaving a sparse collection of fragmented references.

The method introduces an entity-resolution approach that clusters related entities and removes duplicates. Consolidating these references significantly reduces sparsity in the resulting graphs. The authors also introduce MINE, the Measure of Information in Nodes and Edges, as a benchmark for evaluating whether a text extractor produces a useful knowledge graph.

Comparisons with leading generators, including Microsoft’s GraphRAG, show comparable retrieval accuracy and better retention of information. The authors also report more concise and generalizable entities and relations. These findings distinguish several aspects of graph quality: retrieving information successfully, preserving the source’s information, and organizing it compactly. KGGen’s contribution is to improve that organization through entity consolidation while maintaining retrieval performance.
summary.tldr: KGGen consolidates related entities in language-model-extracted knowledge graphs, improving information retention while maintaining comparable retrieval accuracy.

title: KGGen: Extracting Knowledge Graphs from Plain Text with Language Models

abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have focused on integrating multiple modalities, yet their ability to simultaneously process and reason across different inputs remains underexplored. We introduce OmniBench, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate models’ ability to recognize, interpret, and reason across visual, acoustic, and textual inputs simultaneously. We define language models capable of such tri-modal processing as omni-language models (OLMs). OmniBench features high-quality human annotations that require integrated understanding across all modalities. Our evaluation reveals that: i) open-source OLMs show significant limitations in instruction-following and reasoning in tri-modal contexts; and ii) most baseline models perform poorly (below 50% accuracy) even with textual alternatives to image/audio inputs. To address these limitations, we develop OmniInstruct, an 96K-sample instruction tuning dataset for training OLMs. We advocate for developing more robust tri-modal integration techniques and training strategies to enhance OLM performance. Codes and data could be found at https://m-a-p.ai/OmniBench/.

paragraphs: OmniBench evaluates models that must understand visual, acoustic, and textual inputs together. The paper calls systems capable of this three-modality processing omni-language models. Its central question is whether models can combine information across all three inputs to recognize content, interpret it, and reason about it.

The benchmark uses human annotations that require integrated understanding across the modalities. Evaluations reveal substantial instruction-following and reasoning limitations in the tested open-source models. Most baseline models score below 50% accuracy even when textual alternatives replace image or audio inputs. This finding suggests that, in this evaluation, providing information in text does not by itself resolve the difficulty.

The authors also create OmniInstruct, an instruction-tuning dataset containing 96,000 samples intended to train omni-language models. Together, the evaluation and training resources support work on stronger multimodal integration and training strategies. The reported results establish shortcomings in existing models; the abstract presents OmniInstruct as a resource for addressing them without claiming a specific measured improvement from its use.
summary.tldr: OmniBench tests joint image, audio, and text reasoning, revealing major model weaknesses and supplying a complementary instruction-tuning dataset.

title: OmniBench: Towards The Future of Universal Omni-Language Models

abstract: Generating high-fidelity, differentially private (DP) synthetic images offers a promising route to share and analyze sensitive visual data without compromising individual privacy. However, existing DP image synthesis methods struggle to produce high-resolution outputs that faithfully capture the structure of the original data. In this paper, we introduce a novel method, referred to as Synthesis via Private Textual Intermediaries (SPTI), that can generate high-resolution DP images with easy adoptions. The key idea is to shift the challenge of DP image synthesis from the image domain to the text domain by leveraging state-of-the-art DP text generation methods. SPTI first summarizes each private image into a concise textual description using image-to-text models, then applies a modified Private Evolution algorithm to generate DP text, and finally reconstructs images using text-to-image models. Notably, SPTI requires no model training, only inferences with off-the-shelf models. Given a private dataset, SPTI produces synthetic images of substantially higher quality than prior DP approaches. On the LSUN Bedroom dataset, SPTI attains an FID $=$ 26.71 under $\epsilon=1.0$, improving over Private Evolution’s FID of 40.36. Similarly, on MM-CelebA-HQ, SPTI achieves an FID $=$ 33.27 at $\epsilon=1.0$, compared to 57.01 from DP fine-tuning baselines. Overall, our results demonstrate that Synthesis via Private Textual Intermediaries provides a resource-efficient and proprietary-model-compatible framework for generating high-resolution DP synthetic images, greatly expanding access to private visual datasets. Our code release: https://github.com/MarkGodrick/SPTI

paragraphs: SPTI generates differentially private synthetic images by moving the privacy-sensitive synthesis stage into text. The motivation is that existing private image generation methods struggle to produce high-resolution outputs that preserve the structure of the source data. Text descriptions offer an intermediate representation through which established private text generation methods can be applied.

The pipeline first captions each private image with an image-to-text model. A modified Private Evolution algorithm then generates differentially private text, and a text-to-image model converts that text into synthetic images. The method requires only inference with existing models, without model training, making it resource-efficient and compatible with proprietary models.

The reported quality improvements are substantial at ε = 1.0. On LSUN Bedroom, SPTI achieves FID 26.71 compared with 40.36 for Private Evolution. On MM-CelebA-HQ, it achieves 33.27 compared with 57.01 for private fine-tuning baselines. These findings support the textual intermediary as a practical route to higher-quality private image synthesis without training a new image generator.
summary.tldr: SPTI turns private images into differentially private text and then synthetic images, improving image quality without model training.

title: Synthesize Privacy-Preserving High-Resolution Images via Private Textual Intermediaries

abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) measure neural activity non-invasively by capturing electromagnetic fields generated by dendritic currents. Although rooted in the same biophysics, EEG and MEG exhibit distinct signal patterns, further complicated by variations in sensor configurations across modalities and recording devices. Existing approaches typically rely on separate, modality- and dataset-specific models, which limits the performance and cross-domain scalability. This paper proposes BrainOmni, the first brain foundation model that generalises across heterogeneous EEG and MEG recordings. To unify diverse data sources, we introduce BrainTokenizer, the first tokeniser that quantises spatiotemporal brain activity into discrete representations. Central to BrainTokenizer is a novel Sensor Encoder that encodes sensor properties such as spatial layout, orientation, and type, enabling compatibility across devices and modalities. Building upon the discrete representations, BrainOmni learns unified semantic embeddings of brain signals by self-supervised pretraining. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first foundation model to support both EEG and MEG signals, as well as the first to incorporate large-scale MEG pretraining. A total of 1,997 hours of EEG and 656 hours of MEG data are curated and standardised from publicly available sources for pretraining. Experiments show that BrainOmni outperforms both existing foundation models and state-of-the-art task-specific models on a range of downstream tasks. It also demonstrates strong generalisation to unseen EEG and MEG devices. Further analysis reveals that joint EEG-MEG (EMEG) training yields consistent improvements across both modalities. Code and checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/OpenTSLab/BrainOmni

paragraphs: BrainOmni aims to learn a shared representation of EEG and MEG recordings. Both measure neural activity through electromagnetic signals, but their recorded patterns differ, and devices use different sensor configurations. These differences make it difficult to reuse models across recording systems when training is tied to a particular modality or dataset.

The proposed BrainTokenizer converts brain activity across space and time into discrete representations. Its Sensor Encoder explicitly represents sensor layout, orientation, and type, helping accommodate differences between devices and measurement modalities. BrainOmni then uses self-supervised pretraining on these representations to learn unified embeddings. The curated training collection contains 1,997 hours of EEG and 656 hours of MEG from public sources.

Experiments report better performance than existing foundation models and leading task-specific models across several downstream tasks. BrainOmni also generalizes strongly to previously unseen EEG and MEG devices. Joint training on both modalities consistently improves results for each, supporting the value of sharing information across these related measurements while explicitly accounting for how they were recorded.
summary.tldr: BrainOmni unifies EEG and MEG learning through sensor-aware tokenization and joint pretraining, improving downstream performance and generalization to unseen devices.

title: BrainOmni: A Brain Foundation Model for Unified EEG and MEG Signals

abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) commonly relies on adaptive optimizers such as Adam (Kingma & Ba 2015), which accelerate convergence through moment estimates but incur substantial memory overhead. Recent stateless approaches such as SWAN (Ma et al., 2024) have shown that appropriate preprocessing of instantaneous gradient matrices can match the performance of adaptive methods without storing optimizer states. Building on this insight, we introduce \emph{gradient multi-normalization}, a principled framework for designing stateless optimizers that normalize gradients with respect to multiple norms simultaneously. Whereas standard first-order methods can be viewed as gradient normalization under a single norm (Bernstein & Newhouse, 2024), our formulation generalizes this perspective to a multi-norm setting. We derive an efficient alternating scheme that enforces these normalization constraints and show that our procedure can produce, up to an arbitrary precision, a fixed-point of the problem. This unifies and extends prior stateless optimizers, showing that SWAN arises as a specific instance with particular norm choices. Leveraging this principle, we develop SinkGD, a lightweight matrix optimizer that retains the memory footprint of SGD while substantially reducing computation relative to whitening-based methods. On the memory-efficient LLaMA training benchmark (Zhao et al., 2024), SinkGD achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching the same evaluation perplexity as Adam using only 40\% of the training tokens.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam accelerate language-model training by retaining estimates from past gradients, but those stored states consume memory. This paper develops a framework for stateless optimization that instead preprocesses the current gradient. Its central idea is to normalize gradient matrices according to multiple norms simultaneously, extending a perspective that describes standard first-order methods through a single norm.

The authors derive an efficient alternating procedure for enforcing the normalization constraints and show that it can approach a fixed point to arbitrary precision. Their framework includes SWAN as a particular choice of norms, linking an existing stateless optimizer to a broader design principle. They then use that principle to construct a matrix optimizer called SinkGD.

SinkGD retains SGD's memory footprint and reduces computation relative to whitening-based methods. On the reported memory-efficient LLaMA training benchmark, it reaches Adam's evaluation perplexity using 40% of the training tokens and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The finding demonstrates that, in this benchmark, carefully transforming current gradients can combine low optimizer memory with efficient learning.
summary.tldr: SinkGD uses multiple gradient normalizations to achieve low-memory LLM training, matching Adam's perplexity with 40% of the tokens on the reported benchmark.

title: Gradient Multi-Normalization for Efficient LLM Training

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become integral to a wide range of applications worldwide, driving an unprecedented global demand for effective multilingual capabilities. Central to achieving robust multilingual performance is the strategic allocation of language proportions within training corpora. However, determining optimal language ratios is highly challenging due to intricate cross-lingual interactions and sensitivity to dataset scale. This paper introduces CLIMB (Cross-Lingual Interaction-aware Multilingual Balancing), a novel framework designed to systematically optimize multilingual data allocation. At its core, CLIMB introduces a cross-lingual interaction-aware language ratio, explicitly quantifying each language’s effective allocation by capturing inter-language dependencies. Leveraging this ratio, CLIMB proposes a principled two-step optimization procedure—first equalizing marginal benefits across languages, then maximizing the magnitude of the resulting language allocation vectors—significantly simplifying the inherently complex multilingual optimization problem. Extensive experiments confirm that CLIMB can accurately measure cross-lingual interactions across various multilingual settings. LLMs trained with CLIMB-derived proportions consistently achieve state-of-the-art multilingual performance, even achieve competitive performance with open-sourced LLMs trained with more tokens.

paragraphs: Multilingual language-model training requires choosing how much data to allocate to each language. This is difficult because languages interact during learning, and useful proportions depend on the scale of the dataset. CLIMB approaches allocation by explicitly accounting for those interactions when measuring how much training support each language effectively receives.

Its central quantity is an interaction-aware language ratio that incorporates dependencies between languages. The framework then uses a two-step optimization procedure: it first equalizes marginal benefits across languages, then maximizes the magnitude of the resulting allocation vectors. This structure makes a complicated joint allocation problem more manageable while keeping cross-language effects within the calculation.

Experiments show that CLIMB can accurately measure interactions in multiple multilingual settings. Models trained with its chosen proportions consistently achieve state-of-the-art multilingual performance in the reported evaluations and are competitive with open-source models trained on more tokens. The findings suggest that carefully selecting the language mixture can improve the value of a training corpus, alongside decisions about its overall size.
summary.tldr: CLIMB optimizes multilingual training proportions by modeling cross-language interactions and balancing the benefits of additional data.

title: Exploring Polyglot Harmony: On Multilingual Data Allocation for Large Language Models Pretraining

abstract: Multimodal representation learning is critical for a wide range of applications, such as multimodal sentiment analysis. Current multimodal representation learning methods mainly focus on the multimodal alignment or fusion strategies, such that the complementary and consistent information among heterogeneous modalities can be fully explored. However, they mistakenly treat the uncertainty noise within each modality as the complementary information, failing to simultaneously leverage both consistent and complementary information while eliminating the aleatoric uncertainty within each modality. To address this issue, we propose a plug-and-play feature causality decomposition method for multimodal representation learning from causality perspective, which can be integrated into existing models with no affects on the original model structures. Specifically, to deal with the heterogeneity and consistency, according to whether it can be aligned with other modalities, the unimodal feature is first disentangled into two parts: modality-invariant (the synergistic information shared by all heterogeneous modalities) and modality-specific part. To deal with complementarity and uncertainty, the modality-specific part is further decomposed into unique and redundant features, where the redundant feature is removed and the unique feature is reserved based on the backdoor-adjustment. The effectiveness of noise removal is supported by causality theory. Finally, the task-related information, including both synergistic and unique components, is further fed to the original fusion module to obtain the final multimodal representations. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our proposed strategies.

paragraphs: Combining multiple modalities requires preserving both shared information and useful information unique to each source. The paper identifies a problem with existing alignment and fusion approaches: they can mistake noise within a modality for complementary information. Its proposed feature decomposition aims to separate these roles before the original model combines the inputs.

First, each modality’s representation is divided according to whether its features can align with other modalities. This produces a shared, modality-invariant component and a modality-specific component. The latter is then separated into unique and redundant features using backdoor adjustment, a causal method. The redundant component is removed while the unique component is retained.

The shared and unique features are passed into the existing fusion module, allowing the method to be integrated without changing the original model structures. The authors provide causal-theoretical support for noise removal and report effectiveness in extensive experiments. The central contribution is a structured way to preserve agreement and complementarity together while addressing uncertainty within individual modalities.
summary.tldr: A causal feature decomposition separates shared information, useful modality-specific information, and redundant noise before multimodal fusion.

title: Plug-and-play Feature Causality Decomposition for Multimodal Representation Learning

abstract: In this paper, we introduce BMMR, a large-scale bilingual, multimodal, multi-disciplinary reasoning dataset for the community to develop and evaluate large multimodal models (LMMs). BMMR comprises 100k university-level questions drawn from 300 UNESCO-defined subjects, spanning diverse formats—multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and open-ended QA—and sourced from both print and digital media such as books, exams, and quizzes. All data are curated and filtered via a human-in-the-loop, automated, and scalable framework, and each instance is paired with a high-quality reasoning path. The dataset is organized into two parts: BMMR-Eval that comprises 20k high-quality instances to comprehensively assess LMMs’ knowledge and reasoning across multiple disciplines in both Chinese and English; and BMMR-Train that contains 80k instances to support further research and development, extending the current focus on mathematical reasoning to diverse disciplines and domains. In addition, we propose the process-based multi-discipline BMMR-Verifier for accurate and fine-grained evaluation of LMMs’ reasoning. Extensive experiments reveal that (i) even SOTA models leave substantial headroom on BMMR-Eval; (ii) reasoning models exhibit discipline bias and outperform LMMs only on specific subjects; (iii) open-source models still trail their proprietary counterparts; and (iv) fine-tuning on BMMR-Train narrows this gap. Additionally, we conduct reasoning-chain analyses using BMMR-Verifier and other in-depth studies, uncovering the challenges LMMs currently face in multidisciplinary reasoning. We will release the data and models, and we believe our work can offers valuable insights and contributions to the community.

It contains 100,000 university-level questions across 300 UNESCO-defined subjects, with Chinese and English coverage. Questions come from sources including books, examinations, and quizzes, and use multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and open-ended formats. Each instance includes a curated reasoning path.

Its evaluation portion contains 20,000 instances, while 80,000 training instances support model development across disciplines. The authors also introduce BMMR-Verifier, which evaluates reasoning processes at a finer level. This adds a way to examine reasoning chains alongside the broader assessment of knowledge and answers.

Experiments find substantial room for improvement even among leading models. Reasoning models outperform other large multimodal models only in particular subjects, revealing uneven strengths across disciplines. Open-source models trail proprietary models in the reported evaluations, but fine-tuning on BMMR-Train narrows that gap. Together, these findings show why multidisciplinary evaluation matters: success in selected subjects does not establish equally strong reasoning across the full dataset.
summary.tldr: BMMR provides bilingual training and evaluation data that reveal uneven multimodal reasoning ability across academic disciplines.

title: BMMR: A Large-Scale Bilingual Multimodal Multi-Discipline Reasoning Dataset

abstract: We investigate various stochastic bandit problems in the presence of adversarial corruptions. A seminal work for this problem is the BARBAR~\cite{gupta2019better} algorithm, which achieves both robustness and efficiency. However, it suffers from a regret of $O(KC)$, which does not match the lower bound of $\Omega(C)$, where $K$ denotes the number of arms and $C$ denotes the corruption level. In this paper, we first improve the BARBAR algorithm by proposing a novel framework called BARBAT, which eliminates the factor of $K$ to achieve an optimal regret bound up to a logarithmic factor. We also extend BARBAT to various settings, including multi-agent bandits, graph bandits, combinatorial semi-bandits and batched bandits. Compared with the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader framework, our methods are more amenable to parallelization, making them suitable for multi-agent and batched bandit settings, and they incur lower computational costs, particularly in semi-bandit problems. Numerical experiments verify the efficiency of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision-making problems where a learner repeatedly chooses among options with uncertain rewards, while an adversary can corrupt some observations. The goal is to keep regret—the cost of learning compared with choosing well—small despite this interference. An existing method, BARBAR, has a corruption-related regret term that grows with both the number of options and the corruption level.

The proposed framework, BARBAT, removes the factor associated with the number of options. Its regret guarantee matches the optimal bound up to a logarithmic factor. This matters because increasing the number of available choices no longer carries the same multiplicative penalty in that corruption-related term.

The authors also extend the framework to multi-agent, graph, combinatorial semi-bandit, and batched settings. They report easier parallelization than the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader framework and lower computational costs, especially for semi-bandits. Numerical experiments support the methods’ efficiency, complementing the theoretical contribution with evidence that the framework can be useful across several decision-making arrangements.
summary.tldr: BARBAT improves corruption-robust bandit guarantees while supporting efficient computation and parallelization across several bandit settings.

title: A Near-optimal, Scalable and Parallelizable Framework for Stochastic Bandits Robust to Adversarial Corruptions and Beyond

abstract: We rethink test-time scaling laws from a practical efficiency perspective, revealing that the effectiveness of smaller models is significantly overestimated. Prior work, grounded in compute-optimality, overlooks critical memory access bottlenecks introduced by inference-time strategies (e.g., Best-of-N, long CoTs). Our holistic analysis, spanning models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, reveals a new Kinetics Scaling Law that better guides resource allocation by incorporating both computation and memory access costs. The Kinetics Scaling Law suggests that test-time compute is more effective when used on models above a threshold (14B) than on smaller ones. A key reason is that in test-time scaling, attention—rather than parameter count—emerges as the dominant cost factor. Motivated by this, we propose a new scaling paradigm centered on sparse attention, which lowers per-token cost and enables longer generations and more parallel samples within the same resource budget. Empirically, we show that sparse attention models consistently outperform dense counterparts, achieving over 60-point gains in low-cost regimes and over 5-point gains in high-cost regimes for problem-solving accuracy on AIME and LiveCodeBench. These results suggest that sparse attention is essential for realizing the full potential of test-time scaling because, unlike training where parameter scaling saturates, test-time accuracy continues to improve through increased generation.

summary.tldr: Kinetics incorporates memory-access costs into test-time scaling and finds substantial efficiency and accuracy benefits from sparse attention.

title: Kinetics: Rethinking Test-Time Scaling Law

abstract: AI-powered attacks on Learning with Errors (LWE)—an important hard math problem in post-quantum cryptography—rival or outperform "classical" attacks on LWE under certain parameter settings. Despite the promise of this approach, a dearth of accessible data limits AI practitioners' ability to study and improve these attacks. Creating LWE data for AI model training is time- and compute-intensive and requires significant domain expertise. To fill this gap and accelerate AI research on LWE attacks, we propose the TAPAS datasets, a ${\bf t}$oolkit for ${\bf a}$nalysis of ${\bf p}$ost-quantum cryptography using ${\bf A}$I ${\bf s}$ystems. These datasets cover several LWE settings and can be used off-the-shelf by AI practitioners to prototype new approaches to cracking LWE. This work documents TAPAS dataset creation, establishes attack performance baselines, and lays out directions for future work.

paragraphs: Learning with Errors is a mathematical problem important to post-quantum cryptography. Under certain parameter settings, AI-based attacks already rival or outperform classical approaches. Studying those methods is difficult for many AI researchers because generating suitable training data requires substantial computation, time, and specialist knowledge. TAPAS addresses that access barrier through ready-to-use datasets.

The datasets cover several Learning with Errors settings and are intended for prototyping new AI approaches to the problem. The paper documents how the data was created, establishes attack-performance baselines, and identifies directions for further research. These components give researchers both material for training and reference results for evaluating new approaches.

The contribution is research infrastructure for investigating AI-based cryptanalysis, rather than a claim that post-quantum cryptography is generally broken. The motivating comparison with classical attacks is explicitly restricted to certain parameter settings. By making data available off the shelf, TAPAS enables AI practitioners to investigate those settings without first reproducing the demanding data-generation process themselves.
summary.tldr: TAPAS provides ready-to-use datasets and baselines for studying AI attacks on several Learning with Errors settings.

title: TAPAS: Datasets for Learning the Learning with Errors Problem

abstract: We propose efficient methods for solving stochastic simple bilevel optimization problems with convex inner levels, where the goal is to minimize an outer stochastic objective function subject to the solution set of an inner stochastic optimization problem. Existing methods often rely on costly projection or linear optimization oracles over complex sets, limiting their scalability. To overcome this, we propose an iteratively regularized conditional gradient approach that leverages linear optimization oracles exclusively over the base feasible set. Our proposed methods employ a vanishing regularization sequence that progressively emphasizes the inner problem while biasing towards desirable minimal outer objective solutions. In the one-sample stochastic setting and under standard convexity assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic convergence rates of $O(t^{-1/4})$ for both the outer and inner objectives. In the finite-sum setting with a mini-batch scheme, the corresponding rates become $O(t^{-1/2})$. When the outer objective is nonconvex, we prove non-asymptotic convergence rates of $O(t^{-1/7})$ for both the outer and inner objectives in the one-sample stochastic setting, and $O(t^{-1/4})$ in the finite-sum setting. Experimental results on over-parametrized regression and dictionary learning tasks demonstrate the practical advantages of our approach over existing methods, confirming our theoretical findings.
