paragraphs: Simple bilevel optimization seeks a solution that minimizes an outer objective while also solving an inner optimization problem. Even with a convex inner problem, working directly with its solution set can require costly projection or linear optimization operations. This paper develops stochastic methods that only need linear optimization over the original feasible set.

The approach uses conditional gradients with a regularization schedule that shrinks over time. As optimization progresses, the schedule places increasing emphasis on satisfying the inner problem while still favoring solutions with desirable outer objective values. This provides a way to pursue the two objectives without repeatedly invoking optimization routines over a more complicated derived set.

Under the stated convexity assumptions, the authors prove finite-iteration rates of O(t^(-1/4)) for both objectives with one stochastic sample, and O(t^(-1/2)) with finite sums and mini-batches. For a nonconvex outer objective, the corresponding reported rates are O(t^(-1/7)) and O(t^(-1/4)). Experiments on over-parameterized regression and dictionary learning demonstrate practical advantages over existing methods, complementing the convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: Regularized conditional-gradient methods solve stochastic bilevel problems using simpler linear optimization operations while retaining provable convergence rates.

title: Conditional Gradient Methods with Standard LMO for Stochastic Simple Bilevel Optimization

abstract: Conditional generative modeling aims to learn a conditional data distribution from samples containing data-condition pairs. For this, diffusion and flow-based methods have attained compelling results. These methods use a learned (flow) model to transport an initial standard Gaussian noise that ignores the condition to the conditional data distribution. The model is hence required to learn both mass transport \emph{and} conditional injection. To ease the demand on the model, we propose \emph{Condition-Aware Reparameterization for Flow Matching} (CAR-Flow) -- a lightweight, learned \emph{shift} that conditions the source, the target, or both distributions. By relocating these distributions, CAR-Flow shortens the probability path the model must learn, leading to faster training in practice. On low-dimensional synthetic data, we visualize and quantify the effects of CAR-Flow. On higher-dimensional natural image data (ImageNet-256), equipping SiT-XL/2 with CAR-Flow reduces FID from 2.07 to 1.68, while introducing less than \(0.6\%\) additional parameters.

paragraphs: Conditional flow models learn to transform random noise into data matching a supplied condition. Typically, the starting noise distribution ignores that condition. The same learned model therefore has to handle both moving probability mass toward the data and introducing the information that distinguishes one condition from another.

CAR-Flow reduces this burden with a small learned shift that depends on the condition. It can relocate the source distribution, the target distribution, or both before the flow learns the transformation between them. The resulting probability path is shorter, and the authors report faster training in practice. Synthetic examples let them visualize and measure how this relocation changes the transport problem.

On ImageNet-256, adding CAR-Flow to SiT-XL/2 lowers the reported FID from 2.07 to 1.68 while adding less than 0.6% to the parameter count. This result shows that a lightweight change to how the learning problem is parameterized can improve image generation. The contribution centers on making the conditional transport task easier for the main model.
summary.tldr: CAR-Flow uses small condition-dependent shifts to simplify flow matching, improving training speed and reported image-generation quality.

title: CAR-Flow: Condition-Aware Reparameterization Aligns Source and Target for Better Flow Matching

abstract: World models represent a promising approach for training reinforcement learning agents with significantly improved sample efficiency. While most world model methods primarily rely on sequences of discrete latent variables to model environment dynamics, this compression often neglects critical visual details essential for reinforcement learning. Recent diffusion-based world models condition generation on a fixed context length of frames to predict the next observation, using separate recurrent neural networks to model rewards and termination signals. Although this architecture effectively enhances visual fidelity, the fixed context length approach inherently limits memory capacity. In this paper, we introduce EDELINE, a unified world model architecture that integrates state space models with diffusion models. Our approach outperforms existing baselines across visually challenging Atari 100k tasks, memory-demanding Crafter benchmark, and 3D first-person ViZDoom environments, demonstrating superior performance in all these diverse challenges. Code is available at https://github.com/LJH-coding/EDELINE.

paragraphs: World models learn how an environment evolves so reinforcement learning agents can use experience more efficiently. One common approach compresses observations into discrete representations, which can discard visual details relevant to decisions. Diffusion-based alternatives improve visual fidelity, but conditioning predictions on a fixed number of recent frames restricts the history available to the model.

EDELINE addresses this memory problem by combining state space models with diffusion models in a unified architecture. The approach brings sequence modeling into the same world-model design as visual generation. Its motivation is to retain the benefits of detailed observation prediction while improving the ability to account for information beyond a short, fixed frame window.

The authors report better performance than existing baselines across visually challenging Atari 100k tasks, the memory-demanding Crafter benchmark, and first-person 3D ViZDoom environments. These evaluations test the architecture across different demands on perception and memory. The results support integrating temporal sequence modeling with diffusion-based world models as a way to improve reinforcement learning performance across the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: EDELINE combines state space and diffusion models to strengthen world-model memory, outperforming baselines across three reinforcement learning benchmark settings.

title: EDELINE: Enhancing Memory in Diffusion-based World Models via Linear-Time Sequence Modeling

abstract: We study the task of noiseless linear regression under Gaussian covariates in the presence of additive oblivious contamination. Specifically, we are given i.i.d.\ samples from a distribution $(x, y)$ on $\mathbb R^d \times \mathbb R$ with $x \sim \mathcal N(0,I_d)$ and $y = x^\top \beta + z$, where $z$ is drawn from an unknown distribution that is independent of $x$. Moreover, $z$ satisfies $\mathbb P[z = 0] = \alpha>0$. The goal is to accurately recover the regressor $\beta$ to small $\ell_2$-error. Ignoring computational considerations, this problem is known to be solvable using $O(d/\alpha)$ samples. On the other hand, the best known polynomial-time algorithms require $\Omega(d/\alpha^2)$ samples. Here we provide formal evidence that the quadratic dependence in $1/\alpha$ is inherent for efficient algorithms. Specifically, we show that any efficient Statistical Query algorithm for this task requires VSTAT complexity at least $\tilde{\Omega}(d^{1/2}/\alpha^2)$.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression when some responses are exactly clean and others contain additive contamination. The inputs follow a standard Gaussian distribution, and contamination is independent of the inputs. Its distribution is otherwise unknown, with probability alpha of adding exactly zero. The objective is to recover the regression coefficients accurately despite the contaminated responses.

The central question is how computational efficiency changes the amount of information required. Without restricting computation, recovery is known to need O(d/alpha) samples, where d is the input dimension. The best known polynomial-time algorithms require a quadratic dependence on inverse alpha. As the clean fraction shrinks, that difference creates a substantial gap between information availability and efficient recovery.

The authors establish a lower bound for efficient algorithms in the Statistical Query framework, expressed through VSTAT complexity with quadratic dependence on inverse alpha. This gives formal evidence that the less favorable dependence reflects a computational obstacle. The scope of that evidence is the stated algorithmic framework and contamination model; it is not a universal lower bound for every conceivable efficient algorithm.
summary.tldr: A Statistical Query lower bound provides evidence of a computational barrier in recovering linear regressors from independently contaminated responses.

title: Information-Computation Tradeoffs for Noiseless Linear Regression with Oblivious Contamination

abstract: Speech is a fundamental form of human communication, and speech perception constitutes the initial stage of language comprehension. Although brain-to-speech interface technologies have made significant progress in recent years, most existing studies focus on neural decoding during speech production. Such approaches heavily rely on articulatory motor regions, rendering them unsuitable for individuals with speech motor impairments, such as those with aphasia or locked-in syndrome. To address this limitation, we construct and release NeuroListen, the first publicly available stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) dataset specifically designed for auditory reconstruction. It contains over 10 hours of neural–speech paired recordings from 5 clinical participants, covering a wide range of semantic categories. Building on this dataset, we propose HyperSpeech, a multi-band neural decoding framework that employs dynamic spatio-temporal hypergraph neural networks to capture high-order dependencies across frequency, spatial, and temporal dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperSpeech significantly outperforms existing methods across multiple objective speech quality metrics, and achieves superior performance in human subjective evaluations, validating its effectiveness and advancement. This study provides a dedicated dataset and modeling framework for auditory speech decoding, offering foundations for neural language processing and assistive communication systems.

title: Listening to the Brain: Multi-Band sEEG Auditory Reconstruction via Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Hypergraphs

abstract: Lifelong knowledge editing enables continuous, precise updates to outdated knowledge in large language models (LLMs) without computationally expensive full retraining. However, existing methods often accumulate errors throughout the editing process, causing a gradual decline in both editing accuracy and generalization. To tackle this problem, we propose Neuron-Specific Masked Knowledge Editing (NMKE), a novel fine-grained editing framework that combines neuron-level attribution with dynamic sparse masking. Leveraging neuron functional attribution, we identify two key types of knowledge neurons, with knowledge-general neurons activating consistently across prompts and knowledge-specific neurons activating to specific prompts. NMKE further introduces an entropy-guided dynamic sparse mask, locating relevant neurons to the target knowledge. This strategy enables precise neuron-level knowledge editing with fewer parameter modifications. Experimental results from thousands of sequential edits demonstrate that NMKE outperforms existing methods in maintaining high editing success rates and preserving model general capabilities in lifelong editing.

paragraphs: Updating a language model repeatedly creates a cumulative problem: individual knowledge edits can introduce errors that weaken later editing and broader model performance. This paper proposes Neuron-Specific Masked Knowledge Editing, or NMKE, to make these ongoing updates more precise without requiring full retraining. Its central idea is to identify relevant neurons and restrict how much of the model an edit changes.

The method combines neuron-level attribution with a sparse mask that changes dynamically. The attribution analysis distinguishes neurons that activate consistently across prompts from neurons associated with particular prompts. An entropy-guided masking procedure then locates neurons relevant to the knowledge being updated. This gives the editing process a finer target while reducing the number of modified parameters.

Experiments involving thousands of sequential edits show that NMKE outperforms existing methods in maintaining editing success and preserving general capabilities. The result matters because lifelong editing must sustain both objectives through repeated updates. The paper supports selective modification as a way to manage accumulated editing damage while continuing to incorporate new knowledge.
summary.tldr: NMKE targets dynamically selected neurons to sustain successful knowledge edits and preserve general capabilities across thousands of updates.

title: Edit Less, Achieve More: Dynamic Sparse Neuron Masking for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in LLMs

abstract: Vision-language foundation models (VLMs), such as CLIP, exhibit remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks. However, deploying these models can be unreliable when significant distribution gaps exist between training and test data, while fine-tuning for diverse scenarios is often costly. Cache-based test-time adapters offer an efficient alternative by storing representative test samples to guide subsequent classifications. Yet, these methods typically employ naive cache management with limited capacity, leading to severe catastrophic forgetting when samples are inevitably dropped during updates. In this paper, we propose DOTA (DistributiOnal Test-time Adaptation), a simple yet effective method addressing this limitation. Crucially, instead of merely memorizing individual test samples, DOTA continuously estimates the underlying distribution of the test data stream. Test-time posterior probabilities are then computed using these dynamically estimated distributions via Bayes' theorem for adaptation. This distribution-centric approach enables the model to continually learn and adapt to the deployment environment. Extensive experiments validate that DOTA significantly mitigates forgetting and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can become unreliable when deployment data differ substantially from their training data. Updating them for every setting can be expensive. Cache-based adapters offer a lighter approach: they retain representative test examples and use them to help classify later inputs. Their limited storage, however, means examples are eventually discarded, potentially erasing useful information.

DOTA changes what the adapter remembers. Instead of relying only on individual stored examples, it continuously estimates the distribution underlying the incoming test data. It then applies Bayes' theorem to those evolving estimates to compute posterior probabilities for classification. Adaptation therefore depends on a running statistical description of the deployment stream.

This distribution-based representation addresses the forgetting associated with cache replacement and allows the model to keep adapting as test data arrive. The reported experiments show substantially reduced forgetting and state-of-the-art performance compared with existing methods. The central contribution is a different way to preserve deployment experience: maintain estimates of the data distribution rather than only a small collection of examples.
summary.tldr: DOTA adapts vision-language models using continuously estimated test-data distributions, reducing the forgetting associated with limited example caches.

title: DOTA: Distributional Test-time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models

abstract: Existing Multi-fidelity Bayesian Optimization (MFBO) methods ignore the convergence behavior of the multi-fidelity surrogate as the fidelity increases, leading to inefficient exploration and suboptimal performance. We introduce CAMO (Convergence-Aware Multi-fidelity Optimization), a principled framework based on Linear Fidelity Differential Equations (LFiDEs) that explicitly encodes convergence of fidelity-indexed outputs and employs a closed-form nonstationary kernel. We rigorously prove the existence and pointwise/uniform convergence to the high fidelity surrogate under mild restrictions and provide new convergence results for general FiDEs using smooth, non-smooth and even non-convex Lyapunov functions, establishing a bridge between MFBO and the theory of subgradient flows in non-smooth optimisation theory. Combined with a fidelity-aware acquisition function, CAMO outperforms state-of-the-art MFBO methods on a majority of synthetic and real-world benchmarks, with up to a four-fold improvement in optimisation performance and a dramatic speed-up in convergence. CAMO offers a tractable and theoretically grounded approach to convergence-aware MFBO.
originalAbstract: Existing Multi-fidelity Bayesian Optimization (MFBO) methods ignore the convergence behavior of the multi-fidelity surrogate as the fidelity increases, leading to inefficient exploration and suboptimal performance. We introduce CAMO (Convergence-Aware Multi-fidelity Optimization), a principled framework based on Linear Fidelity Differential Equations (LFiDEs) that explicitly encodes convergence of fidelity-indexed outputs and employs a closed-form nonstationary kernel. We rigorously prove the existence and pointwise/uniform convergence to the high fidelity surrogate under mild restrictions and provide new convergence results for general FiDEs using smooth, non-smooth and even non-convex Lyapunov functions, establishing a bridge between MFBO and the theory of subgradient flows in non-smooth optimisation theory. Combined with a fidelity-aware acquisition function, CAMO outperforms state-of-the-art MFBO methods on a majority of synthetic and real-world benchmarks, with up to a four-fold improvement in optimisation performance and a dramatic speed-up in convergence. CAMO offers a tractable and theoretically grounded approach to convergence-aware MFBO.

paragraphs: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization uses evaluations at different levels of fidelity to search efficiently. Its predictive model must connect these levels, including how outputs approach their high-fidelity behavior. The paper argues that existing methods overlook this convergence structure, which can lead to inefficient exploration and weaker optimization results.

They also derive convergence results for more general fidelity differential equations using several classes of Lyapunov functions, connecting the framework to subgradient-flow theory.

A fidelity-aware acquisition function then guides which evaluations to perform. summary.tldr: CAMO models how evaluations converge as fidelity increases, combining conditional convergence guarantees with stronger results on most tested optimization benchmarks.

title: CAMO: Convergence-Aware Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Scaling laws have shaped recent advances in machine learning by enabling predictable scaling of model performance based on model size, computation, and data volume. Concurrently, the rise in computational cost for AI has motivated model compression techniques, notably quantization and sparsification, which have emerged to mitigate the steep computational demands associated with large-scale training and inference. This paper investigates the interplay between scaling laws and compression strategies, exploring whether a unified scaling framework can accurately predict model performance when training occurs over various compressed representations, such as sparse, scalar-quantized, sparse-quantized or even vector-quantized formats. Our key contributions include proposing and validating a general scaling law formulation applicable both individually but also composably across compression types. We demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that a simple metric based on Gaussian mean squared error fitting can robustly predict parameter efficiency across compressed models. Additionally, we extend our formulation to directly compare the accuracy potential of different compressed formats, and to derive better algorithms for training over sparse-quantized formats. Finally, we identify conditions under which these unified scaling laws fail.

paragraphs: Scaling laws help predict how model performance changes with resources such as parameter count, data, and computation. Compression complicates those predictions because parameters can be represented with different precision or sparsity. This paper asks whether one framework can predict performance for models trained using sparse, scalar-quantized, combined sparse-quantized, and vector-quantized representations.

The authors propose and validate a scaling-law formulation that applies to individual compression methods and combinations of them. A central result is that a simple metric based on fitting Gaussian mean squared error can predict parameter efficiency across compressed models. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results support this connection between representation quality and the usefulness of the resulting parameters.

The framework also supports direct comparisons of the accuracy potential of compressed formats and leads to improved algorithms for training sparse-quantized models. The authors identify conditions where the unified laws fail, so the formulation is explicitly bounded in scope. Its value is a common predictive language for comparing compression choices that would otherwise be treated as separate design problems.
summary.tldr: A unified scaling framework predicts parameter efficiency across compression formats and helps compare their accuracy potential.

title: Unified Scaling Laws for Compressed Representations

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in a wide range of applications. However, when trained on limited or low-diversity datasets, GNNs are prone to overfitting and memorization, which impacts their generalization. To address this, graph data augmentation (GDA) has become a crucial task to enhance the performance and generalization of GNNs. Traditional GDA methods employ simple transformations that result in limited performance gains. Although recent diffusion-based augmentation methods offer improved results, they are sparse, task-specific, and constrained by class labels. In this work, we propose a more general and effective diffusion-based GDA framework that is task-agnostic and label-free. For better training stability and reduced computational cost, we employ a graph variational auto-encoder (GVAE) to learn a compact latent graph representation. A diffusion model is used in the learned latent space to generate both consistent and diverse augmentations. For a fixed augmentation budget, our algorithm selects a subset of samples that would benefit the most from the augmentation. To further improve performance, we also perform test-time augmentation, leveraged by the label-free nature of our method. Thanks to the efficient utilization of GVAE and latent diffusion, our algorithm significantly enhances machine learning safety measures, including calibration, robustness to corruptions, and prediction consistency. Moreover, our method has shown improved robustness against four types of adversarial attacks and achieves better generalization performance. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we compare it with 30 existing methods on 12 benchmark datasets across node classification, link prediction, and graph classification in various learning settings, including semi-supervised, supervised, and long-tailed data distributions. The code will soon be made publicly available.

title: Diffusion-Guided Graph Data Augmentation

abstract: What property of the data distribution determines the excess risk of principal component analysis? In this paper, we provide a precise answer to this question. We establish a central limit theorem for the error of the principal subspace estimated by PCA, and derive the asymptotic distribution of its excess risk under the reconstruction loss. We obtain a non-asymptotic upper bound on the excess risk of PCA that recovers, in the large sample limit, our asymptotic characterization. Underlying our contributions is the following result: we prove that the negative block Rayleigh quotient, defined on the Grassmannian, is generalized self-concordant along geodesics emanating from its minimizer of maximum rotation less than $\pi/4$.

We establish a central limit theorem for the error of the principal subspace estimated by PCA, and derive the asymptotic distribution of its excess risk under the reconstruction loss. We obtain a non-asymptotic upper bound on the excess risk of PCA that recovers, in the large sample limit, our asymptotic characterization. Underlying our contributions is the following result: we prove that the negative block Rayleigh quotient, defined on the Grassmannian, is generalized self-concordant along geodesics emanating from its minimizer of maximum rotation less than $\pi/4$.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis finds a lower-dimensional subspace that preserves information for reconstructing data. With a finite sample, its estimated subspace differs from the best one for the underlying distribution. This paper studies the resulting excess reconstruction loss and asks which properties of the data distribution determine that error.

The authors establish a central limit theorem for the estimated subspace’s error, then derive the asymptotic distribution of its excess risk. These results characterize fluctuations as the sample size becomes large. They also provide a finite-sample upper bound that approaches the asymptotic characterization, connecting guarantees for limited data with the large-sample picture.

The analysis rests on the geometry of the space of subspaces, called the Grassmannian. The authors prove a controlled-variation property, generalized self-concordance, for the negative block Rayleigh quotient along certain geometric paths from its minimizer. The stated result applies when maximum rotation is less than π/4. This geometric control underpins the paper’s statistical description of PCA reconstruction error.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis connects PCA’s subspace estimation error to asymptotic risk distributions and a matching finite-sample upper bound.

title: A Geometric Analysis of PCA

abstract: Multi-class tissue-type classification of colorectal cancer (CRC) histopathologic images is a significant step in the development of downstream machine learning models for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, publicly available CRC datasets used to build tissue classifiers often suffer from insufficient morphologic diversity, class imbalance, and low-quality image tiles, limiting downstream model performance and generalizability. To address this research gap, we introduce STARC-9 (STAnford coloRectal Cancer), a large-scale dataset for multi-class tissue classification. STARC-9 comprises 630,000 histopathologic image tiles uniformly sampled across nine clinically relevant tissue classes (each represented by 70,000 tiles), systematically extracted from hematoxylin & eosin-stained whole-slide images (WSI) from 200 CRC patients at the Stanford University School of Medicine. To construct STARC-9, we propose a novel framework, DeepCluster++, consisting of two primary steps to ensure diversity within each tissue class, followed by pathologist verification. First, an encoder from an autoencoder trained specifically on histopathologic images is used to extract feature vectors from all tiles within a given input WSI. Next, K-means clustering groups morphologically similar tiles, followed by an equal-frequency binning method to sample diverse patterns within each tissue class. Finally, the selected tiles are verified by expert gastrointestinal pathologists to ensure classification accuracy. This semi-automated approach significantly reduces the manual effort required for dataset curation while producing high-quality training examples. To validate the utility of STARC-9, we benchmarked baseline convolutional neural networks, transformers, and pathology-specific foundation models on downstream multi-class CRC tissue classification and segmentation tasks when trained on STARC-9 versus publicly available datasets, demonstrating superior generalizability of models trained on STARC-9. Although we demonstrate the utility of DeepCluster++ on CRC as a pilot use-case, it is a flexible framework that can be used for constructing high-quality datasets from large WSI repositories across a wide range of cancer and non-cancer applications.

summary.tldr: STARC-9 combines balanced tissue classes, diversity-aware sampling, and pathologist verification to improve colorectal tissue-model generalizability.

title: STARC-9: A Large-scale Dataset for Multi-Class Tissue Classification for CRC Histopathology

abstract: We develop a machine learning approach to represent and analyze the underlying spatial structure that governs shot selection among professional basketball players in the NBA. Typically, NBA players are discussed and compared in an heuristic, imprecise manner that relies on unmeasured intuitions about player behavior. This makes it difficult to draw comparisons between players and make accurate player specific predictions. Modeling shot attempt data as a point process, we create a low dimensional representation of offensive player types in the NBA. Using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), an unsupervised dimensionality reduction technique, we show that a low-rank spatial decomposition summarizes the shooting habits of NBA players. The spatial representations discovered by the algorithm correspond to intuitive descriptions of NBA player types, and can be used to model other spatial effects, such as shooting accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper develops a data-based representation of where NBA players choose to shoot. Informal descriptions of player styles can be intuitive but difficult to measure or compare systematically. The authors seek a compact account of spatial shooting habits that supports both comparisons between players and player-specific modeling.

They model shot attempts as a point process and use non-negative matrix factorization to obtain a low-dimensional representation of offensive player types. The resulting low-rank spatial decomposition summarizes shooting behavior through a smaller collection of patterns. This connects the locations of individual attempts to a representation of broader player tendencies learned without supervised type labels.

The discovered spatial representations correspond to intuitive descriptions of NBA player types. They can also be used to model other spatial effects, including shooting accuracy. The contribution is a common quantitative basis for describing shot selection and extending that description to related spatial questions. It gives measured structure to comparisons that otherwise depend on loosely specified impressions of player behavior.
summary.tldr: Point-process modeling and non-negative matrix factorization uncover compact spatial patterns that describe NBA players’ shooting habits.

title: Factorized Point Process Intensities: A Spatial Analysis of Professional Basketball

abstract: Markov jump processes (MJPs) are used to model a wide range of phenomenon from disease progression to RNA path folding. However, existing methods suffer from a number of shortcomings: degenerate trajectories in the case of ML estimation of parametric models and poor inferential performance in the case of nonparametric models. We take a small-variance asymptotics (SVA) approach to overcome these limitations. We derive the small-variance asymptotics for parametric and nonparametric MJPs for both directly observed and hidden state models. In the parametric case we obtain a novel objective function which leads to non-degenerate trajectories. To derive the nonparametric version we introduce the gamma-gamma process, a novel extension to the gamma-exponential process. We propose algorithms for each of these formulations, which we call \emphJUMP-means. Our experiments demonstrate that JUMP-means is competitive with or outperforms widely used MJP inference approaches in terms of both speed and reconstruction accuracy.

paragraphs: Markov jump processes model phenomena involving changes between states, including disease progression and RNA folding. The paper addresses two difficulties in existing inference methods: degenerate trajectories from maximum-likelihood estimation of parametric models, and poor inference performance in nonparametric models. Its proposed route is to derive small-variance asymptotic formulations of these processes.

The derivations cover both parametric and nonparametric models, with either directly observed or hidden states. For parametric models, the resulting objective produces nondegenerate trajectories. For the nonparametric formulation, the authors introduce a gamma-gamma process that extends the gamma-exponential process. They then provide algorithms for the different formulations under the shared name JUMP-means.

Experiments compare JUMP-means with widely used Markov-jump-process inference approaches on speed and reconstruction accuracy. The reported performance is competitive with or better than those alternatives. This qualified result matters: the paper presents an effective family of inference procedures across several formulations, rather than claiming that every variant dominates every comparison. Its methodological contribution links asymptotic analysis to concrete inference objectives and algorithms.
summary.tldr: JUMP-means derives practical Markov-jump-process inference algorithms with nondegenerate parametric trajectories and competitive speed and reconstruction accuracy.

title: JUMP-Means: Small-Variance Asymptotics for Markov Jump Processes

abstract: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms are often used for approximate inference inside learning, but their slow mixing can be difficult to diagnose and the resulting approximate gradients can seriously degrade learning. To alleviate these issues, we define a new model family using strong Doeblin Markov chains, whose mixing times can be precisely controlled by a parameter. We also develop an algorithm to learn such models, which involves maximizing the data likelihood under the induced stationary distribution of these chains. We show empirical improvements on two challenging inference tasks.
originalAbstract: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms are often used for approximate inference inside learning, but their slow mixing can be difficult to diagnose and the resulting approximate gradients can seriously degrade learning. To alleviate these issues, we define a new model family using strong Doeblin Markov chains, whose mixing times can be precisely controlled by a parameter. We also develop an algorithm to learn such models, which involves maximizing the data likelihood under the induced stationary distribution of these chains. We show empirical improvements on two challenging inference tasks.

paragraphs: Learning methods sometimes use Markov Chain Monte Carlo to approximate the inference calculations needed during training. If the chain mixes slowly, its samples may poorly represent the distribution being estimated. The resulting approximate gradients can damage learning, and the paper emphasizes that slow mixing itself can be difficult to diagnose.

The authors address this problem by defining a model family through strong Doeblin Markov chains. A parameter precisely controls the mixing time of these chains. This makes mixing behavior part of the model's design, giving the learning procedure explicit control over a property that otherwise can undermine its inference calculations.

The accompanying learning algorithm maximizes the data likelihood under the stationary distribution induced by the chain. In this formulation, the distribution used to model the data is directly linked to the chain whose mixing is controlled. Experiments show improvements on two challenging inference tasks, supporting the practical value of this connection between model construction, inference behavior, and likelihood-based learning.
summary.tldr: A model family built from strong Doeblin chains makes mixing time controllable and supports likelihood-based learning.

title: Learning Fast-Mixing Models for Structured Prediction

abstract: Structured prediction tasks in machine learning involve the simultaneous prediction of multiple labels. This is often done by maximizing a score function on the space of labels, which decomposes as a sum of pairwise elements, each depending on two specific labels. The goal of this paper is to develop a theoretical explanation of the empirical effectiveness of heuristic inference algorithms for solving such structured prediction problems. We study the minimum-achievable expected Hamming error in such problems, highlighting the case of 2D grid graphs, which are common in machine vision applications. Our main theorems provide tight upper and lower bounds on this error, as well as a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves the bound.

This is often done by maximizing a score function on the space of labels, which decomposes as a sum of pairwise elements, each depending on two specific labels. paragraphs: Structured prediction assigns multiple labels jointly, accounting for relationships among them. A common approach scores a complete labeling by adding terms that each depend on a pair of labels. The paper asks how to explain the practical success of heuristic inference methods for such problems through a theoretical analysis of achievable prediction error.

Its focus is expected Hamming error, which counts incorrect labels rather than treating every imperfect overall labeling as equally wrong. The authors study the smallest achievable expected error, with particular attention to two-dimensional grid graphs. These graphs are relevant to machine vision, where the relationships between prediction locations often have a grid structure.

The main results provide tight upper and lower bounds on this error and a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves the bound. Matching an achievable error level to a theoretical lower bound identifies what efficient inference can accomplish in the studied problems. This addresses predictive accuracy directly and supplies a theoretical perspective on why useful structured predictions can be obtained efficiently.
summary.tldr: Tight prediction-error bounds and an efficient algorithm clarify achievable inference accuracy, especially on two-dimensional grids.

title: How Hard is Inference for Structured Prediction?

abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are multi-layer hierarchical generalisations of Gaussian processes (GPs) and are formally equivalent to neural networks with multiple, infinitely wide hidden layers. DGPs are nonparametric probabilistic models and as such are arguably more flexible, have a greater capacity to generalise, and provide better calibrated uncertainty estimates than alternative deep models. This paper develops a new approximate Bayesian learning scheme that enables DGPs to be applied to a range of medium to large scale regression problems for the first time. The new method uses an approximate Expectation Propagation procedure and a novel and efficient extension of the probabilistic backpropagation algorithm for learning. We evaluate the new method for non-linear regression on eleven real-world datasets, showing that it always outperforms GP regression and is almost always better than state-of-the-art deterministic and sampling-based approximate inference methods for Bayesian neural networks. As a by-product, this work provides a comprehensive analysis of six approximate Bayesian methods for training neural networks.

paragraphs: Deep Gaussian processes extend Gaussian processes into multilayer probabilistic models. They are formally equivalent to neural networks with multiple infinitely wide hidden layers. The paper motivates them as potentially offering greater flexibility, generalization capacity, and better-calibrated uncertainty than alternative deep models, while addressing the difficulty of learning them at useful scales.

The main contribution is an approximate Bayesian learning scheme that makes these models applicable to medium- and large-scale regression problems. It combines approximate expectation propagation with an efficient extension of probabilistic backpropagation. This learning procedure is the practical link between the expressive model family and nonlinear regression tasks involving real datasets.

Across eleven real-world datasets, the method outperforms Gaussian-process regression in every reported comparison and almost always exceeds the considered state-of-the-art approximate inference methods for Bayesian neural networks. Those comparisons include deterministic and sampling-based methods. The paper also analyzes six approximate Bayesian neural-network training methods, providing a broader empirical context for assessing the new deep Gaussian-process approach.
summary.tldr: An approximate Bayesian learning scheme makes deep Gaussian processes practical for larger regression tasks and performs strongly across eleven datasets.

title: Deep Gaussian Processes for Regression using Approximate Expectation Propagation

abstract: We study a specific combinatorial pure exploration stochastic bandit problem where the learner aims at finding the set of arms whose means are above a given threshold, up to a given precision, and for a fixed time horizon. We propose a parameter-free algorithm based on an original heuristic, and prove that it is optimal for this problem by deriving matching upper and lower bounds. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-trivial pure exploration setting with fixed budget for which provably optimal strategies are constructed.
originalAbstract: We study a specific combinatorial pure exploration stochastic bandit problem where the learner aims at finding the set of arms whose means are above a given threshold, up to a given precision, and for a fixed time horizon. We propose a parameter-free algorithm based on an original heuristic, and prove that it is optimal for this problem by deriving matching upper and lower bounds. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-trivial pure exploration setting with fixed budget for which provably optimal strategies are constructed.

paragraphs: The paper studies a sampling problem in which a learner must identify every option whose average outcome exceeds a specified threshold. Each option, called an arm, produces uncertain observations. The learner has a fixed sampling budget and only needs to classify the arms up to a requested precision. The objective is therefore to learn which arms qualify, rather than to maximize rewards while collecting observations.

The authors introduce a parameter-free algorithm based on a new heuristic for choosing what to sample. This addresses the central allocation question: how should limited observations be distributed across arms to identify the qualifying set? The algorithm is designed specifically for the thresholding objective and its fixed time horizon.

The main finding is a proof of optimality through matching upper and lower bounds. These bounds establish both what the proposed method can achieve and the corresponding difficulty of the problem. The authors qualify their historical claim: to their knowledge, this is the first nontrivial fixed-budget pure-exploration setting with a provably optimal strategy.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free sampling algorithm provably optimally identifies which bandit arms exceed a threshold within a fixed budget and specified precision.

title: An optimal algorithm for the Thresholding Bandit Problem

abstract: The Multi-Armed Bandit problem with Unobserved Confounders (MABUC) considers decision-making settings where unmeasured variables can influence both the agent’s decisions and received rewards (Bareinboim et al., 2015). Recent findings showed that unobserved confounders (UCs) pose a unique challenge to algorithms based on standard randomization (i.e., experimental data); if UCs are naively averaged out, these algorithms behave sub-optimally, possibly incurring infinite regret. In this paper, we show how counterfactual-based decision-making circumvents these problems and leads to a coherent fusion of observational and experimental data. We then demonstrate this new strategy in an enhanced Thompson Sampling bandit player, and support our findings’ efficacy with extensive simulations.
originalAbstract: The Multi-Armed Bandit problem with Unobserved Confounders (MABUC) considers decision-making settings where unmeasured variables can influence both the agent’s decisions and received rewards (Bareinboim et al., 2015). Recent findings showed that unobserved confounders (UCs) pose a unique challenge to algorithms based on standard randomization (i.e., experimental data); if UCs are naively averaged out, these algorithms behave sub-optimally, possibly incurring infinite regret. In this paper, we show how counterfactual-based decision-making circumvents these problems and leads to a coherent fusion of observational and experimental data. We then demonstrate this new strategy in an enhanced Thompson Sampling bandit player, and support our findings’ efficacy with extensive simulations.

paragraphs: The paper studies bandit decision-making when hidden variables affect both the decisions an agent makes and the rewards it receives. These unobserved confounders complicate learning because the relationship between actions and outcomes reflects influences the learner cannot directly measure. Simply averaging those influences away can make standard approaches based on randomized experiments behave suboptimally, potentially with infinite regret.

The authors develop counterfactual-based decision-making as a way to avoid these problems. The approach provides a coherent way to combine observational data with experimental data. Its central idea is to use counterfactual reasoning in deciding what to do, rather than treating experimental averages alone as sufficient for the confounded decision problem.

They demonstrate the strategy through an enhanced Thompson Sampling bandit player and support its effectiveness with extensive simulations. The contribution concerns how different sources of evidence should inform sequential decisions when hidden influences matter. The reported simulations support the proposed strategy; the abstract's warning about potentially infinite regret describes a possible consequence of naive treatment of confounding, not an inevitable outcome for every randomized learner.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual reasoning combines observational and experimental evidence to improve bandit decisions in the presence of unobserved confounders.

title: Counterfactual Data-Fusion for Online Reinforcement Learners

abstract: The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size, complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net’s internal state in terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important to a classification result–for example, how sensitive a prediction of “zebra” is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a medical application.

summary.tldr: TCAV quantifies prediction sensitivity to human-defined concepts by examining directions in a neural network’s internal representation.

title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)

abstract: We propose Deep Asymmetric Multitask Feature Learning (Deep-AMTFL) which can learn deep representations shared across multiple tasks while effectively preventing negative transfer that may happen in the feature sharing process. Specifically, we introduce an asymmetric autoencoder term that allows reliable predictors for the easy tasks to have high contribution to the feature learning while suppressing the influences of unreliable predictors for more difficult tasks. This allows the learning of less noisy representations, and enables unreliable predictors to exploit knowledge from the reliable predictors via the shared latent features. Such asymmetric knowledge transfer through shared features is also more scalable and efficient than inter-task asymmetric transfer. We validate our Deep-AMTFL model on multiple benchmark datasets for multitask learning and image classification, on which it significantly outperforms existing symmetric and asymmetric multitask learning models, by effectively preventing negative transfer in deep feature learning.

paragraphs: Learning several tasks through shared features can let them benefit from one another, but it can also spread unreliable information. This harmful interaction is called negative transfer. Deep Asymmetric Multitask Feature Learning addresses it by giving tasks different levels of influence over the shared representation instead of treating their contributions symmetrically.

The method introduces an asymmetric autoencoder term. Reliable predictors for easier tasks contribute strongly to feature learning, while unreliable predictors for harder tasks have their influence suppressed. The intended result is a less noisy shared representation. Harder tasks can still benefit from knowledge contributed by reliable predictors through those common latent features.

Sharing knowledge through features is also presented as more scalable and efficient than asymmetric transfer directly between tasks. Across multiple multitask-learning and image-classification benchmarks, the proposed model significantly outperforms the compared symmetric and asymmetric alternatives. The reported results support the value of controlling who shapes shared features, as well as allowing multiple tasks to use them.
summary.tldr: Deep-AMTFL reduces negative transfer by letting reliable task predictors exert more influence on shared features than unreliable ones.

title: Deep Asymmetric Multi-task Feature Learning

abstract: Variational Bayesian neural nets combine the flexibility of deep learning with Bayesian uncertainty estimation. Unfortunately, there is a tradeoff between cheap but simple variational families (e.g. fully factorized) or expensive and complicated inference procedures. We show that natural gradient ascent with adaptive weight noise implicitly fits a variational posterior to maximize the evidence lower bound (ELBO). This insight allows us to train full-covariance, fully factorized, or matrix-variate Gaussian variational posteriors using noisy versions of natural gradient, Adam, and K-FAC, respectively, making it possible to scale up to modern-size ConvNets. On standard regression benchmarks, our noisy K-FAC algorithm makes better predictions and matches Hamiltonian Monte Carlo’s predictive variances better than existing methods. Its improved uncertainty estimates lead to more efficient exploration in active learning, and intrinsic motivation for reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks aim to combine flexible prediction with uncertainty estimates, but approximating their posterior distributions can be costly. Simple approximation families are cheaper, while richer ones often require complicated inference. This paper identifies a connection that turns familiar optimization methods into tools for variational Bayesian learning.

The authors show that natural gradient ascent with adaptive noise on the weights implicitly fits a variational posterior by maximizing the evidence lower bound. Noisy natural gradient, Adam, and K-FAC support full-covariance, fully factorized, and matrix-variate Gaussian posteriors, respectively. This provides several choices of posterior structure and makes training modern-sized convolutional networks feasible.

The paper also reports that improved uncertainty estimates support more efficient exploration in active learning and intrinsic motivation for reinforcement learning. The practical value of the connection therefore extends from scalable inference to decisions that depend on uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Adaptive weight noise turns natural-gradient-based optimization into variational inference, enabling scalable Bayesian neural networks with improved reported uncertainty estimates.

title: Noisy Natural Gradient as Variational Inference

abstract: Our goal is to build systems which write code automatically from the kinds of specifications humans can most easily provide, such as examples and natural language instruction. The key idea of this work is that a flexible combination of pattern recognition and explicit reasoning can be used to solve these complex programming problems. We propose a method for dynamically integrating these types of information. Our novel intermediate representation and training algorithm allow a program synthesis system to learn, without direct supervision, when to rely on pattern recognition and when to perform symbolic search. Our model matches the memorization and generalization performance of neural synthesis and symbolic search, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on a dataset of simple English description-to-code programming problems.

paragraphs: This paper addresses automatic programming from specifications that people can readily provide, including examples and natural-language instructions. The challenge is deciding how these two capabilities should contribute while solving a programming problem, rather than using a fixed division of labor.

The authors introduce an intermediate representation and a training algorithm that allow a synthesis system to learn when to rely on recognized patterns and when to perform symbolic search. That decision is learned without direct supervision. The representation and training procedure therefore provide a way to adapt the balance between the two forms of problem solving.

The reported model matches neural synthesis on memorization and symbolic search on generalization. It also achieves state-of-the-art results on a dataset that maps simple English descriptions to code. These findings support the proposed combination: learning can guide the synthesis process while explicit search contributes the generalization behavior associated with symbolic methods in the reported comparison.
summary.tldr: A program synthesis system learns when to use pattern recognition and when to use symbolic search, combining their reported memorization and generalization strengths.

title: Learning to Infer Program Sketches

abstract: This paper presents the Imputer, a neural sequence model that generates output sequences iteratively via imputations. The Imputer is an iterative generation model, requiring only a constant number of generation steps independent of the number of input or output tokens. The Imputer can be trained to approximately marginalize over all possible alignments between the input and output sequences, and all possible generation orders. We present a tractable dynamic programming training algorithm, which yields a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood. When applied to end-to-end speech recognition, the Imputer outperforms prior non-autoregressive models and achieves competitive results to autoregressive models. On LibriSpeech test-other, the Imputer achieves 11.1 WER, outperforming CTC at 13.0 WER and seq2seq at 12.5 WER.

paragraphs: Imputer generates sequences through iterative imputation, filling in output information over successive rounds. Its number of generation rounds is constant with respect to input and output token counts. This separates the number of sequential generation steps from sequence length, an important property for a model intended to produce an entire output sequence through a limited number of iterations.

Training accounts approximately for alternative alignments between the input and output, as well as alternative orders in which output content could be generated. The authors develop a tractable dynamic-programming algorithm for this purpose. Its objective is a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood, allowing training to incorporate these possibilities without claiming to compute the full marginal likelihood exactly.

In end-to-end speech recognition, Imputer outperforms earlier non-autoregressive models and is competitive with autoregressive models. On LibriSpeech test-other, the reported word error rate is 11.1, compared with 13.0 for CTC and 12.5 for seq2seq. The results show that the proposed generation and training scheme can combine a fixed number of generation rounds with strong recognition accuracy in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Imputer uses iterative imputation and dynamic-programming training to generate sequences in a constant number of rounds, with strong speech-recognition results.

title: Imputer: Sequence Modelling via Imputation and Dynamic Programming

abstract: Contemporary work on learning in continuous games has commonly overlooked the hierarchical decision-making structure present in machine learning problems formulated as games, instead treating them as simultaneous play games and adopting the Nash equilibrium solution concept. We deviate from this paradigm and provide a comprehensive study of learning in Stackelberg games. This work provides insights into the optimization landscape of zero-sum games by establishing connections between Nash and Stackelberg equilibria along with the limit points of simultaneous gradient descent. We derive novel gradient-based learning dynamics emulating the natural structure of a Stackelberg game using the implicit function theorem and provide convergence analysis for deterministic and stochastic updates for zero-sum and general-sum games. Notably, in zero-sum games using deterministic updates, we show the only critical points the dynamics converge to are Stackelberg equilibria and provide a local convergence rate. Empirically, our learning dynamics mitigate rotational behavior and exhibit benefits for training generative adversarial networks compared to simultaneous gradient descent.

Treating both as simultaneous decision makers can overlook this structure. This paper studies learning in Stackelberg games and relates their equilibria to Nash equilibria and the limit points of simultaneous gradient descent in zero-sum settings.

The authors derive gradient-based learning dynamics using the implicit function theorem. The resulting updates reflect the hierarchical structure of a Stackelberg game. They analyze convergence for deterministic and stochastic updates in both zero-sum and general-sum games, connecting the update rules to the kinds of solutions the learning process can approach.

A particularly strong result concerns deterministic updates in zero-sum games: the only critical points to which the proposed dynamics converge are Stackelberg equilibria. The paper also provides a local convergence rate. Experiments show reduced rotational behavior and benefits for GAN training compared with simultaneous gradient descent. The critical-point guarantee is specific to the stated deterministic, zero-sum setting.
summary.tldr: Gradient dynamics designed for hierarchical games provide Stackelberg convergence results and empirically improve GAN training over simultaneous gradient descent.

title: Implicit Learning Dynamics in Stackelberg Games: Equilibria Characterization, Convergence Analysis, and Empirical Study

abstract: We study a general class of bilevel problems, consisting in the minimization of an upper-level objective which depends on the solution to a parametric fixed-point equation. Important instances arising in machine learning include hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, and certain graph and recurrent neural networks. Typically the gradient of the upper-level objective (hypergradient) is hard or even impossible to compute exactly, which has raised the interest in approximation methods. We investigate some popular approaches to compute the hypergradient, based on reverse mode iterative differentiation and approximate implicit differentiation. Under the hypothesis that the fixed point equation is defined by a contraction mapping, we present a unified analysis which allows for the first time to quantitatively compare these methods, providing explicit bounds for their iteration complexity. This analysis suggests a hierarchy in terms of computational efficiency among the above methods, with approximate implicit differentiation based on conjugate gradient performing best. We present an extensive experimental comparison among the methods which confirm the theoretical findings.

This paper considers inner solutions defined by parameter-dependent fixed-point equations. Examples include hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, and certain recurrent and graph neural networks. Computing the outer objective's gradient, called a hypergradient, can be difficult or impossible to do exactly.

The analysis suggests an efficiency hierarchy, with conjugate-gradient-based approximate implicit differentiation performing best among the methods considered. Extensive experiments confirm the theoretical findings. This gives a principled basis for choosing a hypergradient approximation in the studied setting, with the contraction assumption providing the stated foundation for the theoretical comparison.
summary.tldr: Under a contraction assumption, a unified complexity analysis favors conjugate-gradient-based implicit differentiation for approximate hypergradient computation.

title: On the Iteration Complexity of Hypergradient Computation

abstract: Learning how to predict future events from patterns of past events is difficult when the set of possible event types is large. Training an unrestricted neural model might overfit to spurious patterns. To exploit domain-specific knowledge of how past events might affect an event’s present probability, we propose using a temporal deductive database to track structured facts over time. Rules serve to prove facts from other facts and from past events. Each fact has a time-varying state—a vector computed by a neural net whose topology is determined by the fact’s provenance, including its experience of past events. The possible event types at any time are given by special facts, whose probabilities are neurally modeled alongside their states. In both synthetic and real-world domains, we show that neural probabilistic models derived from concise Datalog programs improve prediction by encoding appropriate domain knowledge in their architecture.

paragraphs: Predicting future events becomes difficult when many event types are possible, because an unrestricted neural model may learn accidental patterns. This paper incorporates domain knowledge through a temporal deductive database. Logical rules specify how facts follow from other facts and past events, providing structure for the prediction model.

Each fact carries a changing vector state computed by a neural network. The network’s topology follows the fact’s provenance: the facts and event history that established it. Special facts determine which event types are currently possible, and neural components model their probabilities alongside their states. Logical specification therefore shapes both what can happen and how relevant history enters the prediction.

The authors derive these probabilistic models from concise Datalog programs and evaluate them in synthetic and real-world domains. Encoding appropriate domain knowledge in the architecture improves prediction in those evaluations. The contribution is a way to connect explicit rules about temporal relationships with learned numerical states, allowing the rules to guide the structure of a neural event model.
summary.tldr: Temporal Datalog rules shape neural event-prediction models, improving predictions by incorporating appropriate domain knowledge into their architecture.

title: Neural Datalog Through Time: Informed Temporal Modeling via Logical Specification

abstract: We consider a novel challenge: approximating a distribution without the ability to randomly sample from that distribution. We study how such an approximation can be obtained using *weight queries*. Given some data set of examples, a weight query presents one of the examples to an oracle, which returns the probability, according to the target distribution, of observing examples similar to the presented example. This oracle can represent, for instance, counting queries to a database of the target population, or an interface to a search engine which returns the number of results that match a given search. We propose an interactive algorithm that iteratively selects data set examples and performs corresponding weight queries. The algorithm finds a reweighting of the data set that approximates the weights according to the target distribution, using a limited number of weight queries. We derive an approximation bound on the total variation distance between the reweighting found by the algorithm and the best achievable reweighting. Our algorithm takes inspiration from the UCB approach common in multi-armed bandits problems, and combines it with a new discrepancy estimator and a greedy iterative procedure. In addition to our theoretical guarantees, we demonstrate in experiments the advantages of the proposed algorithm over several baselines. A python implementation of the proposed algorithm and of all the experiments can be found at https://github.com/Nadav-Barak/AWP.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to approximate a population distribution when drawing random samples from it is impossible. Instead, the learner has an existing dataset and can ask an oracle how much probability the target distribution assigns to examples similar to a selected example. Database counts and search-result counts illustrate the kind of access the authors have in mind.

The proposed algorithm repeatedly chooses an example, requests its weight information, and adjusts the dataset’s weights. Its selection strategy draws inspiration from upper confidence bounds in bandit learning. A new discrepancy estimator and a greedy update procedure help guide this interaction, so that a limited number of queries can support a useful reweighting.

The theoretical guarantee measures total variation distance relative to the best reweighting achievable with the available dataset. That comparison matters: the result concerns how effectively the algorithm uses its available examples. Experiments also show advantages over several baselines, supporting the value of actively choosing which weight queries to make.
summary.tldr: An interactive algorithm approximates a target distribution by selectively querying population weights and reweighting an existing dataset.

title: Approximating a Distribution Using Weight Queries

abstract: Consider N players that each uses a mixture of K resources. Each of the players’ reward functions includes a linear pricing term for each resource that is controlled by the game manager. We assume that the game is strongly monotone, so if each player runs gradient descent, the dynamics converge to a unique Nash equilibrium (NE). Unfortunately, this NE can be inefficient since the total load on a given resource can be very high. In principle, we can control the total loads by tuning the coefficients of the pricing terms. However, finding pricing coefficients that balance the loads requires knowing the players’ reward functions and their action sets. Obtaining this game structure information is infeasible in a large-scale network and violates the users’ privacy. To overcome this, we propose a simple algorithm that learns to shift the NE of the game to meet the total load constraints by adjusting the pricing coefficients in an online manner. Our algorithm only requires the total load per resource as feedback and does not need to know the reward functions or the action sets. We prove that our algorithm guarantees convergence in L2 to a NE that meets target total load constraints. Simulations show the effectiveness of our approach when applied to smart grid demand-side management or power control in wireless networks.

paragraphs: A resource-allocation game can settle into an equilibrium while placing excessive load on particular resources. The paper considers players who each use a mixture of resources and whose rewards include linear prices controlled by a manager. Strong monotonicity ensures that player gradient-descent dynamics converge to a unique Nash equilibrium, but that equilibrium need not satisfy desired load constraints.

The manager could adjust prices to shift resource use, yet directly calculating suitable prices would require knowing players' reward functions and action sets. The proposed online algorithm avoids that information requirement. It learns how to adjust pricing coefficients using only the total load observed on each resource, allowing it to steer the equilibrium through aggregate feedback.

Within the studied setting, the authors prove convergence in L2 to an equilibrium satisfying the target total-load constraints. Simulations in smart-grid demand management and wireless-network power control demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution shows how price adjustment can combine decentralized player behavior with system-level load control while avoiding disclosure of individual reward functions and feasible actions.
summary.tldr: Online price adjustments use aggregate resource loads to steer strongly monotone games toward equilibria satisfying load constraints.

title: Online Learning for Load Balancing of Unknown Monotone Resource Allocation Games

abstract: Despite their overwhelming capacity to overfit, deep neural networks trained by specific optimization algorithms tend to generalize relatively well to unseen data. Recently, researchers explained it by investigating the implicit bias of optimization algorithms. A remarkable progress is the work (Lyu & Li, 2019), which proves gradient descent (GD) maximizes the margin of homogeneous deep neural networks. Except the first-order optimization algorithms like GD, adaptive algorithms such as AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam are popular owing to their rapid training process. Mean-while, numerous works have provided empirical evidence that adaptive methods may suffer from poor generalization performance. However, theoretical explanation for the generalization of adaptive optimization algorithms is still lacking. In this paper, we study the implicit bias of adaptive optimization algorithms on homogeneous neural networks. In particular, we study the convergent direction of parameters when they are optimizing the logistic loss. We prove that the convergent direction of Adam and RMSProp is the same as GD, while for AdaGrad, the convergent direction depends on the adaptive conditioner. Technically, we provide a unified framework to analyze convergent direction of adaptive optimization algorithms by constructing novel and nontrivial adaptive gradient flow and surrogate margin. The theoretical findings explain the superiority on generalization of exponential moving average strategy that is adopted by RMSProp and Adam. To the best of knowledge, it is the first work to study the convergent direction of adaptive optimizations on non-linear deep neural networks

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm can influence which solution a neural network approaches, even without explicitly adding a preference to the training objective. This implicit bias offers a way to study generalization. The paper examines adaptive optimizers on homogeneous neural networks, focusing on the direction approached by their parameters when minimizing logistic loss.

The authors prove that Adam and RMSProp approach the same parameter direction as gradient descent in the studied setting. AdaGrad behaves differently: its limiting direction depends on the adaptive conditioner that adjusts its updates. This distinguishes algorithms that might otherwise be grouped together simply because they all adapt their optimization steps.

The findings provide a theoretical explanation for the generalization advantage attributed to the exponential moving average strategy used by Adam and RMSProp. The specific object of analysis is parameter direction for homogeneous networks under logistic loss, making the result a structured account of optimizer bias within that setting.
summary.tldr: For homogeneous networks trained with logistic loss, Adam and RMSProp share gradient descent’s limiting parameter direction, while AdaGrad’s depends on its conditioner.

title: The Implicit Bias for Adaptive Optimization Algorithms on Homogeneous Neural Networks

abstract: This paper considers decentralized stochastic optimization over a network of $n$ nodes, where each node possesses a smooth non-convex local cost function and the goal of the networked nodes is to find an $\epsilon$-accurate first-order stationary point of the sum of the local costs. We focus on an online setting, where each node accesses its local cost only by means of a stochastic first-order oracle that returns a noisy version of the exact gradient. In this context, we propose a novel single-loop decentralized hybrid variance-reduced stochastic gradient method, called GT-HSGD, that outperforms the existing approaches in terms of both the oracle complexity and practical implementation. The GT-HSGD algorithm implements specialized local hybrid stochastic gradient estimators that are fused over the network to track the global gradient. Remarkably, GT-HSGD achieves a network topology-independent oracle complexity of $O(n^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ when the required error tolerance $\epsilon$ is small enough, leading to a linear speedup with respect to the centralized optimal online variance-reduced approaches that operate on a single node. Numerical experiments are provided to illustrate our main technical results.
originalAbstract: This paper considers decentralized stochastic optimization over a network of $n$ nodes, where each node possesses a smooth non-convex local cost function and the goal of the networked nodes is to find an $\epsilon$-accurate first-order stationary point of the sum of the local costs. We focus on an online setting, where each node accesses its local cost only by means of a stochastic first-order oracle that returns a noisy version of the exact gradient. In this context, we propose a novel single-loop decentralized hybrid variance-reduced stochastic gradient method, called GT-HSGD, that outperforms the existing approaches in terms of both the oracle complexity and practical implementation. The GT-HSGD algorithm implements specialized local hybrid stochastic gradient estimators that are fused over the network to track the global gradient. Remarkably, GT-HSGD achieves a network topology-independent oracle complexity of $O(n^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ when the required error tolerance $\epsilon$ is small enough, leading to a linear speedup with respect to the centralized optimal online variance-reduced approaches that operate on a single node. Numerical experiments are provided to illustrate our main technical results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a network of computing nodes can jointly optimize a shared objective when each node knows only its own local cost. Those costs are smooth but nonconvex, and nodes receive noisy gradient information. The target is an approximately stationary point, where the combined objective has a sufficiently small gradient.

The proposed method, GT-HSGD, combines local estimators that reduce gradient noise with communication that tracks the global gradient across the network. It uses a single optimization loop. This design connects two difficulties: making useful progress from noisy local information and coordinating that progress toward the sum of all local costs.

For sufficiently small error tolerance epsilon, the method achieves an oracle complexity of O(n^-1 epsilon^-3), independent of network topology. The authors interpret this as linear speedup with the number of nodes relative to optimal centralized online variance-reduced methods using one node. The small-tolerance qualification matters to that result. Numerical experiments illustrate the theory, while the paper also reports advantages in practical implementation.
summary.tldr: GT-HSGD combines local variance reduction and network gradient tracking to achieve conditional linear speedup in decentralized stochastic optimization.

title: A Hybrid Variance-Reduced Method for Decentralized Stochastic Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: A central goal of machine learning is to learn robust representations that capture the fundamental relationship between inputs and output labels. However, minimizing training errors over finite or biased datasets results in models latching on to spurious correlations between the training input/output pairs that are not fundamental to the problem at hand. In this paper, we define and analyze robust and spurious representations using the information-theoretic concept of minimal sufficient statistics. We prove that even when there is only bias of the input distribution (i.e. covariate shift), models can still pick up spurious features from their training data. Group distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provides an effective tool to alleviate covariate shift by minimizing the worst-case training losses over a set of pre-defined groups. Inspired by our analysis, we demonstrate that group DRO can fail when groups do not directly account for various spurious correlations that occur in the data. To address this, we further propose to minimize the worst-case losses over a more flexible set of distributions that are defined on the joint distribution of groups and instances, instead of treating each group as a whole at optimization time. Through extensive experiments on one image and two language tasks, we show that our model is significantly more robust than comparable baselines under various partitions.
