paragraphs: A model can achieve low training error by using correlations that happen to appear in its dataset but do not reflect the underlying prediction problem. This paper analyzes such spurious representations using minimal sufficient statistics, an information-theoretic way to describe information needed for prediction. The authors prove that even a shift affecting only the input distribution can lead models to learn spurious features.

The paper shows that this approach can fail when the groups do not capture the spurious correlations present in the data. Protecting each group as a whole may therefore leave important patterns within those groups insufficiently addressed.

Experiments on one image task and two language tasks show significantly greater robustness than comparable baselines across different partitions. The results connect the theoretical diagnosis to a practical change in how robust optimization represents possible distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: Robust optimization over both groups and individual examples helps address spurious correlations that predefined groups can miss.

title: Examining and Combating Spurious Features under Distribution Shift

abstract: We study reinforcement learning for partially observed Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with infinite observation and state spaces, which remains less investigated theoretically. To this end, we make the first attempt at bridging partial observability and function approximation for a class of POMDPs with a linear structure. In detail, we propose a reinforcement learning algorithm (Optimistic Exploration via Adversarial Integral Equation or OP-TENET) that attains an $\epsilon$-optimal policy within $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ episodes. In particular, the sample complexity scales polynomially in the intrinsic dimension of the linear structure and is independent of the size of the observation and state spaces. The sample efficiency of OP-TENET is enabled by a sequence of ingredients: (i) a Bellman operator with finite memory, which represents the value function in a recursive manner, (ii) the identification and estimation of such an operator via an adversarial integral equation, which features a smoothed discriminator tailored to the linear structure, and (iii) the exploration of the observation and state spaces via optimism, which is based on quantifying the uncertainty in the adversarial integral equation.

paragraphs: In partially observed reinforcement learning, an agent must act without directly seeing the full state of its environment. This paper studies a class of these problems with linear structure, allowing both the hidden-state space and the observation space to be infinite. The aim is learning efficiency governed by structure rather than space size.

The proposed algorithm, OP-TENET, combines three ingredients. A finite-memory Bellman operator describes values recursively. An adversarial integral equation identifies and estimates that operator using a smoothed discriminator tailored to the linear structure. Finally, uncertainty in this estimation drives optimistic exploration of the environment.

The authors prove that OP-TENET reaches an ε-optimal policy within O(1/ε²) episodes. Its sample complexity depends polynomially on the intrinsic dimension of the linear structure and does not depend on the sizes of the observation or state spaces. This provides a theoretical bridge between partial observability and function approximation. The guarantee applies to the structured class studied, showing how suitable low-dimensional organization can make very large partially observed problems statistically manageable.
summary.tldr: OP-TENET learns near-optimal policies in linearly structured partially observed environments with sample complexity independent of state and observation space sizes.

title: Reinforcement Learning from Partial Observation: Linear Function Approximation with Provable Sample Efficiency

abstract: In this paper, we study the non-local convergence properties of deep linear networks. Specifically, under the quadratic loss, we consider optimizing deep linear networks in which there is at least a layer with only one neuron. We describe the convergent point of trajectories with an arbitrary balanced starting point under gradient flow, including the paths which converge to one of the saddle points. We also show specific convergence rates of trajectories that converge to the global minimizers by stages. We conclude that the rates vary from polynomial to linear. As far as we know, our results are the first to give a non-local analysis of deep linear neural networks with arbitrary balanced initialization, rather than the lazy training regime which has dominated the literature on neural networks or the restricted benign initialization.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes optimization trajectories in deep linear networks under quadratic loss. Its setting includes a structural restriction: at least one layer has only one neuron. Within that setting, the authors study gradient flow from arbitrary balanced initializations, allowing a broader range of starting points within the balanced class.

The analysis characterizes where trajectories converge, including those that end at saddle points. Accounting for these paths matters because a description of successful trajectories alone would not explain the behavior across all of the allowed initializations. The result therefore concerns both the destination of optimization and the possibility of convergence to points other than global minimizers.

For trajectories that do reach global minimizers, the authors give convergence rates across different stages. These rates range from polynomial to linear. The work's non-local perspective extends beyond analyses restricted to lazy training or specially favorable initializations. Its contribution is a more detailed description of optimization dynamics under the stated network and initialization conditions, including how the speed of convergence can change along successful paths.
summary.tldr: For deep linear networks with a one-neuron layer, the paper characterizes gradient-flow limits and staged convergence rates from arbitrary balanced initializations.

title: On Non-local Convergence Analysis of Deep Linear Networks

abstract: We study the problem of learning a mixture of multiple linear dynamical systems (LDSs) from unlabeled short sample trajectories, each generated by one of the LDS models. Despite the wide applicability of mixture models for time-series data, learning algorithms that come with end-to-end performance guarantees are largely absent from existing literature. There are multiple sources of technical challenges, including but not limited to (1) the presence of latent variables (i.e. the unknown labels of trajectories); (2) the possibility that the sample trajectories might have lengths much smaller than the dimension $d$ of the LDS models; and (3) the complicated temporal dependence inherent to time-series data. To tackle these challenges, we develop a two-stage meta-algorithm, which is guaranteed to efficiently recover each ground-truth LDS model up to error $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d/T})$, where $T$ is the total sample size. We validate our theoretical studies with numerical experiments, confirming the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper considers short time series generated by several different linear dynamical systems. Each observed trajectory comes from one system, but the learner is not told which one. The goal is to recover the underlying systems from this unlabeled collection, rather than treating all trajectories as observations of a single model.

Three difficulties interact. The trajectory assignments are hidden, individual sequences may be much shorter than the dimension of the systems, and observations within a sequence depend on one another over time. These features make it challenging to provide a guarantee covering the entire learning procedure, which the authors identify as largely absent from existing work.

The proposed solution is a two-stage meta-algorithm with an efficient recovery guarantee. Its stated error scales as the square root of system dimension divided by total sample size, up to logarithmic factors. This expresses how recovery benefits from more observations across the dataset while becoming harder as dimension increases. Numerical experiments support the theoretical study and the effectiveness of the algorithm for recovering multiple systems from short unlabeled trajectories.
summary.tldr: A two-stage algorithm recovers mixtures of linear dynamical systems from short unlabeled trajectories with an end-to-end error guarantee.

title: Learning Mixtures of Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: We analyze the role of rotational equivariance in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) applied to spherical images. We compare the performance of the group equivariant networks known as S2CNNs and standard non-equivariant CNNs trained with an increasing amount of data augmentation. The chosen architectures can be considered baseline references for the respective design paradigms. Our models are trained and evaluated on single or multiple items from the MNIST- or FashionMNIST dataset projected onto the sphere. For the task of image classification, which is inherently rotationally invariant, we find that by considerably increasing the amount of data augmentation and the size of the networks, it is possible for the standard CNNs to reach at least the same performance as the equivariant network. In contrast, for the inherently equivariant task of semantic segmentation, the non-equivariant networks are consistently outperformed by the equivariant networks with significantly fewer parameters. We also analyze and compare the inference latency and training times of the different networks, enabling detailed tradeoff considerations between equivariant architectures and data augmentation for practical problems.

paragraphs: This paper compares two ways of handling rotations in images defined on a sphere. One builds rotational equivariance into the network architecture through S2CNNs. The other trains standard convolutional networks with increasing amounts of data augmentation. The comparison uses baseline architectures and images containing one or several MNIST or FashionMNIST items projected onto a sphere.

The results depend on the task. For classification, the desired label stays the same when an image rotates. Standard networks can reach at least the performance of the equivariant network when their size and the amount of augmentation increase considerably. In these experiments, augmentation and additional model capacity can therefore compensate for the architectural difference.

For semantic segmentation, the output must move consistently with the rotated input. Here, equivariant networks consistently outperform the standard networks while using significantly fewer parameters. The paper also compares training time and inference latency. These measurements help frame the practical choice around task behavior, model size, and computation rather than accuracy alone.
summary.tldr: On spherical-image tasks, augmentation can close the classification gap, while equivariant networks retain a clear segmentation advantage.

title: Equivariance versus Augmentation for Spherical Images

abstract: Transformer has achieved great successes in learning vision and language representation, which is general across various downstream tasks. In visual control, learning transferable state representation that can transfer between different control tasks is important to reduce the training sample size. However, porting Transformer to sample-efficient visual control remains a challenging and unsolved problem. To this end, we propose a novel Control Transformer (CtrlFormer), possessing many appealing benefits that prior arts do not have. Firstly, CtrlFormer jointly learns self-attention mechanisms between visual tokens and policy tokens among different control tasks, where multitask representation can be learned and transferred without catastrophic forgetting. Secondly, we carefully design a contrastive reinforcement learning paradigm to train CtrlFormer, enabling it to achieve high sample efficiency, which is important in control problems. For example, in the DMControl benchmark, unlike recent advanced methods that failed by producing a zero score in the “Cartpole” task after transfer learning with 100k samples, CtrlFormer can achieve a state-of-the-art score with only 100k samples while maintaining the performance of previous tasks. The code and models are released in our project homepage.

paragraphs: Visual-control agents must turn images into representations useful for choosing actions. Reusing those representations across control tasks could reduce the amount of training experience required. This paper introduces CtrlFormer, a transformer architecture designed to learn transferable representations while retaining performance on tasks the agent has already learned.

CtrlFormer jointly learns self-attention relationships involving visual tokens and policy tokens across different control tasks. This provides a structure for learning and transferring multitask representations. The authors pair the architecture with a contrastive reinforcement learning training approach intended to make learning efficient when environment interactions are limited.

The reported DMControl results illustrate both transfer and retention. In the Cartpole example, CtrlFormer reaches a state-of-the-art score with 100,000 samples after transfer while maintaining earlier task performance. Recent advanced methods described in the abstract instead obtain zero scores in that transfer setting with the same sample count. The example supports the proposed combination of architecture and training for efficient transfer; it does not establish that forgetting is absent in every possible task sequence.
summary.tldr: CtrlFormer combines multitask transformer representations with contrastive reinforcement learning to improve visual-control transfer while preserving prior-task performance.

title: CtrlFormer: Learning Transferable State Representation for Visual Control via Transformer

abstract: This paper considers the problem of measure estimation under the barycentric coding model (BCM), in which an unknown measure is assumed to belong to the set of Wasserstein-2 barycenters of a finite set of known measures. Estimating a measure under this model is equivalent to estimating the unknown barycentric coordinates. We provide novel geometrical, statistical, and computational insights for measure estimation under the BCM, consisting of three main results. Our first main result leverages the Riemannian geometry of Wasserstein-2 space to provide a procedure for recovering the barycentric coordinates as the solution to a quadratic optimization problem assuming access to the true reference measures. The essential geometric insight is that the parameters of this quadratic problem are determined by inner products between the optimal displacement maps from the given measure to the reference measures defining the BCM. Our second main result then establishes an algorithm for solving for the coordinates in the BCM when all the measures are observed empirically via i.i.d. samples. We prove precise rates of convergence for this algorithm—determined by the smoothness of the underlying measures and their dimensionality—thereby guaranteeing its statistical consistency. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of the BCM and associated estimation procedures in three application areas: (i) covariance estimation for Gaussian measures; (ii) image processing; and (iii) natural language processing.

paragraphs: The barycentric coding model assumes that an unknown probability measure is a Wasserstein-2 barycenter of finitely many known reference measures. Under this assumption, estimating the measure becomes a problem of finding its barycentric coordinates. These coordinates specify its position within the family of barycenters generated by the references.

The authors use the geometry of Wasserstein-2 space to express coordinate recovery as a quadratic optimization problem when the true reference measures are available. Its coefficients come from inner products between optimal displacement maps from the given measure to the references. This provides a concrete computational problem grounded in the geometry of transporting probability mass.

The paper then develops an algorithm for the more observational setting where all measures are represented by independent, identically distributed samples. It proves statistical consistency with convergence rates governed by dimension and smoothness. Applications in Gaussian covariance estimation, image processing, and natural language processing demonstrate the utility of the model and its estimation procedures across different kinds of data.
summary.tldr: The paper turns estimation within a Wasserstein barycenter model into coordinate recovery, with algorithms and statistical guarantees for sampled measures.

title: Measure Estimation in the Barycentric Coding Model

abstract: In this paper, we revisit Stochastic Continuous Submodular Maximization in both offline and online settings, which can benefit wide applications in machine learning and operations research areas. We present a boosting framework covering gradient ascent and online gradient ascent. The fundamental ingredient of our methods is a novel non-oblivious function $F$ derived from a factor-revealing optimization problem, whose any stationary point provides a $(1-e^{-\gamma})$-approximation to the global maximum of the $\gamma$-weakly DR-submodular objective function $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathcal{X})$. Under the offline scenario, we propose a boosting gradient ascent method achieving $(1-e^{-\gamma}-\epsilon^{2})$-approximation after $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations, which improves the $(\frac{\gamma^2}{1+\gamma^2})$ approximation ratio of the classical gradient ascent algorithm. In the online setting, for the first time we consider the adversarial delays for stochastic gradient feedback, under which we propose a boosting online gradient algorithm with the same non-oblivious function $F$. Meanwhile, we verify that this boosting online algorithm achieves a regret of $O(\sqrt{D})$ against a $(1-e^{-\gamma})$-approximation to the best feasible solution in hindsight, where $D$ is the sum of delays of gradient feedback. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result to obtain $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret against a $(1-e^{-\gamma})$-approximation with $O(1)$ gradient inquiry at each time step, when no delay exists, i.e., $D=T$. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our boosting methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic maximization of continuous objectives with a weak diminishing-returns structure, in both offline and online settings. Its key idea is to optimize a specially constructed auxiliary function F. For the stated smooth, gamma-weakly DR-submodular objectives, every stationary point of F gives a 1 − exp(−gamma) approximation to the original objective’s global maximum.

The offline algorithm uses this auxiliary function to boost gradient ascent. It achieves an approximation factor of 1 − exp(−gamma) − epsilon squared after O(1/epsilon squared) iterations, improving the stated approximation ratio of classical gradient ascent. The construction therefore changes what reaching a stationary point can guarantee about the original maximization problem.

For online learning, the same function supports an algorithm with adversarially delayed stochastic gradient feedback. Its regret is O(square root of D) relative to an approximate hindsight benchmark, where D summarizes feedback delays. Without delay, it obtains O(square root of T) regret with constant gradient queries per step. Numerical experiments also demonstrate the effectiveness of the boosting methods.
summary.tldr: An auxiliary objective strengthens gradient-based approximation guarantees for stochastic submodular maximization and supports online learning with delayed feedback.

title: Stochastic Continuous Submodular Maximization: Boosting via Non-oblivious Function

abstract: This paper focuses on the cluster description problem where, given a dataset and its partition into clusters, the task is to explain the clusters. We introduce a new approach to explain clusters by constructing a polyhedron around each cluster while minimizing either the complexity of the resulting polyhedra or the number of features used in the description. We formulate the cluster description problem as an integer program and present a column generation approach to search over an exponential number of candidate half-spaces that can be used to build the polyhedra. To deal with large datasets, we introduce a novel grouping scheme that first forms smaller groups of data points and then builds the polyhedra around the grouped data, a strategy which out-performs the common approach of sub-sampling data. Compared to state of the art cluster description algorithms, our approach is able to achieve competitive interpretability with improved description accuracy.

paragraphs: Once a dataset has been divided into clusters, a separate problem remains: explaining what distinguishes each group. This paper starts with an existing partition and constructs a geometric description around each cluster. Each description is a polyhedron, a region defined by combining linear boundaries, so cluster membership can be described through a collection of conditions on the data features.

The method explicitly optimizes for simpler descriptions, either by reducing the complexity of the polyhedra or by reducing the number of features they use. The authors formulate this choice as an integer program. Because there are exponentially many candidate half-spaces from which to construct the regions, they use column generation to search the candidate space.

For larger datasets, the authors first combine points into smaller groups and then construct descriptions around those groups. They report that this strategy performs better than subsampling the data. Against existing cluster description algorithms, the approach achieves improved description accuracy with competitive interpretability. The result shows how optimization can balance faithful explanations of an existing clustering with descriptions that remain manageable to inspect.
summary.tldr: The paper explains existing clusters using optimized polyhedra, improving description accuracy while retaining competitive interpretability.

title: Cluster Explanation via Polyhedral Descriptions

abstract: In this manuscript we consider the problem of generalized linear estimation on Gaussian mixture data with labels given by a single-index model. Our first result is a sharp asymptotic expression for the test and training errors in the high-dimensional regime. Motivated by the recent stream of results on the Gaussian universality of the test and training errors in generalized linear estimation, we ask ourselves the question: "when is a single Gaussian enough to characterize the error?". Our formula allows us to give sharp answers to this question, both in the positive and negative directions. More precisely, we show that the sufficient conditions for Gaussian universality (or lack thereof) crucially depend on the alignment between the target weights and the means and covariances of the mixture clusters, which we precisely quantify. In the particular case of least-squares interpolation, we prove a strong universality property of the training error and show it follows a simple, closed-form expression. Finally, we apply our results to real datasets, clarifying some recent discussions in the literature about Gaussian universality of the errors in this context.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a single Gaussian distribution can adequately characterize prediction errors for data drawn from a mixture of Gaussian clusters. The setting is generalized linear estimation, with labels produced by a single-index model. The authors derive a sharp expression for training and test errors in a high-dimensional asymptotic regime.

That expression lets them identify both situations where Gaussian universality holds and situations where it fails. Their sufficient conditions depend on how the target weights align with the cluster means and covariances. In plain language, the relationship between the prediction task and the geometry of the data clusters matters for whether a simpler Gaussian description captures the errors.

For least-squares interpolation, the authors establish a strong universality result specifically for training error and give a simple closed-form expression. They also apply their results to real datasets. The contribution is a more precise account of when Gaussian simplification is justified, with distinctions between the general estimation setting and this particular training-error result.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when Gaussian mixtures can be replaced by a single Gaussian for error analysis, depending on task–cluster alignment.

title: Are Gaussian Data All You Need? The Extents and Limits of Universality in High-Dimensional Generalized Linear Estimation

abstract: We study off-policy evaluation (OPE) of contextual bandit policies for large discrete action spaces where conventional importance-weighting approaches suffer from excessive variance. To circumvent this variance issue, we propose a new estimator, called OffCEM , that is based on the conjunct effect model (CEM), a novel decomposition of the causal effect into a cluster effect and a residual effect. OffCEM applies importance weighting only to action clusters and addresses the residual causal effect through model-based reward estimation. We show that the proposed estimator is unbiased under a new assumption, called local correctness , which only requires that the residual-effect model preserves the relative expected reward differences of the actions within each cluster. To best leverage the CEM and local correctness, we also propose a new two-step procedure for performing model-based estimation that minimizes bias in the first step and variance in the second step. We find that the resulting OffCEM estimator substantially improves bias and variance compared to a range of conventional estimators. Experiments demonstrate that OffCEM provides substantial improvements in OPE especially in the presence of many actions.

This paper proposes OffCEM, an estimator that divides the action effect into a shared cluster effect and an action-specific residual effect.

The authors report substantial bias and variance improvements over a range of conventional estimators, with experiments showing particular benefits when the action space is large. The result connects reduced weighting variance to a precise modeling requirement, making the role of within-cluster reward accuracy explicit.
summary.tldr: OffCEM combines cluster-level importance weighting with residual reward modeling to improve evaluation of policies with many actions.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation for Large Action Spaces via Conjunct Effect Modeling

abstract: Domain decomposition methods (DDMs) are popular solvers for discretized systems of partial differential equations (PDEs), with one-level and multilevel variants. These solvers rely on several algorithmic and mathematical parameters, prescribing overlap, subdomain boundary conditions, and other properties of the DDM. While some work has been done on optimizing these parameters, it has mostly focused on the one-level setting or special cases such as structured-grid discretizations with regular subdomain construction. In this paper, we propose multigrid graph neural networks (MG-GNN), a novel GNN architecture for learning optimized parameters in two-level DDMs. We train MG-GNN using a new unsupervised loss function, enabling effective training on small problems that yields robust performance on unstructured grids that are orders of magnitude larger than those in the training set. We show that MG-GNN outperforms popular hierarchical graph network architectures for this optimization and that our proposed loss function is critical to achieving this improved performance.

paragraphs: Domain decomposition methods solve discretized partial differential equations by working with subdomains. The approach is trained on small problems and evaluated on unstructured grids orders of magnitude larger, directly testing whether learned parameter choices remain useful as problem size increases.

The reported results show robust performance on these larger grids and better optimization performance than popular hierarchical graph-network architectures. The authors also find that the new loss is critical to the improvement. The contribution therefore combines an architecture with a training objective, demonstrating that both matter when learning parameters for numerical solvers that must work beyond training-scale problems.
summary.tldr: MG-GNN learns two-level domain-decomposition parameters on small problems and performs robustly on much larger unstructured grids.

title: MG-GNN: Multigrid Graph Neural Networks for Learning Multilevel Domain Decomposition Methods

abstract: In personalized federated learning (PFL), multiple clients train customized models to fulfill their personal objectives, which, however, are prone to overfitting to local data due to the heterogeneity and scarcity of local data. To address this, we propose from the information-theoretic perspective a personalized federated learning framework based on the common representation learned across clients, named FedCR. Specifically, we introduce to the local client update a regularizer that aims at minimizing the discrepancy between local and global conditional mutual information (CMI), such that clients are encouraged to learn and exploit the common representation. Upon this, each client learns individually a customized predictor (head), while the extractor (body) remains to be aggregated by the server. Our CMI regularizer leads to a theoretically sound alignment between the local and global stochastic feature distributions in terms of their Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. More importantly, by modeling the global joint feature distribution as a product of multiple local feature distributions, clients can efficiently extract diverse information from the global data but without need of the raw data from other clients. We further show that noise injection via feature alignment and ensemble of local predictors in FedCR would help enhance its generalization capability. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate a consistent performance gain and better generalization behavior of FedCR.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning gives each client a model suited to its own objectives. However, scarce and heterogeneous local data can make those models overfit. FedCR addresses this by encouraging clients to learn representations shared across the federation while retaining individually trained prediction heads.

During local updates, FedCR adds a regularizer that reduces disagreement between local and global conditional mutual information. The server aggregates the feature extractor, while each client customizes its predictor. The authors theoretically connect this regularization to alignment between local and global stochastic feature distributions, measured through Kullback-Leibler divergence.

Benchmark experiments report consistent performance gains and better generalization behavior. The overall approach balances shared feature learning with client-specific decisions, addressing overfitting without giving up personalization.
summary.tldr: FedCR combines shared feature learning, information-based regularization, and personalized prediction heads to improve federated generalization.

title: FedCR: Personalized Federated Learning Based on Across-Client Common Representation with Conditional Mutual Information Regularization

abstract: Simple regret is a natural and parameter-free performance criterion for pure exploration in multi-armed bandits yet is less popular than the probability of missing the best arm or an $\epsilon$-good arm, perhaps due to lack of easy ways to characterize it. In this paper, we make a significant progress on minimizing simple regret in both data-rich ($T\ge n$) and data-poor regime ($T \le n$) where $n$ is the number of arms and $T$ is the number of samples. At its heart is our improved instance-dependent analysis of the well-known Sequential Halving (SH) algorithm where we bound the probability of returning an arm whose mean reward is not within $\epsilon$ from the best (i.e., not $\epsilon$-good) for any choice of $\epsilon>0$, although $\epsilon$ is not an input to SH. Our bound not only leads to an optimal worst-case simple regret bound of $\sqrt{n/T}$ up to logarithmic factors but also essentially matches the instance-dependent lower bound for returning an $\epsilon$-good arm reported by Katz-Samuels and Jamieson (2020). For the more challenging data-poor regime, we propose Bracketing SH (BSH) that enjoys the same improvement even without sampling each arm at least once. Our empirical study shows that BSH outperforms existing methods on real-world tasks.

paragraphs: In pure-exploration bandit problems, sampling serves to identify a good option for eventual use. Simple regret measures how far the selected option’s mean reward falls below the best. This paper improves guarantees for that criterion both when the sampling budget is at least the number of options and when there are too few samples to inspect every option.

The central result is a sharper, instance-dependent analysis of Sequential Halving. It bounds the probability of selecting an option more than epsilon below the best for every positive epsilon, even though the algorithm does not take epsilon as an input. The analysis yields a worst-case simple regret rate of square root of n/T, optimal up to logarithmic factors.

The bound also essentially matches an existing instance-dependent lower bound for identifying an epsilon-good option. For the data-poor setting, the authors introduce Bracketing Sequential Halving, which obtains the same improvement without requiring every option to be sampled. Experiments on real-world tasks show this variant outperforming the compared methods. The contribution combines stronger guarantees for a familiar algorithm with a variant designed for limited sampling budgets.
summary.tldr: Sharper Sequential Halving analysis and a bracketing variant improve guarantees for selecting a good bandit arm, including when samples are scarce.

title: Revisiting Simple Regret: Fast Rates for Returning a Good Arm

abstract: The popularity of federated learning comes from the possibility of better scalability and the ability for participants to keep control of their data, improving data security and sovereignty. Unfortunately, sharing model updates also creates a new privacy attack surface. In this work, we characterize the privacy guarantees of decentralized learning with random walk algorithms, where a model is updated by traveling from one node to another along the edges of a communication graph. Using a recent variant of differential privacy tailored to the study of decentralized algorithms, namely Pairwise Network Differential Privacy, we derive closed-form expressions for the privacy loss between each pair of nodes where the impact of the communication topology is captured by graph theoretic quantities. Our results further reveal that random walk algorithms tends to yield better privacy guarantees than gossip algorithms for nodes close from each other. We supplement our theoretical results with empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world graphs and datasets.

paragraphs: Keeping training data with individual participants does not eliminate privacy risks, because shared model updates can still expose information. This paper studies decentralized learning in which a model travels between connected participants and is updated as it goes. The route follows a random walk on the network’s communication graph.

The authors analyze this process using Pairwise Network Differential Privacy, a privacy notion tailored to decentralized algorithms. They derive closed-form expressions for privacy loss between pairs of nodes. Graph-theoretic quantities describe how the communication topology affects those expressions, making the arrangement of connections an explicit part of the privacy analysis rather than treating all participants identically.

The results indicate that random-walk algorithms tend to provide stronger privacy guarantees than gossip algorithms for nodes that are close to one another. This is a qualified comparison tied to network proximity. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world graphs and datasets supplement the theory, helping connect the mathematical characterization to decentralized learning settings.
summary.tldr: Pairwise privacy formulas reveal how network structure shapes privacy in random-walk learning, with advantages over gossip methods for nearby nodes.

title: Differentially Private Decentralized Learning with Random Walks

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm that safeguards privacy by retaining client data on edge devices. However, optimizing FL in practice can be challenging due to the diverse and heterogeneous nature of the learning system. Though recent research has focused on improving the optimization of FL when distribution shifts occur among clients, ensuring global performance when multiple types of distribution shifts occur simultaneously among clients—such as feature distribution shift, label distribution shift, and concept shift—remain under-explored. In this paper, we identify the learning challenges posed by the simultaneous occurrence of diverse distribution shifts and propose a clustering principle to overcome these challenges. Through our research, we find that existing methods fail to address the clustering principle. Therefore, we propose a novel clustering algorithm framework, dubbed as FedRC, which adheres to our proposed clustering principle by incorporating a bi-level optimization problem and a novel objective function. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedRC significantly outperforms other SOTA cluster-based FL methods. Our code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps training data on clients, but those clients can differ in several ways at once. Their input features may have different distributions, their label frequencies may differ, and the relationship between inputs and labels may change. This paper focuses on the challenge of maintaining global performance when these forms of distribution shift occur together.

The authors identify learning difficulties created by simultaneous shifts and propose a principle for clustering clients to address them. They find that existing methods do not satisfy this principle. Their framework, FedRC, introduces a new objective and a bi-level optimization problem, using two linked levels of optimization to implement the proposed clustering approach.

Extensive experiments report significant gains over other state-of-the-art cluster-based federated learning methods. The findings support treating the coexistence of different shifts as a distinct design problem for client clustering. FedRC's contribution is therefore both conceptual and algorithmic: it specifies a clustering principle for this setting and provides a framework intended to follow it.
summary.tldr: FedRC uses a new clustering principle and bi-level optimization to improve federated learning when multiple distribution shifts coexist.

title: FedRC: Tackling Diverse Distribution Shifts Challenge in Federated Learning by Robust Clustering

abstract: We propose a model-based offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for confounded partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) under general function approximations and show it is provably efficient under some technical conditions such as the partial coverage imposed on the offline data distribution. Specifically, we first establish a novel model-based identification result for learning the effect of any action on the reward and future transitions in the confounded POMDP. Using this identification result, we then design a nonparametric two-stage estimation procedure to construct an estimator for off-policy evaluation (OPE), which permits general function approximations. Finally, we learn the optimal policy by performing a conservative policy optimization within the confidence regions based on the proposed estimation procedure for OPE. Under some mild conditions, we establish a finite-sample upper bound on the suboptimality of the learned policy in finding the optimal one, which depends on the sample size and the length of horizons polynomially.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from recorded experience becomes harder when the environment is only partially observed and the data are confounded. This paper develops a model-based offline reinforcement learning algorithm for that setting. It permits general function approximation and establishes efficiency under technical conditions that include partial coverage by the offline data.

The first contribution is an identification result for the effects of actions on rewards and future transitions. Building on it, the authors construct a nonparametric two-stage estimator for off-policy evaluation, which assesses policies using the existing dataset. They then optimize conservatively within confidence regions derived from that estimation procedure, connecting policy selection to uncertainty in the evaluation.

Under the stated conditions, the paper gives a finite-sample upper bound on how far the learned policy is from optimal. The bound has polynomial dependence on sample size and horizon length. The result provides a theoretical learning route through identification, evaluation, and conservative optimization, with its guarantee explicitly depending on the assumptions imposed on the problem and available data.
summary.tldr: A model-based offline RL method learns policies in confounded, partially observed environments with finite-sample guarantees under technical coverage and estimation conditions.

title: Model-based Reinforcement Learning for Confounded POMDPs

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have gained considerable attention for their excellent natural language processing capabilities. Nonetheless, these LLMs present many challenges, particularly in the realm of trustworthiness. This paper introduces TrustLLM, a comprehensive study of trustworthiness in LLMs, including principles for different dimensions of trustworthiness, established benchmark, evaluation, and analysis of trustworthiness for mainstream LLMs, and discussion of open challenges and future directions. Specifically, we first propose a set of principles for trustworthy LLMs that span eight different dimensions. Based on these principles, we further establish a benchmark across six dimensions including truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, and machine ethics. We then present a study evaluating 16 mainstream LLMs in TrustLLM, consisting of over 30 datasets. Our findings firstly show that in general trustworthiness and capability (i.e., functional effectiveness) are positively related. Secondly, our observations reveal that proprietary LLMs generally outperform most open-source counterparts in terms of trustworthiness, raising concerns about the potential risks of widely accessible open-source LLMs. However, a few open-source LLMs come very close to proprietary ones, suggesting that open-source models can achieve high levels of trustworthiness without additional mechanisms like *moderator*, offering valuable insights for developers in this field. Thirdly, it is important to note that some LLMs may be overly calibrated towards exhibiting trustworthiness, to the extent that they compromise their utility by mistakenly treating benign prompts as harmful and consequently not responding. Besides these observations, we've uncovered key insights into the multifaceted trustworthiness in LLMs. We emphasize the importance of ensuring transparency not only in the models themselves but also in the technologies that underpin trustworthiness. We advocate that the establishment of an AI alliance between industry, academia, the open-source community to foster collaboration is imperative to advance the trustworthiness of LLMs.

The authors interpret those exceptions as evidence that open-source models can achieve high trustworthiness without additional mechanisms such as a moderator.

The paper also observes that some models refuse benign prompts after mistakenly treating them as harmful, sacrificing usefulness through excessive caution. Its findings therefore concern both harmful behavior and unnecessary restrictions on legitimate use. Beyond evaluation, the authors advocate transparency in models and in the technologies used to support trustworthiness, along with collaboration among industry, academia, and the open-source community.
summary.tldr: TrustLLM evaluates multiple dimensions of language-model trustworthiness, finding broad capability correlations alongside model differences and unnecessary refusals.

title: Position: TrustLLM: Trustworthiness in Large Language Models

abstract: This work studies algorithms for learning from aggregate responses. We focus on the construction of aggregation sets (called bags in the literature) for event-level loss functions. We prove for linear regression and generalized linear models (GLMs) that the optimal bagging problem reduces to one-dimensional size-constrained $k$-means clustering. Further, we theoretically quantify the advantage of using curated bags over random bags. We then propose the $\texttt{PriorBoost}$ algorithm, which adaptively forms bags of samples that are increasingly homogeneous with respect to (unobserved) individual responses to improve model quality. We study label differential privacy for aggregate learning, and we also provide extensive experiments showing that $\texttt{PriorBoost}$ regularly achieves optimal model quality for event-level predictions, in stark contrast to non-adaptive algorithms.

paragraphs: Learning from aggregate responses means training with information about groups of samples while seeking predictions for individual events. This paper focuses on how those groups, called bags, should be constructed. The grouping decision matters because a model trained on aggregate responses must still support an objective defined at the individual-event level.

For linear regression and generalized linear models, the authors prove that optimal bag construction reduces to one-dimensional k-means clustering with size constraints. They also quantify the advantage of deliberately curated bags over random ones. This analysis makes grouping a central part of the learning problem rather than a fixed preprocessing choice.

PriorBoost uses these ideas to form bags adaptively, making their members increasingly similar in their unobserved individual responses. The intended effect is to improve model quality as the grouping process evolves. The paper also studies label differential privacy in aggregate learning. Extensive experiments report that PriorBoost regularly reaches optimal quality for individual-event predictions, unlike non-adaptive alternatives. The empirical claim is about its recurring success, not a guarantee that every adaptive grouping achieves the optimum.
summary.tldr: PriorBoost adaptively groups samples with increasingly similar hidden responses to improve individual predictions learned from aggregate labels.

title: PriorBoost: An Adaptive Algorithm for Learning from Aggregate Responses

abstract: We focus on s-rectangular robust Markov decision processes (MDPs), which capture interconnected uncertainties across different actions within each state. This framework is more general compared to sa-rectangular robust MDPs, where uncertainties in each action are independent. However, the introduced interdependence significantly amplifies the complexity of the problem. Existing methods either have slow performance guarantees or are inapplicable to even moderately large state spaces. In this work, we derive optimal robust Bellman operators in explicit forms. This leads to robust value iteration methods with significantly faster time complexities than existing approaches, which can be used in large state spaces. Further, our findings reveal that the optimal policies demonstrate a novel threshold behavior, selectively favoring a limited set of actions based on their respective advantage functions. Additionally, our study uncovers a noteworthy connection between the robustness of a policy and the variance in its value function, highlighting that policies with lower variance exhibit greater resilience.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes account for uncertainty when choosing actions. This paper studies the s-rectangular setting, where uncertainties for different actions at the same state can be interconnected. That coupling makes the framework more general than one that treats each action's uncertainty independently, but also makes the planning problem harder to solve.

The authors derive explicit expressions for optimal robust Bellman operators, the updates used to compute robust values. These expressions lead to value iteration algorithms with substantially faster time complexity than existing approaches. The improvement matters because previous methods either had slow guarantees or became impractical even with moderately many states.

The analysis also reveals structure in the resulting decisions. Optimal policies exhibit threshold behavior, selecting a limited collection of actions according to their advantage functions. The authors additionally connect robustness to variation in the value function: lower variance corresponds to greater resilience in their analysis. Together, these results provide faster planning methods and a clearer account of how robust policies select actions under coupled uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Explicit robust Bellman updates make planning with coupled action uncertainties faster and reveal threshold structure in optimal policies.

title: Efficient Value Iteration for s-rectangular Robust Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Amortized variational inference is an often employed framework in simulation-based inference that produces a posterior approximation that can be rapidly computed given any new observation. Unfortunately, there are few guarantees about the quality of these approximate posteriors. We propose Conformalized Amortized Neural Variational Inference (CANVI), a procedure that is scalable, easily implemented, and provides guaranteed marginal coverage. Given a collection of candidate amortized posterior approximators, CANVI constructs conformalized predictors based on each candidate, compares the predictors using a metric known as predictive efficiency, and returns the most efficient predictor. CANVI ensures that the resulting predictor constructs regions that contain the truth with a user-specified level of probability. CANVI is agnostic to design decisions in formulating the candidate approximators and only requires access to samples from the forward model, permitting its use in likelihood-free settings. We prove lower bounds on the predictive efficiency of the regions produced by CANVI and explore how the quality of a posterior approximation relates to the predictive efficiency of prediction regions based on that approximation. Finally, we demonstrate the accurate calibration and high predictive efficiency of CANVI on a suite of simulation-based inference benchmark tasks and an important scientific task: analyzing galaxy emission spectra.

Unfortunately, there are few guarantees about the quality of these approximate posteriors. We propose Conformalized Amortized Neural Variational Inference (CANVI), a procedure that is scalable, easily implemented, and provides guaranteed marginal coverage. Given a collection of candidate amortized posterior approximators, CANVI constructs conformalized predictors based on each candidate, compares the predictors using a metric known as predictive efficiency, and returns the most efficient predictor. CANVI ensures that the resulting predictor constructs regions that contain the truth with a user-specified level of probability. CANVI is agnostic to design decisions in formulating the candidate approximators and only requires access to samples from the forward model, permitting its use in likelihood-free settings. We prove lower bounds on the predictive efficiency of the regions produced by CANVI and explore how the quality of a posterior approximation relates to the predictive efficiency of prediction regions based on that approximation. Finally, we demonstrate the accurate calibration and high predictive efficiency of CANVI on a suite of simulation-based inference benchmark tasks and an important scientific task: analyzing galaxy emission spectra.

paragraphs: Amortized variational inference produces fast approximate posteriors for new observations, but those approximations often come with few quality guarantees. CANVI adds a conformal procedure that constructs regions with a user-chosen probability of containing the truth. Its guarantee is marginal coverage, describing coverage across the relevant collection of cases rather than a separate guarantee for each observation.

Given several candidate posterior approximators, CANVI constructs conformalized predictors from each and compares their predictive efficiency. It returns the most efficient predictor while retaining the stated coverage guarantee. The procedure does not depend on particular design choices for the candidate approximators and only requires samples from the forward model, allowing use when likelihoods are unavailable.

The authors prove lower bounds on predictive efficiency and examine how posterior approximation quality relates to the efficiency of the resulting regions. Experiments on simulation-based inference benchmarks and galaxy emission spectra demonstrate accurate calibration and high predictive efficiency. The contribution connects fast approximate inference with guaranteed coverage while also comparing how efficiently candidate models produce useful prediction regions.
summary.tldr: CANVI converts approximate posteriors into prediction regions with guaranteed marginal coverage and selects among candidates by predictive efficiency.

title: Variational Inference with Coverage Guarantees in Simulation-Based Inference

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) from temporal logical specifications is a fundamental problem in sequential decision making. One of the basic and core such specification is the reachability specification that requires a target set to be eventually visited. Despite strong empirical results for RL from such specifications, the theoretical guarantees are bleak, including the impossibility of Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) guarantee for reachability specifications. Given the impossibility result, in this work we consider the problem of RL from reachability specifications along with the information of expected conditional distance (ECD). We present (a) lower bound results which establish the necessity of ECD information for PAC guarantees and (b) an algorithm that establishes PAC-guarantees given the ECD information. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first RL from reachability specifications that does not make any assumptions on the underlying environment to learn policies.

They consider providing the learner with expected conditional distance information, abbreviated ECD. summary.tldr: Expected conditional distance information enables PAC-guaranteed reachability learning, with lower bounds establishing its necessity in the studied setting.

title: Reinforcement Learning from Reachability Specifications: PAC Guarantees with Expected Conditional Distance

abstract: In this work, we investigate how people use text-to-image models to generate desired target images. To study this interaction, we created ArtWhisperer, an online game where users are given a target image and are tasked with iteratively finding a prompt that creates a similar-looking image as the target. Through this game, we recorded over 50,000 human-AI interactions; each interaction corresponds to one text prompt created by a user and the corresponding generated image. The majority of these are repeated interactions where a user iterates to find the best prompt for their target image, making this a unique sequential dataset for studying human-AI collaborations. In an initial analysis of this dataset, we identify several characteristics of prompt interactions and user strategies. People submit diverse prompts and are able to discover a variety of text descriptions that generate similar images. Interestingly, prompt diversity does not decrease as users find better prompts. We further propose a new metric to quantify AI model steerability using our dataset. We define steerability as the expected number of interactions required to adequately complete a task. We estimate this value by fitting a Markov chain for each target task and calculating the expected time to reach an adequate score. We quantify and compare AI steerability across different types of target images and two different models, finding that images of cities and nature are more steerable than artistic and fantasy images. We also evaluate popular vision-language models to assess their image understanding and ability to incorporate feedback. These findings provide insights into human-AI interaction behavior, present a concrete method of assessing AI steerability, and demonstrate the general utility of the ArtWhisperer dataset.

title: ArtWhisperer: A Dataset for Characterizing Human-AI Interactions in Artistic Creations

abstract: In this work, we investigate an intriguing and prevalent phenomenon of diffusion models which we term as "consistent model reproducibility”: given the same starting noise input and a deterministic sampler, different diffusion models often yield remarkably similar outputs. We confirm this phenomenon through comprehensive experiments, implying that different diffusion models consistently reach the same data distribution and score function regardless of diffusion model frameworks, model architectures, or training procedures. More strikingly, our further investigation implies that diffusion models are learning distinct distributions influenced by the training data size. This is evident in two distinct training regimes: (I) "memorization regime,” where the diffusion model overfits to the training data distribution, and (ii) "generalization regime,” where the model learns the underlying data distribution. Our study also finds that this valuable property generalizes to many variants of diffusion models, including those for conditional generation and solving inverse problems. Lastly, we discuss how our findings connect to existing research and highlight the practical implications of our discoveries.

This paper investigates that phenomenon experimentally under the name consistent model reproducibility. The comparison concerns agreement across models, extending the idea of reproducibility beyond rerunning a single fixed model.

The experiments suggest that different frameworks, architectures, and training procedures can lead models toward the same data distribution and score function. Further investigation points to training-data size as an influence on which distribution is learned. The authors distinguish a memorization regime, in which models overfit the training-data distribution, from a generalization regime, in which they learn the underlying data distribution.

The study also observes the reproducibility property in variants used for conditional generation and inverse problems. These findings suggest that shared generation behavior is a broader empirical pattern across diffusion approaches. The same-noise and deterministic-sampling conditions are central to the observation, while the distinction between memorization and generalization clarifies that similar outputs across models need to be interpreted alongside the distribution those models have learned.
summary.tldr: Experiments find that different diffusion models often generate similar outputs from identical noise, with training-data size influencing memorization and generalization regimes.

title: The Emergence of Reproducibility and Consistency in Diffusion Models

abstract: Existing analysis of Local (Stochastic) Gradient Descent for heterogeneous objectives requires stepsizes $\eta \leq 1/K$ where $K$ is the communication interval, which ensures monotonic decrease of the objective. In contrast, we analyze Local Gradient Descent for logistic regression with separable, heterogeneous data using any stepsize $\eta > 0$. With $R$ communication rounds and $M$ clients, we show convergence at a rate $\mathcal{O}(1/\eta K R)$ after an initial unstable phase lasting for $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\eta K M)$ rounds. This improves upon the existing $\mathcal{O}(1/R)$ rate for general smooth, convex objectives. Our analysis parallels the single machine analysis of Wu et al. (2024) in which instability is caused by extremely large stepsizes, but in our setting another source of instability is large local updates with heterogeneous objectives.

paragraphs: Local gradient descent lets clients perform multiple updates between communication rounds. Existing analyses for heterogeneous objectives restrict the stepsize to at most 1/K, where K is the communication interval, to keep the objective decreasing monotonically. This paper examines whether that restriction is needed for logistic regression with separable, heterogeneous data.

The authors allow any positive constant stepsize η. They show that, after an initial unstable phase, convergence follows a rate of O(1/(ηKR)), where R is the number of communication rounds. The initial phase lasts roughly O(ηKM) rounds, up to the factors suppressed by the stated bound, with M denoting the number of clients.

The result exposes a trade-off: larger stepsizes or longer local update intervals improve the eventual rate while lengthening the bound on the unstable phase. The analysis improves on the cited O(1/R) rate for general smooth convex objectives in this specific setting. It also identifies heterogeneous local updates as a source of instability, alongside extremely large stepsizes.
summary.tldr: For separable heterogeneous logistic regression, Local GD can converge faster after an unstable phase without restricting the positive constant stepsize.

title: Constant Stepsize Local GD for Logistic Regression: Acceleration by Instability

abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) aim to constrain the outputs and gradients of deep learning models to satisfy specified governing physics equations, which have demonstrated significant potential for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). Although existing PINN methods have achieved pleasing performance, they always treat both easy and hard sample points indiscriminately, especially ones in the physical boundaries. This easily causes the PINN model to fall into undesirable local minima and unstable learning, thereby resulting in an Unbalanced Prediction Problem (UPP). To deal with this daunting problem, we propose a novel framework named Cognitive Physical Informed Neural Network (CoPINN) that imitates the human cognitive learning manner from easy to hard. Specifically, we first employ separable subnetworks to encode independent one-dimensional coordinates and apply an aggregation scheme to generate multi-dimensional predicted physical variables. Then, during the training phase, we dynamically evaluate the difficulty of each sample according to the gradient of the PDE residuals. Finally, we propose a cognitive training scheduler to progressively optimize the entire sampling regions from easy to hard, thereby embracing robustness and generalization against predicting physical boundary regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our CoPINN achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly significantly reducing prediction errors in stubborn regions.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions while encouraging their outputs and gradients to satisfy governing physical equations. The paper identifies a training problem: treating easy and difficult sample locations alike can lead to unstable learning and uneven prediction quality. Physical boundaries are a particular concern because errors can remain concentrated in difficult regions.

CoPINN introduces an easy-to-hard training process inspired by human learning. Its architecture first encodes individual one-dimensional coordinates with separate subnetworks, then combines them to predict multidimensional physical variables. During training, it dynamically estimates each sample's difficulty using gradients of the residuals of the partial differential equation, which measure departures from satisfying the equation.

A training scheduler uses those difficulty estimates to progressively optimize across the sampled regions. This links the order of learning to the model's changing assessment of the problem. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, with especially substantial error reductions in stubborn regions. The findings support the value of difficulty-aware scheduling for more robust predictions, particularly around physical boundaries.
summary.tldr: CoPINN schedules physics-informed learning from easy to difficult locations, reporting especially strong error reductions in challenging physical regions.

title: CoPINN: Cognitive Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: This paper introduces Graphon Attachment Network Models (GAN-M), a novel framework for modeling evolving networks with rich structural dependencies, grounded in graphon theory. GAN-M provides a flexible and interpretable foundation for studying network formation by leveraging graphon functions to define attachment probabilities, thereby combining the strengths of graphons with a temporal perspective. A key contribution of this work is a methodology for learning structural changes in these networks over time. Our approach uses graph counts—frequencies of substructures such as triangles and stars—to capture shifts in network topology. We propose a new statistic designed to learn changes in the resulting piecewise polynomial signals and develop an efficient method for change detection, supported by theoretical guarantees. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across various network settings, highlighting its potential for dynamic network analysis.

Graphon functions determine attachment probabilities, giving the framework a temporal perspective alongside a flexible and interpretable description of connection structure.

This connects observable substructure frequencies to changes in the evolving network.

Together, the modeling framework and detection procedure provide a route for studying structural transitions through small-pattern counts, with the reported results highlighting its potential for dynamic network analysis.
summary.tldr: GAN-M models evolving network attachment and detects structural changes through signals built from small-subgraph counts.

title: Learning Changes in Graphon Attachment Network Models

abstract: Extending the context length of Language Models (LMs) by improving Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) has become a trend. While prior works mainly address RoPE’s limitations within attention, this paper uncovers the adverse effects on length generalization from nearly all parts of LMs. Using Discrete Signal Processing theory, we show that RoPE enables periodic attention by implicitly achieving Non-Uniform Discrete Fourier Transform. However, this periodicity is undermined by the spectrum damage caused by: 1) linear layers and activation functions outside of attention; 2) insufficiently trained frequency components brought by time-domain truncation. Building on our observations, we propose Fourier Position Embedding (FoPE), which enhances attention’s frequency-domain properties to improve both its periodic extension and length generalization. FoPE constructs Fourier Series and zero-outs the destructive frequency components, increasing model robustness against the spectrum damage. Experiments across various model scales and benchmarks show that, within varying context windows, FoPE maintains a more stable performance compared to other baselines. Several analyses and ablations bring further support to our method and theoretical modeling.

paragraphs: Position embeddings help language models use token order, but extending their behavior to longer contexts remains difficult. This paper studies Rotary Position Embedding through discrete signal processing. It argues that length generalization depends on operations throughout the model, extending beyond the attention mechanism where many earlier improvements have concentrated.

The findings suggest that preserving useful frequency behavior is a productive direction for improving context-length generalization.
summary.tldr: Fourier Position Embedding removes destructive frequency components to make attention more robust and performance more stable across context lengths.

title: Fourier Position Embedding: Enhancing Attention’s Periodic Extension for Length Generalization

abstract: With large language models (LLMs) increasingly deployed as cognitive engines for AI agents, the reliability and effectiveness critically hinge on their intrinsic epistemic agency, which remains understudied. Epistemic agency, the ability to flexibly construct, adapt, and monitor beliefs about dynamic environments, represents a base-model-level capacity independent of specific tools, modules, or applications. We characterize the holistic process underlying epistemic agency, which unfolds in seven interrelated dimensions: prediction, decision-making, perception, memory, counterfactual thinking, belief updating, and meta-reflection. Correspondingly, we propose Reflection-Bench, a cognitive-psychology-inspired benchmark consisting of seven tasks with long-term relevance and minimization of data leakage. Through a comprehensive evaluation of 16 models using three prompting strategies, we identify a clear three-tier performance hierarchy and significant limitations of current LLMs, particularly in meta-reflection capabilities. While state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate rudimentary signs of epistemic agency, our findings suggest several promising research directions, including enhancing core cognitive functions, improving cross-functional coordination, and developing adaptive processing mechanisms. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/ReflectionBench.

paragraphs: An AI agent needs to form beliefs about its environment, revise them when circumstances change, and monitor its own reasoning. This paper studies that collection of abilities under the name epistemic agency. It treats them as capacities of the underlying language model, independent of the particular tools, extra modules, or applications surrounding the model.

The benchmark makes these interconnected abilities explicit targets for evaluating the reliability of model-based agents.
summary.tldr: Reflection-Bench evaluates seven belief-management abilities and finds substantial weaknesses in current models, particularly in meta-reflection.

title: Reflection-Bench: Evaluating Epistemic Agency in Large Language Models

abstract: Text-to-SQL, which enables natural language interaction with databases, serves as a pivotal method across diverse industries. With new, more powerful large language models (LLMs) emerging every few months, fine-tuning has become incredibly costly, labor-intensive, and error-prone. As an alternative, zero-shot Text-to-SQL, which leverages the growing knowledge and reasoning capabilities encoded in LLMs without task-specific fine-tuning, presents a promising and more challenging direction. To address this challenge, we propose Alpha-SQL, a novel approach that leverages a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework to iteratively infer SQL construction actions based on partial reasoning states. To enhance the framework’s reasoning capabilities, we introduce LLM-as-Action-Model to dynamically generate SQL construction actions during the MCTS process, steering the search toward more promising SQL queries. Moreover, Alpha-SQL employs a self-supervised reward function to evaluate the quality of candidate SQL queries, ensuring more accurate and efficient query generation. Experimental results show that Alpha-SQL achieves 69.7% execution accuracy on the BIRD development set, using a 32B open-source LLM without fine-tuning. Alpha-SQL outperforms the best previous zero-shot approach based on GPT-4o by 2.5% on the BIRD development set.

paragraphs: Turning a natural-language question into SQL requires choosing a sequence of query-building decisions. Alpha-SQL tackles this task without task-specific fine-tuning, motivated by the expense and effort of repeatedly adapting newly released language models. Its central idea is to search through possible constructions instead of relying on a single generated query.

The method uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to explore SQL construction from partially completed reasoning states. A language model acts as an action generator, proposing possible next construction steps during the search. This makes the available actions responsive to the current reasoning state. summary.tldr: Alpha-SQL uses language-model-guided tree search to build SQL queries without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: Alpha-SQL: Zero-Shot Text-to-SQL using Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Protein sequence design has seen significant advances through discrete diffusion and autoregressive approaches, yet the potential of continuous diffusion remains underexplored. Here, we present DiMA, a latent diffusion framework that operates on protein language model representations. Through systematic exploration of architectural choices and diffusion components, we develop a robust methodology that generalizes across multiple protein encoders ranging from 8M to 3B parameters. We demonstrate that our framework achieves consistently high performance across sequence-only (ESM-2, ESMc), dual-decodable (CHEAP), and multimodal (SaProt) representations using the same architecture and training approach. We conduct extensive evaluation of existing methods alongside DiMA using multiple metrics across two protein modalities, covering quality, diversity, novelty, and distribution matching of generated proteins. DiMA consistently produces novel, high-quality and diverse protein sequences and achieves strong results compared to baselines such as autoregressive, discrete diffusion and flow matching language models. The model demonstrates versatile functionality, supporting conditional generation tasks including protein family-generation, motif scaffolding and infilling, and fold-specific sequence design, despite being trained solely on sequence data. This work provides a universal continuous diffusion framework for protein sequence generation, offering both architectural insights and practical applicability across various protein design scenarios. Code is released at GitHub.

Evaluation examines quality, diversity, novelty, and distribution matching across two protein modalities. DiMA produces novel, diverse, high-quality sequences and reports strong results against autoregressive, discrete diffusion, and flow-matching language models. It also supports protein-family generation, motif scaffolding, infilling, and fold-specific sequence design despite training solely on sequence data. The findings position continuous diffusion over language-model encodings as a flexible approach to several protein sequence design tasks.
summary.tldr: DiMA applies continuous diffusion to protein language-model representations, generating diverse sequences and supporting multiple conditional design tasks.

title: Diffusion on Language Model Encodings for Protein Sequence Generation

abstract: Recently, latent action learning, pioneered by Latent Action Policies (LAPO), have shown remarkable pre-training efficiency on observation-only data, offering potential for leveraging vast amounts of video available on the web for embodied AI. However, prior work has focused on distractor-free data, where changes between observations are primarily explained by ground-truth actions. Unfortunately, real-world videos contain action-correlated distractors that may hinder latent action learning. Using Distracting Control Suite (DCS) we empirically investigate the effect of distractors on latent action learning and demonstrate that LAPO struggle in such scenario. We propose LAOM, a simple LAPO modification that improves the quality of latent actions by 8x, as measured by linear probing. Importantly, we show that providing supervision with ground-truth actions, as few as 2.5% of the full dataset, during latent action learning improves downstream performance by 4.2x on average. Our findings suggest that integrating supervision during Latent Action Models (LAM) training is critical in the presence of distractors, challenging the conventional pipeline of first learning LAM and only then decoding from latent to ground-truth actions.
