paragraphs: Latent action learning aims to extract action-like representations from observations without requiring action labels throughout pre-training. That makes video a potentially valuable resource for embodied AI. This paper examines a complication: real videos contain distracting changes correlated with actions, whereas earlier work mainly studied observations whose changes were explained by the actual actions.

Using the Distracting Control Suite, the authors show empirically that Latent Action Policies, or LAPO, struggle with these distractors. They introduce LAOM, a simple modification that improves latent-action quality eightfold according to linear probing. This evaluates the learned representation separately from its eventual use in a downstream task.

The authors also provide ground-truth action supervision during representation learning. With labels for as little as 2.5% of the full dataset, downstream performance improves by 4.2 times on average. These findings suggest that early supervision can be critical when distractors are present. They challenge the conventional sequence of first learning latent actions without labels and only afterward learning how those representations correspond to real actions.
summary.tldr: Experiments with distractors show that small amounts of action supervision during latent-action learning can substantially improve downstream performance.

title: Latent Action Learning Requires Supervision in the Presence of Distractors

abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) algorithms alter models’ weights to perform targeted updates to incorrect, outdated, or otherwise unwanted factual associations. However, recent work has shown that applying KE can adversely affect models’ broader factual recall accuracy and diminish their reasoning abilities. Although these studies give insights into the potential harms of KE algorithms, e.g., performance evaluations on benchmarks, little is understood about why such destructive failures occur. Motivated by this, we define a novel synthetic task in which a Transformer is trained from scratch to internalize a "structured" knowledge graph. The structure enforces relationships between entities of the graph, such that editing a factual association has "trickling effects" on other entities (e.g., altering X’s parent is Y to Z affects who X’s siblings’ parent is). Through evaluations of edited models on this task, we show that KE inadvertently affects representations of entities beyond the targeted one, distorting relevant structures that allow a model to infer unseen knowledge about an entity. We call this phenomenon representation shattering and demonstrate that it degrades models’ factual recall and reasoning performance. We further corroborate our findings in naturalistic settings with pre-trained Llama and Mamba models as well. Overall, our work yields a precise mechanistic hypothesis to explain why KE has adverse effects on model abilities.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing changes model weights to update particular factual associations. Such edits can also damage broader recall and reasoning, but performance measurements alone do not explain why. This paper constructs a synthetic task to examine that mechanism in a Transformer trained from scratch on a structured knowledge graph.

The graph links facts so that changing one association has implications for other entities. This makes it possible to inspect whether an edit preserves the relationships needed for additional inferences. The evaluations show that editing can alter representations beyond the intended entity and distort the structure supporting inference about knowledge the model has not directly seen.

The authors call this phenomenon representation shattering and demonstrate that it harms factual recall and reasoning on the task. They also corroborate the findings in more naturalistic settings with pretrained Llama and Mamba models. The result is a mechanistic hypothesis for editing failures: targeted weight changes can disrupt shared representational relationships that support capabilities beyond the fact being edited.
summary.tldr: Knowledge edits can distort representations of related entities, offering a mechanistic explanation for damage to recall and reasoning.

title: Representation Shattering in Transformers: A Synthetic Study with Knowledge Editing

abstract: Recent studies show that in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of large language models (LLMs), data quality matters more than quantity. While most data cleaning methods concentrate on filtering entire samples, the quality of individual tokens within a sample can vary significantly. After pre-training, even in high-quality samples, patterns or phrases that are not task-related can be redundant, uninformative, or even harmful. Continuing to fine-tune on these patterns may offer limited benefit and even degrade downstream task performance. In this paper, we investigate token quality from a noisy-label perspective and propose a generic token cleaning pipeline for SFT tasks. Our method filters out uninformative tokens while preserving those carrying key task-specific information. Specifically, we first evaluate token quality by examining the influence of model updates on each token, then apply a threshold-based separation. The token influence can be measured in a single pass with a fixed reference model or iteratively with self-evolving reference models. The benefits and limitations of both methods are analyzed theoretically by error upper bounds. Extensive experiments show that our framework consistently improves downstream performance. Code is available at https://github.com/UCSC-REAL/TokenCleaning.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning datasets can contain useful examples whose individual tokens vary in relevance. Even a high-quality sample may include phrases that add little task information after pretraining, and continued training on them can hurt downstream performance. This paper therefore studies data selection at the token level rather than only at the example level.

The proposed pipeline treats token quality through a noisy-label perspective. It estimates quality by examining how model updates influence each token, then applies a threshold to separate informative tokens from uninformative ones. The influence measurement can use one pass with a fixed reference model or an iterative process with reference models that evolve.

The authors analyze the benefits and limitations of both variants using theoretical error upper bounds. Extensive experiments show consistent downstream improvements from the framework. The contribution is a finer-grained way to direct fine-tuning toward task-specific information: useful content can be retained even when other tokens in the same sample contribute little or potentially interfere with learning.
summary.tldr: Token Cleaning improves supervised fine-tuning by using update-based influence estimates to filter uninformative tokens within training examples.

title: Token Cleaning: Fine-Grained Data Selection for LLM Supervised Fine-Tuning

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are the dominant approach to solving machine learning problems defined over graphs. Despite much theoretical and empirical work in recent years, our understanding of finer-grained aspects of architectural design for GNNs remains impoverished. In this paper, we consider the benefits of architectures that maintain and update edge embeddings. On the theoretical front, under a suitable computational abstraction for a layer in the model, as well as memory constraints on the embeddings, we show that there are natural tasks on graphical models for which architectures leveraging edge embeddings can be much shallower. Our techniques are inspired by results on time-space tradeoffs in theoretical computer science. Empirically, we show architectures that maintain edge embeddings almost always improve on their node-based counterparts—frequently significantly so in topologies that have "hub" nodes.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can maintain learned representations on nodes, but they can also maintain and update representations on edges. This paper examines what the latter architectural choice contributes. The question is more specific than whether a network can solve a graph task: it asks whether edge representations change how much depth the computation requires.

Under a particular abstraction of layer computation and memory constraints on embeddings, the authors identify natural tasks on graphical models for which edge-based architectures can be much shallower. Their analysis draws on time-space tradeoffs from theoretical computer science. The depth advantage is conditional on this computational setup and the embedding-memory restrictions.

Empirically, architectures maintaining edge embeddings almost always improve on their node-based counterparts in the reported comparisons. Improvements are frequently substantial in graphs containing hub nodes. The theoretical and experimental results together provide evidence that edge representations are a consequential design choice, with potential benefits in both required network depth and measured task performance.
summary.tldr: Edge embeddings can reduce required GNN depth under stated computational assumptions and improve performance in nearly all reported empirical comparisons.

title: Towards characterizing the value of edge embeddings in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Human mesh recovery (HMR) from a single image is inherently ill-posed due to depth ambiguity and occlusions. Probabilistic methods have tried to solve this by generating numerous plausible 3D human mesh predictions, but they often exhibit misalignment with 2D image observations and weak robustness to in-the-wild images. To address these issues, we propose ADHMR, a framework that Aligns a Diffusion-based HMR model in a preference optimization manner. First, we train a human mesh prediction assessment model, HMR-Scorer, capable of evaluating predictions even for in-the-wild images without 3D annotations. We then use HMR-Scorer to create a preference dataset, where each input image has a pair of winner and loser mesh predictions. This dataset is used to finetune the base model using direct preference optimization. Moreover, HMR-Scorer also helps improve existing HMR models by data cleaning, even with fewer training samples. Extensive experiments show that ADHMR outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/shenwenhao01/ADHMR.

paragraphs: Recovering a three-dimensional human body from one image is ambiguous: hidden body parts and uncertain depth allow several plausible reconstructions. Generating many candidates can represent that uncertainty, but plausible bodies can still disagree with the visible image. ADHMR addresses this mismatch by teaching a diffusion-based reconstruction model to prefer better mesh predictions.

The method first trains HMR-Scorer, a model that assesses predicted human meshes. It can evaluate predictions for images captured in uncontrolled settings even when those images lack three-dimensional annotations. The scorer then selects a better and worse prediction for each image, producing paired preferences. Direct preference optimization uses these pairs to fine-tune the original mesh generator.

The experiments report performance beyond current state-of-the-art methods. The scorer also improves existing reconstruction models through data cleaning, even when the resulting training set contains fewer examples. Together, these findings suggest that evaluating prediction quality can help both align a generator with image evidence and improve the usefulness of its training data.
summary.tldr: ADHMR uses scored pairs of human-mesh predictions to improve a diffusion model through direct preference optimization.

title: ADHMR: Aligning Diffusion-based Human Mesh Recovery via Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: Benchmark Data Contamination (BDC)—the inclusion of benchmark testing samples in the training set—has raised increasing concerns in Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation, leading to falsely inflated performance estimates and undermining evaluation reliability. To address this, researchers have proposed various mitigation strategies to update existing benchmarks, including modifying original questions or generating new ones based on them. However, a rigorous examination of the effectiveness of these mitigation strategies remains lacking. In this paper, we design a systematic and controlled pipeline along with two novel metrics—fidelity and contamination resistance—to provide a fine-grained and comprehensive assessment of existing BDC mitigation strategies. Previous assessment methods, such as accuracy drop and accuracy matching, focus solely on aggregate accuracy, often leading to incomplete or misleading conclusions. Our metrics address this limitation by emphasizing question-level evaluation result matching. Extensive experiments with 10 LLMs, 5 benchmarks, 20 BDC mitigation strategies, and 2 contamination scenarios reveal that no existing strategy effectively balances fidelity and contamination resistance. No semantic-preserving strategy yields a significant improvement in resistance over the vanilla case (i.e., no benchmark update) across all benchmarks, while semantic-altering strategies sacrifice fidelity for resistance. These findings underscore the urgent need for designing more effective BDC mitigation strategies. Our code repository is available at https://github.com/ASTRAL-Group/BDC_mitigation_assessment.

paragraphs: When benchmark questions appear in language-model training data, test scores can overstate capability. Researchers try to mitigate this contamination by modifying questions or generating replacements. This paper examines whether those changes both resist contamination and preserve the evaluation behavior of the original benchmark.

The authors build a controlled assessment pipeline with two metrics: fidelity and contamination resistance. Both emphasize matching evaluation outcomes at the question level, addressing information that aggregate accuracy comparisons can hide. Their experiments cover 10 language models, five benchmarks, 20 mitigation strategies, and two contamination scenarios, allowing them to examine the tradeoff across many tested configurations.

No tested strategy effectively balances the two objectives. Strategies that preserve semantics do not significantly improve contamination resistance over unchanged benchmarks across all five benchmarks, while strategies that alter semantics gain resistance at the expense of fidelity. The findings question whether updating benchmark questions reliably fixes contamination: an update may either leave the problem insufficiently addressed or change what the evaluation is measuring.
summary.tldr: A controlled study finds that tested benchmark updates fail to balance contamination resistance with fidelity to the original evaluation.

title: The Emperor’s New Clothes in Benchmarking? A Rigorous Examination of Mitigation Strategies for LLM Benchmark Data Contamination

abstract: Although Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have achieved remarkable success across various tasks, they still suffer from limited generalization. We hypothesize that this limitation arises from the traditional sample-based (0–dimensionnal) regularization used in ANNs. To overcome this, we introduce Deep Sturm-Liouville (DSL), a novel function approximator that enables continuous 1D regularization along field lines in the input space by integrating the Sturm-Liouville Theorem (SLT) into the deep learning framework. DSL defines field lines traversing the input space, along which a Sturm-Liouville problem is solved to generate orthogonal basis functions, enforcing implicit regularization thanks to the desirable properties of SLT. These basis functions are linearly combined to construct the DSL approximator. Both the vector field and basis functions are parameterized by neural networks and learned jointly. We demonstrate that the DSL formulation naturally arises when solving a Rank-1 Parabolic Eigenvalue Problem. DSL is trained efficiently using stochastic gradient descent via implicit differentiation and achieves competitive performance on diverse multivariate datasets, including high-dimensional image datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: The authors hypothesize that conventional regularization applied at individual samples contributes to neural networks' limited generalization. Deep Sturm–Liouville, or DSL, explores a different construction: applying continuous one-dimensional regularization along field lines that pass through the input space. The motivation is a hypothesis, while the proposed function approximator is a concrete implementation of that idea.

Along each field line, DSL solves a Sturm–Liouville problem to obtain orthogonal basis functions. It forms its predictions by combining those functions linearly. Neural networks parameterize both the vector field and the basis functions, and these components are learned together, allowing the regularized representation to adapt during training.

The paper connects this construction to a rank-one parabolic eigenvalue problem and trains it through stochastic gradient descent using implicit differentiation. Experiments show competitive performance on varied multivariate datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10. The results demonstrate the practicality of this mathematically structured approximator, including on high-dimensional images, without establishing that sample-based regularization explains all generalization failures.
summary.tldr: DSL learns orthogonal basis functions along input-space field lines to introduce continuous one-dimensional regularization into a neural function approximator.

title: Deep Sturm–Liouville: From Sample-Based to 1D Regularization with Learnable Orthogonal Basis Functions

abstract: As deep learning continues to evolve, the need for data efficiency becomes increasingly important. Considering labeling large datasets is both time-consuming and expensive, active learning (AL) provides a promising solution to this challenge by iteratively selecting the most informative subsets of examples to train deep neural networks, thereby reducing the labeling cost. However, the effectiveness of different AL algorithms can vary significantly across data scenarios, and determining which AL algorithm best fits a given task remains a challenging problem. This work presents the first differentiable AL strategy search method, named AutoAL, which is designed on top of existing AL sampling strategies. AutoAL consists of two neural nets, named SearchNet and FitNet, which are optimized concurrently under a differentiable bi-level optimization framework. For any given task, SearchNet and FitNet are iteratively co-optimized using the labeled data, learning how well a set of candidate AL algorithms perform on that task. With the optimal AL strategies identified, SearchNet selects a small subset from the unlabeled pool for querying their annotations, enabling efficient training of the task model. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoAL consistently achieves superior accuracy compared to all candidate AL algorithms and other selective AL approaches, showcasing its potential for adapting and integrating multiple existing AL methods across diverse tasks and domains.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces annotation effort by choosing which unlabeled examples should receive labels next. However, the usefulness of a particular selection strategy varies across tasks and datasets. AutoAL addresses this additional decision problem: how to identify suitable active learning strategies for the task being learned, using existing sampling methods as its candidates.

The framework contains two neural networks, SearchNet and FitNet, trained together through differentiable bi-level optimization. Their iterative updates use labeled examples to learn how well candidate strategies perform on the current task. SearchNet then uses the identified strategies to select a small subset of the unlabeled pool for annotation, providing additional training data for the task model.

The reported experiments show higher accuracy than every candidate algorithm and the other selective active learning approaches evaluated. This supports learning how to adapt and integrate selection strategies rather than fixing one strategy for all data scenarios. The contribution is an automated search mechanism built on existing active learning methods, with evidence of effectiveness across diverse tasks and domains.
summary.tldr: AutoAL learns which existing active learning strategies suit a task and uses them to choose examples for annotation.

title: AutoAL: Automated Active Learning with Differentiable Query Strategy Search

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at aggregating neighbor information for classification, yet their performance is hindered by graph structural entanglement, where spurious correlations from semantically irrelevant neighbors contaminate node embeddings. This challenge is most acute for nodes near class boundaries in the embedding space, where amplified structural noise blurs decision boundaries and destabilizes predictions. Existing robust GNN methods largely treat all nodes uniformly, ignoring boundary vulnerabilities. In this paper, to improve classification performance, we tackle graph structural disentanglement by identifying boundary-region entanglement as the primary bottleneck and propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning GNN plug-in module that selectively suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries with minimal model parameter perturbation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms existing leading methods. Notably, BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks build node representations by combining information from neighboring nodes. This becomes problematic when neighbors are connected structurally but are irrelevant to the node’s meaning or class. Their information can introduce misleading correlations, especially for nodes whose representations already lie near the boundary between classes.

The paper identifies these boundary regions as the main bottleneck in graph structural entanglement. It proposes Boundary Embedding Shaping, or BES, a plug-in module that uses adaptive contrastive learning to selectively suppress misleading structural information near decision boundaries. The approach focuses its intervention on vulnerable representations while making only small changes to model parameters.

Experiments report consistently improved separation at class boundaries and performance above existing leading methods. For GCN, the reported average improvement in node classification is 3.3%, reaching 5.0% on WikiCS; BES also achieves superior link prediction accuracy. These findings support targeted treatment of boundary vulnerabilities as a useful way to improve graph representations and their downstream predictions.
summary.tldr: BES improves graph predictions by selectively reducing misleading neighbor information near class boundaries.

title: Boundary Embedding Shaping with Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Graph Structural Disentanglement

abstract: Data augmentation is a widely used strategy to improve model robustness and generalization by enriching training datasets with synthetic examples. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong generative capabilities for this purpose, their applications in high-stakes domains like healthcare present unique challenges due to the risk of generating clinically incorrect or misleading information. In this work, we propose a novel query-based model collaboration framework that integrates expert-level domain knowledge to guide the augmentation process to preserve critical medical information. Compared to existing LLM-based and traditional augmentation methods, our generated data significantly improves preservation of critical medical information and reduces hallucinations at both the token and concept levels. Experiments on downstream clinical prediction tasks demonstrate consistent performance gains over existing augmentation methods. This lightweight collaborative framework addresses the gap between LLM augmentation potential and the safety requirements of specialized domains.

paragraphs: Synthetic training examples can help models become more robust and generalize better, but generating clinical text introduces a specific concern: altered or invented medical information can make an example misleading. This paper develops an augmentation framework intended to preserve the critical clinical content while still benefiting from a language model's ability to generate text.

The proposed framework uses query-based collaboration between models to bring expert-level domain knowledge into the generation process. That knowledge guides augmentation toward medically faithful examples. Its central design choice is to make domain guidance part of producing the augmented data, connecting the flexibility of text generation with the need to retain information that matters for clinical interpretation.

Compared with both existing language-model augmentation and traditional augmentation methods, the authors report significantly better preservation of critical medical information and fewer hallucinations at the token and concept levels. Downstream clinical prediction experiments also show consistent performance gains. Together, these findings support the lightweight collaborative approach as a way to improve both the faithfulness and practical training value of synthetic clinical text.
summary.tldr: Query-based model collaboration guides clinical text augmentation with expert knowledge, improving medical-information preservation and downstream prediction in reported experiments.

title: Expert-guided Clinical Text Augmentation via Query-Based Model Collaboration

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is critical for reliable deployment of vision models, and Mahalanobis-based detectors remain strong baselines. However, their performance varies widely across modern pretrained representations, making it unclear which feature-space properties determine success or failure. Across diverse foundation-model backbones and Mahalanobis variants, we show that performance is highly representation-dependent and can shift substantially with pretraining data and fine-tuning. We link this variability to in-distribution geometry and identify a two-term ID summary that consistently tracks Mahalanobis OOD behavior across detectors: within-class spectral structure and local intrinsic dimensionality. Finally, we introduce radially scaled $\ell_2$ normalization, $\phi_\beta(z)=z/\|z\|^\beta$, a direction-preserving transformation that changes feature radii and exposes a different ID geometry to the same quadratic detector. Selecting $\beta$ from ID-only geometry signals generally outperforms fixed normalization baselines.

Across diverse foundation-model backbones and Mahalanobis variants, we show that performance is highly representation-dependent and can shift substantially with pretraining data and fine-tuning. We link this variability to in-distribution geometry and identify a two-term ID summary that consistently tracks Mahalanobis OOD behavior across detectors: within-class spectral structure and local intrinsic dimensionality. Finally, we introduce radially scaled $\ell_2$ normalization, $\phi_\beta(z)=z/\|z\|^\beta$, a direction-preserving transformation that changes feature radii and exposes a different ID geometry to the same quadratic detector. Selecting $\beta$ from ID-only geometry signals generally outperforms fixed normalization baselines.

paragraphs: Mahalanobis detectors try to identify unfamiliar inputs using the geometry of a model’s learned features. This paper investigates why these detectors work well with some pretrained vision representations and poorly with others. Across different foundation-model backbones and detector variants, the authors find that detection performance depends strongly on the representation and can change substantially after different pretraining or fine-tuning.

The authors connect those changes to two properties of familiar, in-distribution data: within-class spectral structure and local intrinsic dimensionality. These describe how features vary within a class and how many dimensions their local structure effectively occupies. Together, the two measurements consistently track detector behavior across the studied settings.

The paper also introduces a transformation that preserves each feature vector’s direction while adjusting its length through an exponent, beta. This changes the geometry seen by the same detector. Selecting beta using only in-distribution geometry generally beats fixed normalization choices, suggesting a practical way to adapt detection to a representation without using out-of-distribution examples for that selection.
summary.tldr: Two properties of familiar-data geometry help explain Mahalanobis detection performance and guide a normalization that generally improves it.

title: A Geometry-Based View of Mahalanobis OOD Detection

abstract: We can often verify the correctness of neural network outputs using ground truth labels, but we cannot reliably determine whether the output was produced by normal or anomalous internal mechanisms. Mechanistic anomaly detection (MAD) aims to flag these cases, but existing methods either depend on latent space analysis, which is vulnerable to obfuscation, or are specific to particular architectures and modalities. We reframe MAD as a functional attribution problem: asking to what extent samples from a trusted set can explain the model’s output, where attribution failure signals anomalous behavior. We operationalize this using influence functions, measuring functional coupling between test samples and a small reference set via parameter-space sampling. We evaluate across multiple anomaly types and modalities. For backdoors in vision models, our method achieves state-of-the-art detection on BackdoorBench, with an average Defense Effectiveness Rating (DER) of 0.93 across seven attacks and four datasets (next best 0.83). For LLMs, we similarly achieve a significant improvement over baselines for several backdoor types, including on explicitly obfuscated models. Beyond backdoors, preliminary evidence shows our method can detect adversarial and out-of-distribution samples, and distinguishes multiple anomalous mechanisms within a single model. Our results establish functional attribution as an effective, modality-agnostic tool for detecting anomalous behavior in deployed models.

title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection via Functional Attribution

abstract: Saliency maps are widely used to interpret image classification models and build trust in their predictions; however, their reliability remains a central concern, as randomized networks can produce saliency maps that closely resemble those of trained models. We identify a previously underappreciated architectural contributor to this phenomenon: a center-focused saliency bias induced by common convolutional design choices. Through controlled ablations, we show that architectural components such as zero padding and receptive field growth induce a center-focused saliency prior that is already present in randomly initialized CNNs and under randomized inputs. In contrast, this behavior is largely absent in non-convolutional architectures such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) and multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). To investigate the interaction between architectural priors and learning, we introduce a corner-shift benchmark and a Center-Shift Index that quantify how saliency redistributes under object relocation. We show that training can partially shift saliency toward object regions, while randomized models remain dominated by architectural center bias, providing one mechanism by which trained-random similarity can be inflated and clarifying how architectural priors can confound standard saliency evaluations.

These observations show that a visually structured saliency map can partly reflect network design.

This provides one mechanism that inflates trained–random similarity and shows why saliency evaluations need to distinguish learned responses from architectural spatial preferences.
summary.tldr: Convolutional design choices can create center-focused saliency before training, confounding comparisons between trained and randomized networks.

title: When Random Saliency Looks Trained: Architectural Center Bias in CNN Interpretability

abstract: Logistic regression is widely used in applications; however, when the dimension scales with the sample size, theory reveals that the asymptotic behavior of common M-estimators depends on nonzero bias and variance factors, which are functions of the signal strength. To leverage the theory to design valid statistical methodologies, it is essential to obtain accurate estimates of the signal strength. In this work, we utilize a data-splitting strategy to efficiently estimate the signal strength. To alleviate issues caused by separable data, we analyze the exact asymptotics of an M-estimator with a data-driven, non-decomposable regularizer that adapts to the true covariance structure. We justify the validity of our method through both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments.

paragraphs: When the number of variables in logistic regression grows with the sample size, common estimators have asymptotic behavior involving nonzero bias and variance factors. Those factors depend on signal strength. Accurately estimating signal strength is therefore an important step toward turning high-dimensional theory into valid statistical methods.

This paper develops an efficient estimation strategy based on splitting the data. It also addresses difficulties caused by separable data through an M-estimator with a data-driven regularizer. The regularizer is non-decomposable and adapts to the true covariance structure, making the dependence among variables part of the analysis rather than treating regularization as independent adjustments to individual coordinates.

The authors derive exact asymptotic behavior for this estimator and support the method with numerical experiments. The stated contribution is both an estimator of the signal strength needed by the theory and an analysis that accommodates the separability issue. Its significance lies in connecting a difficult underlying quantity to usable statistical methodology in the regime where dimension grows alongside sample size.
summary.tldr: A data-splitting method estimates signal strength in high-dimensional logistic regression, with theory addressing separability through covariance-adaptive regularization.

title: Signal Strength Estimation in Logistic Regression Using Data Splitting

abstract: LLM-augmented database analytics face a major bottleneck in the costly prefill phase. Although relational tables inherently contain repeated attribute values, standard row-by-row processing produces fragmented prompt layouts that obscure shared prefixes, thereby minimizing opportunities for prefix KV cache reuse and constraining system efficiency. Existing solutions typically employ heuristic or exhaustive search methods to reorder prompt layouts, but these approaches can be inefficient and may not leverage the structural properties of relational tables. We address this challenge by formulating prefix-cache-aware prompt layout optimization as a problem rooted in the isomorphism between prefix-cache reuse and the radix tree topology induced by the relational data distribution. Building on this perspective, we introduce a practical greedy tree-shaping algorithm that efficiently selects row and column orderings to maximize prefix overlap. Our approach, SOLO, improves prefill throughput by up to 90.3% under fixed prefix-cache budget. Moreover, it reduces planning overhead by up to 242$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

summary.tldr: SOLO reorders database rows and columns to expose shared prompt prefixes, improving cache reuse and reducing layout-planning overhead.

title: Prefix-Cache-Aware Data Reordering for LLM-Augmented Database Analytics

abstract: Protein sequence generation for engineering requires samples that are biophysically plausible and, when targeting a family/domain, remain recognizable members while exploring within-family diversity. Current discrete generative models typically start from uniform or masked-token noise, which discards strong position-specific constraints induced by evolution and forces the model to reconstruct conserved residues from scratch, leading to weak family control and low foldability. We propose LineageFlow, a simplex-valued flow-matching model that initializes generation from lineage priors derived from ancestral sequence reconstruction, turning generation into structured mutation from an evolved scaffold. Across diverse protein families, LineageFlow achieves family validity close to held-out natural sequences and improves predicted structural confidence over uniform-/mask-initialized baselines while maintaining substantial within-family novelty and diversity, even surpassing a large pretrained baseline trained on substantially more data. Finally, we introduce rerouting, a single intermediate-time mutate–select–amplify intervention that enables objective-guided sampling without per-step predictor guidance and yields further gains in plausibility, including a zero-shot enzyme generation case study.

paragraphs: Protein generation must balance plausible sequences with diversity, while retaining membership in a desired family. LineageFlow starts from the observation that uniform or masked-token noise discards evolutionary constraints at individual sequence positions. Reconstructing those constraints from scratch can weaken family control and foldability, so the method begins with a more informative starting point.

Its flow-matching model operates on amino-acid probability distributions and initializes generation from lineage priors obtained through ancestral sequence reconstruction. Generation therefore becomes structured mutation of an evolved scaffold. The paper also introduces rerouting: one intermediate mutate-select-amplify intervention that steers sampling toward an objective without requiring predictor guidance at every step.

They retain substantial novelty and diversity within families, and the reported results even surpass a large pretrained baseline trained on considerably more data. Rerouting further improves plausibility, including in a zero-shot enzyme-generation case study. The structural-confidence findings concern predictions.
summary.tldr: LineageFlow generates diverse, family-consistent protein sequences by starting flow matching from reconstructed evolutionary priors.

title: LineageFlow: Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Family-Aware Protein Sequence Generation

abstract: LLMs achieve remarkable multi-step reasoning capabilities, yet effectively transferring these skills via post-training distillation remains challenging. Existing data selection methods, ranging from manual curation to heuristics based on length, entropy, or overall loss, fail to capture the causal importance of individual reasoning steps, limiting distillation efficiency. To address this, we propose Attention Influence for Reasoning (AIR), a principled, unsupervised and training-free framework that leverages mechanistic insights of the retrieval head to select high-value post-training data. AIR first identifies reasoning-critical attention heads of an off-the-shelf model, then constructs a weakened reference model with disabled head influence, and finally quantifies the resulting loss divergence as the Attention Influence Score. This score enables fine-grained assessment at both the step and sample levels, supporting step-level weighted fine-tuning and global sample selection. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that AIR consistently improves reasoning accuracy, surpassing heuristic baselines and effectively isolating the most critical steps and samples. Our work establishes a mechanism-driven, data-efficient approach for reasoning distillation in LLMs.

paragraphs: AIR addresses the problem of choosing training examples that effectively transfer reasoning skills between language models. Common selection rules use properties such as response length, uncertainty, or overall prediction loss. The paper argues that these signals miss which individual reasoning steps depend most strongly on mechanisms important to reasoning.

The framework identifies reasoning-critical attention heads in an existing model, then constructs a weakened reference by disabling their influence. It measures the resulting divergence in prediction loss to produce an Attention Influence Score. This intervention supplies a mechanism-based signal for assessing both complete examples and individual steps within an example. The selection procedure itself is unsupervised and requires no training.

The scores support two uses: selecting samples for post-training and assigning different fine-tuning weights to reasoning steps. Experiments across several reasoning benchmarks report consistent accuracy improvements over heuristic selection methods and effective identification of important steps and samples. The contribution is a way to allocate training effort according to measured attention-head influence, connecting internal model behavior to practical data selection.
summary.tldr: AIR selects and weights reasoning data by measuring how prediction loss changes when reasoning-critical attention heads are weakened.

title: AIR: Post-training Data Selection for Reasoning via Attention Head Influence

abstract: Recent works introduce Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) into vision transformers (ViTs) to enhance their extrapolation capability, i.e., maintaining performance when inference is conducted on higher resolution images. RoPE encodes positions via rotating phases whose change is controlled by frequency components. Strandard 2D RoPE does not generalize well to input resolution changes as it only applies axial frequencies separately along each individual axis. To solve this issue, Mix-RoPE combines xy-axis frequencies, such that it can model position relations in diagonal direction. However, in practice, we observe that the learned 2D frequencies become anisotropic in their direction distributions due to the axial spectral bias in image features, limiting the extrapolation ability of ViTs. Motivated by this observation, we propose Compass-RoPE. We replace the xy cartesian coordinates with a polar parameterization that explicitly decouples frequency scale and angle. By initializing the angle vectors uniformly over [0,2$\pi$), it ensures the isotropic direction coverage. Besides, we further introduce discrete Fourier transform (DFT) mixing for the angle vectors, allowing each transformed individual angle vector element to nest multipule angles and thus to enrich angular expressiveness. Extensive experiments on multi-resolution classification and dense prediction tasks show that our Compass-RoPE achieves more stable extrapolation performance under large-scale resolution changes.

Standard two-dimensional versions handle the image axes separately, while mixed versions combine them to represent diagonal relationships as well.

title: Compass-RoPE: Isotropic Rotary Position Embeddings for Vision Transformers

abstract: Reward design remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Hand-crafted rewards are often difficult to specify and may lead to suboptimal policies, while learned rewards from preferences can suffer from inefficiency and unstable training. Inspired by the dual nature of human learning explored in cognitive science, we decompose rewards into two complementary components: Formal Rewards (FR), explicitly designed based on task knowledge, and Residual Rewards (RR), learned from observations to capture implicit and nuanced preferences. Based on this decomposition, we propose CoRe, a hybrid framework that integrates FR and RR with vision-language models (VLMs) feedback to achieve preference-aligned policies without human involvement. Our contributions are twofold: (1) We propose a Formal Reward Module (FRM) that leverages VLMs to iteratively design and optimize FR based on task knowledge and preference feedback, enabling the continual improvement of policy during training; (2) We introduce a Residual Reward Module (RRM) that learns RR from video-level preference by employing VLMs to generate preference labels and capturing nuanced rewards that complement FR, ensuring alignment with human intent. Through the synergy of FRM and RRM, CoRe enables the automatic construction of reliable rewards that are efficient and preference-aligned. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoRe outperforms existing approaches in terms of policy learning effectiveness and efficiency on ten robotic manipulation tasks in simulation and five real-worlds.

The framework combines them using vision-language model feedback to train preference-aligned policies without human involvement in the feedback process.

Experiments span ten simulated robotic manipulation tasks and five real-world tasks. The authors report better policy learning effectiveness and efficiency than existing approaches. These findings support combining the two reward sources: explicit specifications provide one part of the learning signal, while learned preferences supply additional guidance for behavior that task rules alone may not capture.
summary.tldr: CoRe combines explicit task rewards with learned video preferences from vision-language models to improve robotic policy learning.

title: CoRe: Combined Rewards with Vision-Language Model Feedback for Preference-Aligned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Class imbalance poses a critical challenge in federated learning (FL), where underrepresented classes suffer from poor predictive performance yet cannot be addressed by standard centralized techniques due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints. We propose FedCGNM (Federated Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum), a client-side optimizer in FL that partitions classes into a small number of groups based on minimum within-group variance, maintains a momentum per group, normalizes each group momentum to unit length, and uses the summation of the normalized group momentums as an update direction. This design both equalizes gradient magnitude across majority and minority groups and mitigates the noise inherent in rare-class gradients. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis explicitly accounting for time-varying resampling-rates. Additionally, to efficiently optimize these rates in small-client regimes, we introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) based algorithm that exploits federated parallelism that evaluates many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset demonstrates that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines, with FedHOO yielding further gains in small-scale federations.

paragraphs: Federated learning must learn from data distributed across clients, where privacy and differences between local datasets complicate class balancing. Underrepresented classes can consequently receive poor predictions. FedCGNM addresses this problem through the optimizer used on each client, changing how updates from different class groups contribute to learning.

The method partitions classes into a small number of groups using a minimum within-group variance criterion. It maintains momentum for each group, normalizes each momentum vector to unit length, and sums those vectors to determine the update direction. This equalizes the magnitude of majority- and minority-group contributions while reducing noise in rare-class gradients. Its bandit-based search exploits federated parallelism to evaluate many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Across four public long-tailed benchmarks and a chip-defect dataset, FedCGNM consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines; FedHOO supplies additional gains in small federations.
summary.tldr: FedCGNM balances class-group updates in federated learning, while FedHOO efficiently tunes resampling rates for smaller federations.

title: Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum and Faster Hyperparameter Exploration to Tackle Class Imbalance in Federated Learning

abstract: A central goal of large language model (LLM) research is to build agentic systems that can plan, act, and adapt through sustained interaction with dynamic environments. While recent LLM-based agents exhibit impressive contextual reasoning, their long-horizon decision-making remains fragile, often suffering from $\textit{objective drift}$, where goals and plans drift over extended interactions. We introduce $\texttt{Multi}^2$, a hierarchical multi-agent decision-making framework that explicitly decomposes agent behavior into complementary roles. A high-level agent ($\texttt{System 1}$) focuses on context-aware sub-goal generation using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while a low-level agent ($\texttt{System 2}$) executes atomic actions through offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) in interactive environments. This separation enables stable long-horizon control, mitigates objective drift, and allows efficient adaptation. Across diverse interactive environments, $\texttt{Multi}^2$ consistently outperforms strong agentic baselines, demonstrating improved robustness and coordination in multi-turn interaction. Beyond performance, we introduce and release three hierarchical benchmark datasets, filling a long-standing gap in training and evaluating hierarchical decision-making for LLM-based agents.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can lose track of their goals during extended interaction, even when their immediate reasoning appears strong. Multi² addresses this objective drift through a hierarchy of complementary agents. The design separates deciding what subgoal to pursue from selecting the individual actions needed to carry it out.

The high-level agent, called System 1, uses supervised fine-tuning to generate subgoals appropriate to the current context. The low-level agent, System 2, learns atomic actions through reinforcement learning that moves from offline to online interaction. This division assigns planning and execution distinct roles and training procedures, supporting sustained control and efficient adaptation.

Across diverse interactive environments, Multi² consistently outperforms the strong agentic baselines evaluated, with better robustness and coordination over multiple turns. The authors also release three hierarchical benchmark datasets for training and evaluating this kind of decision-making. Together, the framework and datasets address both how to organize long-horizon agents and how to study that organization, with the reported results supporting hierarchy as a way to mitigate goal drift.
summary.tldr: Multi² separates subgoal planning from action execution to improve sustained interaction and reduce objective drift in language-model agents.

title: $\texttt{Multi}^2$: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Decision-Making with LLM-Based Agents in Interactive Environments

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is highly sensitive to which demonstrations appear in the prompt, but selecting them is expensive because candidate contexts must be validated with repeated LLM calls. We argue that demonstration selection is easier to judge than to find: predicting whether a specific query–context pair $(q,D)$ will succeed is cheaper and more general than searching for an optimal $D^\star$. Based on this insight, we propose DiSP, a sample-and-judge framework that stratifies queries by difficulty. DiSP runs random demonstration trials to estimate each training query’s success rate, trains a lightweight router to predict difficulty from the query, and trains level-specific judges to score sampled contexts. At inference, DiSP performs stop-on-acceptance judging under an explicit budget and typically makes a single LLM call, emitting diagnostic risk tags when no suitable context is found. Across five classification datasets with Llama 3–8B and Qwen 2.5–7B, DiSP achieves the best average accuracy, improving over strong learned selection baselines by up to 3.4%, while achieving up to 23$\times$ end-to-end wall-clock speedup.

paragraphs: Examples placed in a prompt can strongly affect a language model's answer, but testing many candidate example sets requires expensive model calls. This paper proposes judging whether a particular query and context will work as a more economical basis for selection. Its DiSP framework samples possible contexts and predicts their suitability.

During training, random demonstration trials estimate how often each query succeeds. A lightweight router learns to predict query difficulty, and separate judges learn to score contexts for different difficulty levels. At inference, the system evaluates sampled contexts within an explicit budget and stops when one is accepted. It typically makes a single language-model call and emits diagnostic risk tags when no suitable context is found.

Across five classification datasets using Llama 3–8B and Qwen 2.5–7B, DiSP achieves the best average accuracy. Reported improvements reach 3.4% over strong learned selection baselines, with up to 23-fold end-to-end speedup. The findings support spending inexpensive judgment computation on context selection before invoking the larger model.
summary.tldr: DiSP uses difficulty-specific judges to select prompt examples efficiently, improving classification accuracy while typically requiring one language-model call.

title: Easier to Judge than to Find: Predicting In-Context Learning Success for Demonstration Selection

abstract: The trajectory prediction of N-body systems is of great significance and remains challenging with broad applications across various fields such as physics, chemistry and biology. Recent advances in generative models including flow matching and diffusion models have emerged as effective solutions to this problem, owing to their capacity to model the stochasticity and underlying distributions of complex system trajectories. However, existing approaches typically adopt trivial prior distributions that neglect the temporal correlations and spatial symmetries of N-body trajectories, which not only complicates the generation process but also limits model performance. To address these limitations, we propose GP-EquiFlow, an SE(3)-equivariant flow matching model incorporating vector-valued Gaussian processes. Based on observed trajectories, we employ vector-valued Gaussian processes to construct SE(3)-equivariant prior distributions, which exhibit enhanced consistency with the target data distribution in both spatial and temporal dynamics. Extensive experiments on N-body simulations and molecular dynamics demonstrate that the proposed GP-EquiFlow delivers more accurate predictions while requiring fewer sampling steps, underscoring the effectiveness of integrating Gaussian process-based SE(3)-equivariant prior distributions in geometric trajectory prediction.

paragraphs: Predicting trajectories of interacting bodies requires modeling both uncertainty and structured motion. Generative methods can represent distributions of possible trajectories, but their starting distributions often ignore relationships across time and spatial symmetries. The paper argues that this makes generation harder by requiring the model to transform a poorly matched prior into physically structured trajectory data.

GP-EquiFlow builds more suitable priors using vector-valued Gaussian processes conditioned on observed trajectories. These priors capture temporal relationships and are SE(3)-equivariant, meaning they respond consistently when the spatial coordinate system is rotated or translated. The flow-matching model therefore begins with a distribution that better agrees with the target trajectories’ spatial and temporal organization.

Experiments on N-body simulations and molecular dynamics show more accurate predictions with fewer sampling steps. The reported benefit comes from incorporating trajectory structure into the prior rather than leaving it entirely for the generative transformation to learn. These results support combining Gaussian-process temporal modeling with spatial equivariance when constructing starting distributions for geometric trajectory prediction.
summary.tldr: GP-EquiFlow uses temporally structured, spatially equivariant Gaussian-process priors to improve trajectory prediction with fewer sampling steps.

title: SE(3)-Equivariant Flow Matching with Gaussian Process Priors for Geometric Trajectory Prediction

abstract: We propose a frequency-aware perceptual optimization framework for low-complexity image compression, realized as a Realism-enhanced Region-based Implicit Codec (Re2IC). Re2IC models visual perception via saliency-guided region partitioning and local–global perceptual modulation. To enhance realism under complexity constraints, we introduce wavelet–Wasserstein distortion (WA-WD), a frequency-decomposed perceptual distortion that balances fidelity and realism through subband-aware modeling and provides a more reliable approximation than standard Wasserstein distortion. Together, these designs enable fine-grained spatial–spectral optimization, allowing Re2IC to achieve superior rate–perception trade-offs, outperforming generative codecs such as HiFiC while using less than 1% of their decoding cost. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art perceptual performance among overfitted codecs. Beyond compression, WA-WD serves as a standalone, tunable perceptual metric with strong alignment to human preference (Pearson 94.6%, Spearman 92.3%) and competitive performance across multiple IQA benchmarks. Project page: https://eedavidwu.github.io/ReReIC/

paragraphs: Image compression must balance storage size, visual appearance, and the computation needed to reconstruct an image. Re2IC targets perceptual quality under tight decoding budgets. It partitions an image using visual saliency and combines local and global perceptual adjustments, allowing optimization to account for differences between image regions.

The authors introduce wavelet–Wasserstein distortion, or WA-WD, to evaluate visual differences across frequency subbands. This gives the optimization a way to balance fidelity and realism at different spatial and frequency scales. The paper describes WA-WD as a more reliable approximation than standard Wasserstein distortion, supporting more detailed control over the compressed image’s appearance.

Experiments report better rate–perception trade-offs than generative codecs such as HiFiC while using less than 1% of their decoding cost, along with state-of-the-art perceptual results among overfitted codecs. WA-WD also functions independently as a tunable image-quality metric. Its reported alignment with human preference reaches Pearson correlation of 94.6% and Spearman correlation of 92.3%, with competitive results across multiple image-quality assessment benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Re2IC optimizes image regions and frequency bands to improve perceptual compression quality at very low decoding cost.

title: Frequency-Aware Perceptual Optimization for Low-Complexity Implicit Image Compression

abstract: We introduce physics-as-representation, a learning paradigm that encodes physical structure and geometric laws into visual representations, enabling models to see the unseen—the underlying 3D geometry and motion dynamics not apparent in raw pixels. We instantiate this paradigm in gaze perception by proposing SG-Gaze, a framework that learns a Structurally and Geometrically Consistent Representation (SGR) through dual-branch adversarial learning. An analytical branch embeds appearance features onto a spherical manifold aligned with gaze geodesics, while a model-guided branch reconstructs the 3D eyeball with weak 2D edge supervision. We further introduce View-Consistent Regularization, which augments SGR learning with synthetic view perturbations and enforces rotation-equivariant consistency across gaze vectors and structural projections, eliminating the need for multi-view calibration or explicit 3D labels. Extensive experiments across 12 challenging cross-domain transfers demonstrate that SG-Gaze achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and strong generalization. Our work highlights that enforcing structural and geometric consistency with equivariant regularization serves as effective inductive biases for interpretable and generalizable representation learning—a step toward machines that perceive the world not only from pixels, but from physics.

paragraphs: SG-Gaze explores how encoding physical and geometric structure can help gaze estimation generalize across domains. The broader proposal, physics-as-representation, builds underlying structure into visual features instead of relying only on appearance. For gaze perception, the relevant structure includes the eye’s three-dimensional geometry and the geometric relationships between viewing directions.

The framework learns through two adversarial branches. An analytical branch places appearance features on a spherical manifold aligned with gaze geometry. A model-guided branch reconstructs a three-dimensional eyeball using weak supervision from two-dimensional edges. Together, they encourage a representation that agrees with both structural and geometric constraints.

View-Consistent Regularization adds synthetic viewpoint perturbations and requires gaze vectors and structural projections to transform consistently under rotation. This removes the need for multi-view calibration or explicit three-dimensional labels in the proposed approach. Across 12 challenging cross-domain transfers, experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy and strong generalization. The results support structural consistency and rotation-aware regularization as useful biases for learning gaze representations that extend beyond the appearance patterns of one domain.
summary.tldr: SG-Gaze combines eye geometry and rotation-consistent learning to improve cross-domain gaze estimation without explicit 3D labels or multi-view calibration.

title: Seeing the Unseen: Physics-as-Representation for Generalizable Gaze Perception

abstract: Existing contrastive multi-view clustering methods rely on a pre-defined cluster number, limiting their flexibility in real-world scenarios lacking prior knowledge. To address this, we propose GROK, a novel framework driven by a cluster decision agent for unknown-$K$ multi-view clustering. It pioneers the adaptation of group relative policy optimization (GRPO) —a reinforcement learning strategy for LLM reasoning— into the unsupervised domain to autonomously determine the optimal $K$. Specifically, the agent orchestrates the clustering process through three synergistic phases. First, in the state perception phase, we employ a structure-aware adaptive backbone to aggregate multi-view data, providing the agent with consistent and discriminative consensus observations. Second, in the group decision phase, we introduce an action space divide-and-conquer strategy and an adaptive reward function. Equipped with these mechanisms, the agent performs group sampling and relative advantage estimation within the discrete action space of candidate $K$ values, autonomously searching for the optimal $K$ via reward maximization. Finally, via geometric feedback, geometric clustering guidance mechanism transforms the agent’s structural hypotheses into explicit differentiable constraints to reshape feature manifolds, thereby closing the perception-decision-feedback loop. Experimental results demonstrate that GROK achieves superior clustering performance in unknown-$K$ scenarios by autonomously exploring the cluster structure.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples using several views of the same data, but many contrastive approaches require the number of clusters to be supplied beforehand. GROK addresses cases where that number is unknown. It introduces a cluster decision agent that uses group relative policy optimization, adapting a reinforcement-learning strategy used for language-model reasoning to an unsupervised clustering problem.

The framework forms a loop with three stages. First, a structure-aware backbone combines the views into consistent, discriminative observations. Next, the agent searches candidate cluster counts using a divided action space, group sampling, and an adaptive reward. Relative advantage estimates help compare sampled decisions, guiding the search toward cluster counts that maximize the reward.

Finally, geometric feedback turns the agent's hypotheses about cluster structure into differentiable constraints that reshape the learned feature space. Cluster-count selection therefore influences the representation used for subsequent decisions. The authors report superior clustering performance in unknown-count settings. The finding supports coupling the search for cluster structure with representation learning, allowing the two processes to inform one another instead of fixing the cluster count before learning begins.
summary.tldr: GROK uses a reinforcement-learning agent and geometric feedback to jointly explore cluster counts and improve multi-view clustering when the count is unknown.

title: GRPO-based Cluster Decision Agent for Unknown-$\boldsymbolK$ Multi-view Clustering

abstract: Current chemical large language models (LLMs) predominantly rely on explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to solve complex reasoning problems. However, forcing nonverbal tacit chemical logic into discrete natural language imposes a fundamental “modality mismatch,” creating an artificial bottleneck for reasoning. We introduce LatentChem, a reasoning interface that decouples chemical logic from linguistic generation, enabling the model to process information via continuous thought vectors and dynamic perception. Our investigation reveals a pivotal emergent behavior: spontaneous internalization, defined here as self-selected under outcome-only optimization. When optimized for task success, the model abandons verbose textual derivations in favor of implicit latent computation, suggesting that it identifies the continuous manifold as a more native substrate for chemical logic. This paradigm shift also proves to be a superior computational strategy: LatentChem achieves a 59.88% non-tie win rate against the strong CoT baseline on the rigorous ChemCoTBench, while delivering a broad 10.84$\times$ average reduction in reasoning step overhead (5.96$\times$ wall-clock speedup) across all evaluated benchmarks. Our results provide empirical evidence that chemical reasoning is more naturally and effectively realized as continuous latent dynamics rather than discretized linguistic trajectories.

paragraphs: Chemical language models often express intermediate reasoning as a written chain of thought. LatentChem investigates whether requiring this verbal form constrains chemical reasoning that could instead proceed internally. Its reasoning interface separates chemical computation from language generation, allowing the model to use continuous thought vectors together with dynamic perception.

A central observation is spontaneous internalization under optimization based only on task outcomes. The model increasingly chooses implicit latent computation over lengthy written derivations without being directly rewarded for that choice. The authors interpret this behavior as evidence that continuous representations provide a useful substrate for the chemical reasoning tasks they study.

On ChemCoTBench, LatentChem achieves a 59.88% win rate against a strong chain-of-thought baseline when ties are excluded. Across all evaluated benchmarks, it reduces reasoning-step overhead by an average factor of 10.84 and delivers a 5.96-fold wall-clock speedup. These findings connect the change in reasoning interface to both task performance and computational efficiency, providing empirical support for latent chemical reasoning in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: LatentChem lets chemical reasoning proceed through continuous internal representations, improving benchmark outcomes while substantially reducing reasoning time.

title: LatentChem: From Textual CoT to Latent Thinking in Chemical Reasoning

abstract: Feature learning strength (FLS), i.e., the inverse of the effective output scaling of a model, plays a critical role in shaping the optimization dynamics of neural nets. While its impact has been extensively studied under the asymptotic regimes—both in training time and FLS—existing theory offers limited insight into how FLS affects generalization in practical settings, such as when training is stopped upon reaching a target training risk. In this work, we investigate the impact of FLS on generalization in deep networks under such practical conditions. Through empirical studies, we first uncover the emergence of an optimal FLS—neither too small nor too large—that yields substantial generalization gains. This finding runs counter to the prevailing intuition that stronger feature learning universally improves generalization. To explain this phenomenon, we develop a theoretical analysis of gradient flow dynamics in two-layer ReLU nets trained with logistic loss, where FLS is controlled via initialization scale. Our main theoretical result establishes the existence of an optimal FLS arising from a trade-off between two competing effects: An excessively large FLS induces an over-alignment phenomenon that degrades generalization, while an overly small FLS leads to over-fitting.

paragraphs: Feature learning strength controls an important aspect of how neural-network representations evolve during optimization. The paper defines it through the inverse of effective output scaling and asks how it affects generalization under a practical stopping rule: ending training once a target training risk is reached. This differs from studying only extreme strengths or indefinitely long training.

Empirical studies in deep networks reveal an intermediate strength that generalizes better than settings that are either too weak or too strong. This challenges the intuition that increasing feature learning must always help. The result motivates an explanation of why two models reaching a training target can nevertheless differ in performance beyond their training data.

The theoretical analysis studies gradient flow in two-layer ReLU networks trained with logistic loss, controlling feature learning strength through initialization scale. It establishes an optimum arising from competing effects: excessive strength causes over-alignment, while insufficient strength causes over-fitting. The contribution links the empirical pattern to a specific theoretical setting and makes feature learning strength a meaningful quantity to balance.
summary.tldr: The paper finds and theoretically explains an intermediate feature learning strength that balances over-alignment against over-fitting.

title: Over-Alignment vs Over-Fitting: The Role of Feature Learning Strength in Generalization

abstract: Motivated by discrete diffusion’s success in language-vision modeling, we explore its potential for multi-view generation, a task dominated by continuous approaches. We introduce ViewMask-1-to-3, formulating multi-view generation as a discrete sequence modeling problem where each viewpoint is represented as visual tokens from MAGVIT-v2. Through discrete diffusion via masked token prediction, our approach enables progressive multi-view generation via iterative token unmasking, unifying language and vision in a shared token space. Importantly, simple random masking combined with self-attention naturally encourages cross-view consistency without specialized architectures or 3D geometric priors. Our method outperforms the baseline on the GSO and 3D-FUTURE benchmarks, ranking first on average across standard image metricsand, and achieving a 10.6% higher IoU than continuous diffusion models on 3D-FUTURE. Furthermore, the proposed framework can be naturally extended to support text-to-image generation and multimodal understanding, highlighting its potential toward a more unified paradigm for multimodal understanding and generation.

paragraphs: Generating images of the same object from different viewpoints requires those images to agree about what they depict. ViewMask-1-to-3 approaches this task as discrete sequence modeling. Each view is encoded as visual tokens from MAGVIT-v2, allowing generation to operate through token prediction in a shared language-and-vision representation.

The model progressively fills masked tokens through discrete diffusion. Random masking and self-attention encourage agreement across views without specialized architectural components or explicit 3D geometric priors. This makes the relationship between viewpoints something the token model learns through its shared prediction process, rather than something imposed through a dedicated geometric design.

On GSO and 3D-FUTURE, the authors report stronger performance than the baseline and first-place average ranking across standard image metrics. On 3D-FUTURE, they report 10.6% higher IoU than continuous diffusion models. The framework can also be extended to text-to-image generation and multimodal understanding. These results support discrete masked-token generation as a promising common foundation for multiple visual and language-related tasks.
summary.tldr: ViewMask-1-to-3 generates consistent viewpoints through iterative visual-token unmasking without specialized architectures or explicit 3D priors.

title: ViewMask-1-to-3: Multi-View Consistent Image Generation via Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Models

abstract: The allocation of scarce donor organs constitutes one of the most consequential algorithmic challenges in healthcare. While the field is rapidly transitioning from rigid, rule-based systems to machine learning and data-driven optimization, we argue that current approaches often overlook a fundamental barrier: incentives. In this position paper, we highlight that organ allocation is not merely an optimization problem, but rather a complex game involving organ procurement organizations, transplant centers, clinicians, patients, and regulators. Focusing on US adult heart transplant allocation, we identify critical incentive misalignments across the decision-making pipeline, and present data showing that they are having adverse consequences today. Our main position is that the next generation of allocation policies should be incentive aware. We outline a research agenda for the machine learning community, calling for the integration of mechanism design, strategic classification, causal inference, and social choice to ensure robustness, efficiency, fairness, and trust in the face of strategic behavior from the various constituent groups.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that better prediction and optimization alone are insufficient foundations for heart transplant allocation policy. Allocation decisions involve organizations and people whose incentives can differ, including procurement organizations, transplant centers, clinicians, patients, and regulators. A policy therefore operates within an interacting decision system where strategic behavior matters.

Focusing on adult heart transplant allocation in the United States, the authors identify incentive misalignments across the decision pipeline. They also present data indicating that these misalignments already have adverse consequences. This motivates treating incentives as part of the problem that an allocation policy must address when using machine learning and data-driven optimization.

The proposed research agenda brings together mechanism design, strategic classification, causal inference, and social choice. The authors call for these perspectives to support robust, efficient, fair, and trusted allocation in the presence of strategic behavior. The contribution is a case for incentive-aware policy development and a research direction, rather than a reported demonstration of a completed replacement allocation system.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that heart transplant allocation policies must account for participants’ incentives and strategic behavior.

abstract: We study the problem of modeling species geographic distributions, a criticalproblem in conservation biology. We propose the use of maximum-entropytechniques for this problem, specifically, sequential-update algorithms thatcan handle a very large number of features. We describe experiments comparingmaxent with a standard distribution-modeling tool, called GARP, on a dataset containing observationdata for North American breeding birds. We also study how well maxent performsas a function of the number of training examples and training time, analyzethe use of regularization to avoid overfitting when the number of examples issmall, and explore the interpretability of models constructed using maxent.
