paragraphs: The paper investigates how to model where species occur geographically, a problem that matters for conservation biology. It proposes maximum entropy methods and focuses on sequential update algorithms that can handle very large collections of features. This makes the computational approach an important part of the contribution: the proposed modeling framework is intended to work with many descriptive inputs.

The experiments compare the maximum entropy approach with GARP, an established distribution modeling tool, using observations of North American breeding birds. The study also examines how performance changes with the amount of training data and the time spent training. These questions connect model choice to the resources available for constructing a useful distribution model.

The authors additionally analyze regularization as a way to control overfitting when observations are scarce, and explore whether the resulting models can be interpreted. The abstract describes these investigations without announcing a comparative winner. Its contribution is therefore a proposed approach and an evaluation of its computational, statistical, and interpretive properties.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes maximum entropy models for species distributions and studies their performance, regularization, and interpretability using bird observations.

title: A maximum entropy approach to species distribution modeling

abstract: We consider online learning where the target concept can change over time. Previous work on expert prediction algorithms has bounded the worst-case performance on any subsequence of the training data relative to the performance of the best expert. However, because these “experts” may be difficult to implement, we take a more general approach and bound performance relative to the actual performance of any online learner on this single subsequence. We present the additive expert ensemble algorithm AddExp, a new, general method for using any online learner for drifting concepts. We adapt techniques for analyzing expert prediction algorithms to prove mistake and loss bounds for a discrete and a continuous version of AddExp. Finally, we present pruning methods and empirical results for data sets with concept drift.
originalAbstract: We consider online learning where the target concept can change over time. Previous work on expert prediction algorithms has bounded the worst-case performance on any subsequence of the training data relative to the performance of the best expert. However, because these “experts” may be difficult to implement, we take a more general approach and bound performance relative to the actual performance of any online learner on this single subsequence. We present the additive expert ensemble algorithm AddExp, a new, general method for using any online learner for drifting concepts. We adapt techniques for analyzing expert prediction algorithms to prove mistake and loss bounds for a discrete and a continuous version of AddExp. Finally, we present pruning methods and empirical results for data sets with concept drift.

paragraphs: Online learning becomes harder when the relationship being learned changes over time. This paper introduces AddExp, an additive expert ensemble method designed to use an online learner under such concept drift. It also changes the reference point used to assess performance over a subsequence of the training data.

Earlier expert-prediction analyses compare worst-case performance with the best expert on a subsequence, but those experts may be difficult to implement. The authors instead bound performance relative to what an actual online learner achieves on that same subsequence. This makes the comparison depend on an operational learning procedure and its observed performance over the relevant segment.

Using techniques adapted from expert-prediction analysis, the paper proves mistake and loss bounds for discrete and continuous versions of AddExp. It also presents pruning methods and empirical results on datasets with concept drift. The contribution combines a general way to use online learners for changing targets with theoretical guarantees framed around their actual subsequence performance, alongside empirical investigation of the ensemble approach.
summary.tldr: AddExp adapts online learners to concept drift with mistake and loss bounds relative to a learner’s actual performance on a subsequence.

title: Using additive expert ensembles to cope with concept drift

abstract: Classifiers that refrain from classification in certain cases can significantly reduce the misclassification cost. However, the parameters for such abstaining classifiers are often set in a rather ad-hoc manner. We propose a method to optimally build a specific type of abstaining binary classifiers using ROC analysis. These classifiers are built based on optimization criteria in the following three models: cost-based, bounded-abstention and bounded-improvement. We demonstrate the usage and applications of these models to effectively reduce misclassification cost in real classification systems. The method has been validated with a ROC building algorithm and cross-validation on 15 UCI KDD datasets.

paragraphs: A classifier can sometimes reduce the cost of errors by declining to make a prediction. The practical question is how to set the parameters governing that choice. This paper addresses a specific type of binary classifier with an abstention option, replacing ad hoc parameter selection with an optimization method based on ROC analysis.

The method considers three formulations: cost-based, bounded-abstention, and bounded-improvement. These organize the choice around an explicit cost objective or bounds concerning abstention and improvement. Having different formulations matters because a classification system's requirements can concern both the expense of mistakes and how much freedom the classifier has to withhold decisions.

The authors demonstrate applications that effectively reduce misclassification cost and validate the method using a ROC-building algorithm and cross-validation on 15 datasets. The optimality claim is tied to the specified classifier type and optimization criteria. The work supplies a principled way to choose abstention behavior within those formulations, supported by evaluations on real classification data.
summary.tldr: ROC analysis optimizes a specific class of abstaining binary classifiers under cost, abstention, or improvement criteria.

title: Optimizing abstaining classifiers using ROC analysis

abstract: We introduce an expectation maximizationtype (EM) algorithm for maximum likelihood optimization of conditional densities. It is applicable to hidden variable models where the distributions are from the exponential family. The algorithm can alternatively be viewed as automatic step size selection for gradient ascent, where the amount of computation is traded off to guarantees that each step increases the likelihood. The tradeoff makes the algorithm computationally more feasible than the earlier conditional EM. The method gives a theoretical basis for extended Baum Welch algorithms used in discriminative hidden Markov models in speech recognition, and compares favourably with the current best method in the experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops an expectation-maximization-type algorithm for maximizing conditional likelihood. The relevant models contain hidden variables and use distributions from the exponential family. Conditional likelihood focuses estimation on the distribution of an outcome given the observed input, making the method relevant to discriminative training of models with unobserved internal structure.

The algorithm also has an interpretation as gradient ascent with automatically selected step sizes. Its design exposes a tradeoff between computation and guarantees that each update increases likelihood. This tradeoff makes the procedure more computationally feasible than an earlier conditional EM method, addressing the effort needed to obtain dependable optimization steps.

The work also provides a theoretical foundation for extended Baum–Welch algorithms used to train discriminative hidden Markov models in speech recognition. Experiments compare favorably with the method described as the current best alternative. The contribution combines a conditional-likelihood optimization procedure, an explanation of its relationship to gradient updates, and a theoretical account of an existing family of training algorithms.
summary.tldr: An EM-type method makes conditional-likelihood optimization more feasible by trading computation against guarantees of likelihood-increasing updates.

title: Expectation maximization algorithms for conditional likelihoods

abstract: We consider the problem of multi-task reinforcement learning, where the agent needs to solve a sequence of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) chosen randomly from a fixed but unknown distribution. We model the distribution over MDPs using a hierarchical Bayesian infinite mixture model. For each novel MDP, we use the previously learned distribution as an informed prior for modelbased Bayesian reinforcement learning. The hierarchical Bayesian framework provides a strong prior that allows us to rapidly infer the characteristics of new environments based on previous environments, while the use of a nonparametric model allows us to quickly adapt to environments we have not encountered before. In addition, the use of infinite mixtures allows for the model to automatically learn the number of underlying MDP components. We evaluate our approach and show that it leads to significant speedups in convergence to an optimal policy after observing only a small number of tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies an agent solving a sequence of environments represented as Markov decision processes. These tasks are assumed to be drawn randomly from a fixed but unknown distribution. The learning challenge is to use experience from earlier tasks to understand and solve later ones more quickly.

The authors model the task distribution with a hierarchical Bayesian infinite mixture. For a new environment, the distribution learned from previous environments becomes an informed prior for model-based Bayesian reinforcement learning. This prior carries information across tasks, while the nonparametric model supports adaptation to environments not previously encountered. The infinite mixture also allows the number of underlying MDP components to be learned automatically.

The evaluation reports significant improvements in the speed of convergence to an optimal policy after only a small number of observed tasks. This supports the usefulness of learning a distribution over environments instead of treating every task as a fresh start. The result is situated within the stated setting of tasks sampled from a fixed distribution, which supplies the basis for sharing information.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian mixture transfers knowledge across reinforcement-learning tasks and yields faster convergence in the reported evaluation.

title: Multi-task reinforcement learning: a hierarchical Bayesian approach
